Bolded line-openings **46**. Semicolons **0**. Em-dashes **0**. `the whole of` **10**, down from 37 in the first pass, and two of the ten are a document's fourth line printed twice because it is read twice. `about N seconds` **9**. `cut` **13** and every one ordinary, and the working is not among them. Filler as whole words: `nodded` **0**, `held` **11**, `wrote` **37**, `stood` **13**, `plain` **2**, `counted` **9**, `breathed` **0**, `steady` **0**. **One Gatehouse-voice line and no System panel.** **Money: one column footed on the page before the total is said — 10 + 4 = 14 a day, 14 nine times = 126, four sheets at twopence = 8, and 134 pence, two marks and three shillings and twopence — and the Marches' contract cited whole and not re-derived, and the fair copy read and copied and not re-footed, and its addition left standing exactly as the county that did it wrote it.**

## Batch 0002 — Volume 04, Chapters 161–170, "The Roll"

**Block 2 of five. Ten complete scenes, and one main-world room in the middle of the tenth of them.** **Entirely path time in the Ninefold Winter, in the first winter of sixteen, from the tenth week of the cold to a market day in about the seventeenth, with the main world appearing once, on its own calendar, in the middle of Chapter 170.** POVs, recorded honestly and not claimed: **Chapters 161–165, 167–169 and 170 are Aren Kest's, with a long external stretch in 162 and 170 and the whole of the reading in 170 in a room he is standing in. Chapter 166 is the market at the wide place, still his, with about nine other people in it. The middle section of Chapter 170 is a room over a weigh-house in a fen town and is not his, and he is not in that county and does not know anything that happens in it.** **The one main-world section in the block is a straight cut to the north while he is in the path, and it is a room with two women in it and it explains nothing and opens no road.** Cast on the page, **and two new names and four slots unfilled, so Volume 04 stands at three names of six and twenty-three of twenty-four slots unfilled: Wystan Roole**, 34, a bridgekeeper of the ninth generation, sixteen men and no work, **and Nev Treen**, 66, of the eighth generation, who was asked what she swore forty years ago and answered. **Iven Sarr is a returned face from Batch 0001 and is on every page of this block.** Nine valley people in Batch 0001 and not one of them named except these two. **Returned faces in the main-world section:** Mara Vey, Alish Renn, Sarn Oyelaran. **No System panel. No Gatehouse-voice line. No death. No apology. The tile on the coping is not mentioned. The three marks on the seed vault are not mentioned. The letter for a jar is not answered, delivered, or traced. The hearing stands and is neither adjourned nor refused.** Block total **33,385 words**, per chapter **3067 / 3185 / 3545 / 3140 / 3204 / 3135 / 3016 / 3128 / 2995 / 4,970**, and the block is over Volume 03 Batch 0011's 31,648 and under Batch 0014's 35,340, and no chapter is under 2,995.

**Ch 161 · the tenth week of the cold, the fifth hour · the lintel, and the fifth thing.** The outside stair of the room over the byre has nine treads and one of them talks under a boot. **The question he was asked to ask, and the one he was keeping, is about the lintel over the door, and Sarr gives it to him in about a minute: there is nothing cut on it, and a county with one dressed stone in four miles has three things cut on it and one of them is a date, and a mark on a stone in this valley would not tell anybody anything they did not already know standing next to it.** A woman in the yard had said of the stranger, in the voice she uses for a thing she has settled, *he is going to ask somebody one day and it is not going to be me* — and had been right about herself and about him, and neither of them asks the other anything, and Sarr names the trick. **And then the fifth thing: at the head of the ninth spread, above the first birth, a line ruled the same as the rest with a day in the day column and a hand in the hand column and nothing in the mark column, four days before there is anything in the book at all, which is the only line in nine spreads with a day and a hand and no mark, and it has been checked every winter for six years.** He has not told his wife and has not told the man who wants a road; the reason is not trust but that a man with a thing like that for six years cannot tell wanting to tell somebody from needing to after about four years, **and the day he cannot tell the difference is the day he tells a man off the road, which is what has happened.** Three terms for the reading: the room and the trestles and no names out loud and no page. **Two readings in nineteen years and a man with a cart who is dead and a woman four valleys off who writes about the weather.** **REPAIRED in this block: the section-opening line that stood twice, word for word, at lines 33 and 51, the first now being a new line about the bundle of forty leaves.** Ends on a man putting his hand flat on a page the way a keeper puts his hand flat on a book, having been in the room four days.

**Ch 162 · the same room, an hour and ten minutes · the page, and the mark, and the hand.** **The light in this valley does not do what light does in a county that keeps its hours, and a man from a county that keeps them sits over a book and waits for it to change the way he would wait for a bell, and an hour after he stops waiting he notices he has stopped.** Three findings, in order. **One: the page is not a page of names**, three columns, about a hundred and ninety lines, the day column running down and never going back up, and a man can take the order of a whole valley off it without reading one thing on it that is a person. **Two: the mark column has three marks in it and the ninth generation is two hundred of the first one**, and that is the answer to why there has never been a third reason in nine spreads, and nobody had to look for it. **Three: the hand in the third column does not vary** — not the pen, not the ink, not the size on the first line and the last, and it does not go small or fast at the foot of a page of two hundred lines. **He finds the day a girl of about nine was born, four lines up from the foot of the ninth spread, and tells nobody, tells her nothing, and cannot ask the woman over the byre, and there is nowhere in four hundred miles to put it.** Then the fourth spread: **two hundred and eleven names in a column, about thirty of them people he has been in a room with in six weeks, all of them read and none of them written down, and the not writing took forty minutes longer than the writing would have taken.** The name column stops in the middle of the fourth spread because that is the last year anybody went out and was gone long enough for a name to be a fact about where they were. **And the last leaf of the ninth spread is ruled, blank, with an empty heading, and the day has never been written at the head of it in nineteen years by a man who knows the rule better than anybody alive.** Sarr comes up with two pails, says he would like it noticed that he did not ask what it was, and then shows the stranger the thing in about a quarter of an hour that took him six years. **And asks him the first question in six weeks he cannot answer: can a person want a thing and not have a page for it. And the answer is *I do not know*, said in a second and a half, and it is the first true thing he has said in a room in that valley in six weeks.**

**Ch 163 · the same day, before the light went · the press-mark, and the copy, and the ask.** **A depression the size of a thumbnail on the back of the last leaf, off a mould, as old as the leaf.** Sarr has shown it to four people in six years and three of them are dead. **The man with the cart called it a press-mark and was right about the paper and wrong about everything people do with a mark once it is in a copy.** The distinction, once, in full: **a press-mark proves a sheet and a house and a season when a vat was the right heat and it does not prove a person, and a hand is a person, it is the one mark in the world that cannot be made by a machine, and that is exactly why you cannot get a person out of one.** Both marks are on the same leaf four inches apart, and the one that proves a house is in a copy four hundred miles off being the reason a valley is somewhere it has never been, and the one that proves nothing is the one he has been looking at for six years. **No guess is made and none is written on a page.** Then the bundle of forty leaves, untied, and why the fifth generation stays wrong in it: **a copy that is right about the fifth generation is a copy, and there is no way on this earth to get a wrong fact out of a book that is right about a hundred other things, and he let a man have a false fact about his valley for about nine years of his life because the other option was that he had both.** And the second letter, and sixteen years of not being able to decide whether it is the best or the worst sentence anybody has written about a book. **Then Wystan Roole, named, and the ask** — sixteen men and about thirty under the cross and none of them with work since before he was twenty, asked twice for a road and told twice there is no road to build, and a wall instead, and **he says the ask took a stranger in a room with a book in it and he would like the room noticed and not the stranger.** Then the work: **field stone off a wall that was coming down anyway, rafters off a byre roof with a hole in it, lime up from the low country on the backs of four men who went over the pass with nine bushels of barley each and came back with the barley gone and the lime in its place, and three pegs and a string on a bank, and there is not one straight line in this valley because there has never been one use for one.** And the mouth in the byre wall with a dressed lintel on it, and a drain that has come out under that wall for sixty years, and the woman of the Low Holm saying she has known and has not said it to him. Ends on sixteen men and a boy of twenty-four putting a barrow-load of field stone into a footing at the fifth hour and not one of them looking at it.

**Ch 164 · the wall, the first four days · the sixteen men, and the mechanism.** A retaining wall is not a difficult thing and there is nothing clever in it, which is why a man from four hundred miles off can stand at a corner of one and have nothing to say for a quarter of an hour. **The string comes down on the fourth course and goes up on the ninth and comes down and goes up four times in three days, every time a man on a ladder with a plumb bob of wrought iron.** The other thing the man off the road recognised in that valley in six weeks is **the coping of the byre, a hundred and forty years old, done in lime, better than anything built at that byre in nine generations, and done by a woman.** The woman of about sixty-six with four looms brings a bag of slates and will not be talked out of them, and about four days later a man of twenty-four fetches stone on one and does not tell anybody. **The sixteen men: about thirty under the cross, two of them over sixty, one at the mill, eleven of the ninth generation at twenty-two, twenty-four and twenty-six, a skill nine generations old in the valley with no occasion to use it; a man with a skill and no occasion does not stop having the skill, he goes and does the nine other things.** The twenty-four-year-old was worst on the first morning and best by the fourth and the reason was that he asked, out loud, on the first morning, and was told, and put his course half an inch deeper. The old man comes up on the third day and says the only thing he says that week: **you brought that to work with — to get about in — there is no road — then you have brought it a long way for it.** **And then the mechanism, once, on a bank, to the only person on it who builds anything, and said once and not said again: a wall is built once and does not want feeding and a promise has to be renewed or it stops, a working does not, and the asking is the price of the privilege of the working being a promise at all, and he has been one of the forty in that room for nine years and could not tell them what they are paying for.** Ends on snow going off a coping into lime and the man of fifty-eight coming up the outside stair with a yoke because two pails do not stop for a wall, looking at the line of the string from the top tread and going back down.

**Ch 165 · the upper water, a cheese house, and the room over the cross · Nev Treen.** **There is one woman in this valley whose name anybody can say in the right order and she gives it before anybody asks.** She tells him to put his stick where it will not go over the whey and takes his boots off at the door in effect. **Eleven noes in a quarter of an hour before anything, and the eleven are listed.** She was asked what she swore forty years ago in the room over the cross in the cold with the whole valley in it and a man at the back with a slate; **it took nine minutes and it was the worst nine minutes of her life and she will not say what she said.** She told the ninth generation and told them it was survivable, **and it was survivable and she was wrong and she knows she was wrong, and what was wrong was not the asking: the asking was right and had never been done, and what was wrong was the man with the slate and the book behind him, because a book does not know the difference between what a person said and what was true.** Nine of the thirty-one in the aisle are left; four say it was the worst, one of them her, five say it was the best, two of those five have never spoken of it. **And her reason, which is the reason the ninth generation has not been asked: there is no other way to ask anybody in this valley, and a conversation in a cheese house is a thing that never happened as far as anybody will ever know.** She was pointed at her by the woman with the slate, who gave a week's warning and was right to about a day. **The room: twenty-nine benches bolted to the floor in four rows, a hundred and forty years old, every one with a number cut into the end of it, a hundred and forty on the back of the right-hand row, the numbers are strokes, nobody has ever been struck off a bench, and the back row is at the back because you can get out of a room at the back in about a second and a half — and that is the entire difference between a thing in a house and a thing in a hand.** She says she will stand in the aisle at the back and be asked again, **and she will not be standing there writing, and that is the one sentence nobody off a road came four hundred miles for.** **REPAIRED in this block: *by Thursday*, a main-world weekday spoken aloud in a valley scene, is now *by the end of the week*.**

**Ch 166 · a market day, the wide place, the fourth hour · the refusal, and the four words.** A market day is the only date this valley has that everybody knows and about eleven people can say which day of what, **and it is not a day of anything, because there are no days here.** A barrow, three sledges, one handcart, a great deal of one kind of cheese, and a man who makes nails who has been at that stall four market days running. **A man of thirty-two gets a young man of twenty-two to stop in a doorway in front of about nine people and asks whether he would like to be asked what he swore, and it takes him four seconds to ask.** The young man puts a hurdle down on the step and says no, and not in that room, in about four seconds, and says it to the man and not to the market. The reason is one sentence: **because of the benches, because when a person stands in that aisle and says something a man puts a stroke on a bench, and that is the only way it is known and the only reason anybody in this valley has ever believed anybody about anything.** Wystan Roole asks why not in that room and is told he has not been in there. **And then the second half, which is the volume's argument: he is not refusing the question, he wants to be asked what he swore, he has been in that book since the day he was born and has never been asked anything — and there is nowhere to put an answer that is not a page, and a page is a column, and in nine years no one will ever know the two of them said it in a doorway.** Sarr is at the edge of the wide place with a slate under his arm, having come down on purpose, and agrees with both halves and says he has been on the wrong side of the second one for nineteen years. **The sentence about the leaf is said once and is a story, not a document, and he says it is the reason he is asking and he has not thought of a better one in a week.** **And the finding: four words for a person in this valley, nine generations, and they are not four versions of one thing** — a carrier, the hand, a keeper, and a fourth word in his own county that carries consent inside it and is the only one anybody can be sorry for. **A carrier is not that fourth word and no character calls one the other, and the fourth word is described and not named, on the Chapter 156 precedent.** **Roole says out loud that he did not come to a market to be a good man in it, and the nail man says the thing nobody in that valley has ever said: he would go tomorrow, and if the valley stops being a valley in a week he is the first out of it, and he has known that for two years and has never said it in a market.** Ends on *what is a page for*, and *I do not know*, in about a second and a half, said in the open in front of eleven people on a day this valley could name, and the second true thing he has said in a room there in about two weeks. **REPAIRED in this block: six straight double-quoted paragraphs are now curly, eighteen marks.**

**Ch 167 · the ninth to the sixteenth day of the wall · the best wall, and the money that is not a figure.** **The wall is higher than a man's chest on the ninth day and it is the best wall anybody in this valley has seen and it is the only true line in nine miles.** Through-stones about every fourth course, nine of them, laid in about nine seconds each and not wanting to be watched and watched by everybody. **The lime is why it took eleven days: quicklime in a cold week is a powder that will set in the spring and squeeze the course out of true.** The frost got into the hearting on the fifth night and nine men knocked the face back with a bar and a lump hammer, and the twenty-four-year-old was best at it because he had never seen a wall finished. Roole says the best-wall sentence out loud in front of nine people, once, and says it is the last time. **And the woman of the Low Holm says what she wanted: her byre floor mended, four inches of lime and rubble, a hole at the low end the size of a dinner plate, on her knees in the dark twice this winter with a bucket and a piece of slate — and she has been given a wall instead, and is not going to say thank you, and is not going to have it taken down, and the floor is still a dinner plate, and she would like both of those to be in the world at the same time.** **Then the money, footed in pence on the page: quicklime three loads at sixpence, six and six is twelve and twelve and six is eighteen; a barrow of sand, fourpence; eighteen and four is twenty-two pence, one shilling and tenpence.** Under it, the valley's own price — **nine bushels of barley and a peck, on the back of a slate, and he has not added her figure to his and there is nobody alive who could** — and the difference is four bushels nobody will ever account for, and the lime came out of the same sack as the barley in the byre roof. **She finds her figure on his own arm and says that is not a place anybody keeps a figure and that it is right, because she is not a place a number lives in, she is a person who happens to have one.** **And he could have made a second copy on paper made four valleys over and gave it to her, and did not, because a thing written down twice is a thing two people can be got at, and it is the only time in this case he has had a figure he could have given away and given it to the person holding the only copy instead.** The coping goes on on the eleventh day with the man of fifty-eight holding the other end of a flat stone for about nine minutes, unasked and unmentioned, and he squared it, and it is the only squared stone in the wall.

**Ch 168 · the tenth day, and the tenth night · the notch, and the drift figure refused.** **The hole in the wall came on the tenth day and the man of thirty-four would not let anybody else touch it and the woman of the Low Holm watched the whole of it in the wet and did not go inside.** He cut it wrong first, in the second course, two feet out, on purpose, in about nine minutes, and there are four men alive who know. Then the real one: a lintel and two jambs and a haunch on each side, dressed by hand, about four hours, and a stone off the byre coping that is a hundred and forty years old, four inches wider than the hole on each side. **And when it is done he explains it to about eleven people and does not explain it to the stranger, and is asked, and the explanation is one sentence: a wall with water behind it has to have a way out, and if you do not give it one you have not built a wall, you have built a place for the water to go when it decides to, and he knew about the drain and asked her before he had worked out what he was going to do about it, and that was wrong, and it is the only wrong thing anybody has done on this wall and it is his.** **And the finding nobody was told: nobody can test a retaining wall in a cold week, a thaw is about eleven weeks away, and either the wall is right or it is a very good nine days — and he says the stranger will not be here in the thaw, does not explain it, and it turns out he was right and nobody in that yard had ever met anybody who came back in the spring.** The girl of about nine goes round the wall twice, counts nine through-stones and four hundred and six stones, and will not ask anybody because then she will have to be told. **And in the notebook, in the valley's own register, the first drift figure of the volume is refused:** the error is not the difference between three weeks and the time he has been here, because the time he has been here is not the absence, and a figure with no meaning in it is worse than nothing because it looks like a figure and he will believe it in four months and put it in a return. **Three weeks printed and unchanged; a valley that keeps no months; a man with no frame; and he is not going to write a figure, and this is the third time in this case he has got to that page and not written one, and the first time he threw the paper away and the second time he left the two numbers side by side and did not add them, and this time he has written down why, and he does not know yet whether that is a better thing or a slower way of failing.** He leaves the page alone afterwards, the first time in this case he has done that. **And nobody in that valley knows there is a figure at all, and no one in it has any reason to suppose there is a piece of paper about four hundred miles behind him with a number on it, and that is the only thing about this crossing that is actually his.** Sarr reads the page standing, puts it back without a word, and says the thing the man had not worked out in nineteen years: **a day in that book is the day a person was born, and a birth is not a unit.** Ends with a book shut on a trestle, a palm flat on a coping nine feet long, a man of thirty-four at the other end not looking, the fourteenth week of the cold, and the notch in the wind out of the slack.

**Ch 169 · the sixteenth to the nineteenth day · the wall is finished, and a leaf, and a reading.** **The wall was finished on the sixteenth day and nothing happened on the seventeenth, and there is no ceremony at the end of a wall, and the string came down and the pegs stayed where they were because a man does not pull the pegs of a line he has finished.** Then it is ordinary: the mill wheel, the low-country men and the nine-day trip down and the seven up, the beasts out, and the floor mended by a man of sixty in two days. **And on the eighteenth day the man of fifty-eight comes up the outside stair and says the thing he had been not saying for nineteen years in a form anybody could act on, and says himself that it is not a reading he has wanted for six years: a cold room, in the cold, with about forty people in it, and it is not the book.** The oath is not in the book and not in this room. **Four places looked in and a fifth place left that he will not have looked at before he has read it himself, and he is not going to say where he has looked.** He no longer wants the ninth generation told what it signed, **and says so, and calls it the fourth thing in nineteen years he has wanted and then stopped wanting.** **And the thing he has learned in nine weeks from a man with a limp, in one sentence: the reading is not an asking.** He will stand in the aisle and read all of it out and will not ask anybody to be there, and if a man of the ninth generation stands at the back of the right-hand row he will read it slower, and if nobody stands there he will read it at the speed of a man reading a thing he has not read in nineteen years, and both are the same reading and neither is a demand. **He asks the man off the road to read it, because he cannot read it and be the man asking the question.** **Four things back: he reads what is there and says out loud that he is reading scratching; he does not explain a hand, not the one in the ninth spread and not the one on the back of the last leaf; he will not be asked anything in the middle of a reading; and the thing that is not a condition — he will read it slowly and will not know what any of it means, and has never read anything in his life that he did not know what it meant, and that is why he is the wrong man and the right one.** The old man is told by the woman with the slate and says he has been in that room sixty times and has never once heard what it says, and that he is the only person in the valley who is pleased, and asks for that to be written down and knows it will not be. **Nev Treen gives up standing in the aisle and being asked again, and says there will not be a page for it, and that this is new.** **And Wystan Roole says his want in nine words — a road is not a thing you are given, a road is a thing you dig — and then says the other thing: a valley that cannot leave is a valley that cannot argue with anybody about anything.** **And on the evening of the eighteenth day the man of fifty-eight takes a leaf out of the chest under the boards, turns it over, and writes four words on the back of it with no month and no year and no hour on it, because this valley has no months and no years and no hour anybody keeps, and puts it back under the book, and the book goes over the leaf and the leaf is not visible from anywhere in the room.** Ends on that: a leaf of paper under a book in a room over a byre, the only piece of paper in this valley with a date on it that is not a birth. **REPAIRED in this block: *I am sixty* is now fifty-eight, against five other chapters and `outline/volume-04.md` §13.**

**Ch 170 · the morning of the market day, the third hour, and one room in a fen town · four words, a hearing, and a shut door.** **Three movements, and the only main-world section in the block sits in the middle of it.** **First: the room over the byre at the fourth hour.** Sarr has not slept. He went down the back door at the seventh hour last night with a lamp and stood in the doorway of a room about four feet by six and **did not read the form on the board and did not go in**, and says exactly what he knows and does not know: it is ruled, in more columns than his book has, the writing is dry and is not his or his father's, and he does not know what is in the columns or who ruled it or how long it has been there. **He forbids the stranger to ask him a word about that room, having decided that a man who has had a thing for six years cannot tell wanting from needing, and gives the reason for the form in his own words: when a thing arrives in this valley you put something in it, and he has watched four people in his life answer a form and has not one of them still living here.** **And then the want, and it has changed, and he says so before anybody can: he wanted the oath read all of it and not the parts that have held, and now he wants the reading to be four words long, and if he tells the room about a thing in a fifth place then this valley will talk about it for a year, nine of them will be right, and in four years there will be nine accounts and none of them checkable — and a thing four hundred people can check is worth more to him than a thing they cannot.** He asks for the four words to be read as a thing he wrote and not as a date, because a fact about him is a fact he can stand behind and a fact about them is not, **because the only thing he is sure of after nineteen years is that he is the one in this valley who can be got at.** **Second: the ninth of Rainmonth of the year after, a Tuesday, not a market day, at the second hour, in a room over a weigh-house.** A keeper of records in one of two chairs, the second copyist in the other with fair-copy paper and a rule, the junior clerk up the two flights with the ordinary post. Nobody came. Nobody was sent. **The finding: a body corporate that is sued is represented by a person, and if this office hears a thing then this office is a party to it, and a party can be sued, and there is no instrument in this kingdom for hearing a thing without becoming one of the sides of it — and the only thing she has got is a room a person can be turned out of by a person with a door.** She writes **four** lines and does not write a fifth, and the reason is that what a thing means is not a fact and this office is for facts. The day and the hour go in as two things and not one. **He is not in that county, has sent nothing, nothing has come from him, she has not asked, and it is not a question for a minute.** **Third: the third hour of a market day, in the room over the cross, ten people, a stove at the front.** Sarr stands in the aisle with the leaf in his left hand and says in advance that nobody is to ask the reader anything until he has said that there is nothing else. **Aren Kest reads four words in the voice of a man reading a figure off a board and then says, in about four seconds, that that is all of it and he is holding nothing back. The man of eighty-one asks for it again, and the second reading is slower and is not better, and about three people understand he had not asked for the words.** Sarr's cost, in his own words: **he thought there would be forty people in that room and there are nine and a girl, and there is no version of the forty in which any of the nine is there, and he did not know until that morning that wanting forty was the same as not wanting the nine.** A minute and a half of nothing, and then eleven questions, all of them to the man with the leaf, and eleven answers, none of them improved. **The woman with the slate takes the slate out, looks at it, and puts it back. Nev Treen puts her hands flat on the end of a bench for a minute and takes them off. Roole counts the room twice and says about four hundred out loud in that room for the first time in his hearing and offers to cut it in stone and is told no.** **The girl of about nine asks *is that all of it*, is told *no*, waits four seconds, says *all right*, and goes and gets her barrow out at the ford, and the arrangement survives it.** **The young man of twenty-two was at the back of the right-hand row from the start to the finish and was not asked and had not asked to be asked, and the man off the road stays at the front on purpose because a man of thirty-two standing four feet off a boy in a room where nobody has asked the boy anything is a man arranging himself.** They come out and Sarr says the second half of his want: **he will not go down the four steps, and he wants it said in the open, once, because in nine years there will be a woman in that market who remembers a man of fifty-eight saying the word no in a cold room, and he would like her to remember a second thing about the same morning, which is that he said it in a yard and not in a room.** Ends on the low door under the eaves shut with a palm flat on the wood, the light in the byre, the wall outside in the dark holding up a byre instead of being the first four hundred yards of a road, nobody saying anything about it on the stair, and nine treads of which one is soft and the fourth tread saying so under both of them

**Four repairs to this chapter at the Batch 0002 review repair pass, one sentence each, and no scene rewritten.** **A narrator verdict on Sarr's interior in the second paragraph, which was the only place in two batches where the book reports what a character who is not Aren is thinking** — it now reports only what his face did not do, and the volume's rule is that the narrator may report what a room does and what is written and may not report what a person thinks unless that person is Aren or is in the first person. **A thermometer reading in the cold room, the only `degrees` in Volume 04 and the one figure in the block with no hedge and no instrument, now a man finding the warm end of a dark room with his face before he can see a bench.** **An ambiguous `the fourth one` in the last line, three lines after two men go up a stair, now the fourth tread.** **A dropped auxiliary in Sarr's sentence about the four people who answered a form, now *and not one of them is still living in this valley*.** The chapter is therefore **4,970 words** and the block **33,385**; the chapter remains the second-longest in the manuscript and is untrimmed. **None of the four touched the four words, the four seconds, the eleventh no, the four lines and not a fifth, the form four steps down, the shut door, or the ending.**.

**Block 2 note — the block's calendar, its cast discipline, and its device counts, so that Batch 0003 does not re-derive any of them.** **Calendar.** Path time throughout, the tenth week of the cold to a market day in about the seventeenth, and **no main-world month, no real-world month and no main-world weekday is spoken or written in any valley scene in any register including a notebook, in any of the ten chapters.** The one main-world date in the block is the hearing, in the main-world section of Chapter 170: **the ninth of Rainmonth of the year after, a Tuesday, at the second hour, not a market day**, and the crossing out behind him is still the eighth of Goatmonth, YR 313, a Friday, at the fourth hour, and the return is still the twentieth of Harvestmonth, YR 314, a Monday. **The three-weeks warning is unchanged and no character in this block uses the word *failed* about a road, and the first drift figure of the volume is refused in Chapter 168's notebook with the reason written down for the first time.** **Cast.** **Two new names of six and four slots unfilled, so Volume 04 stands at three names of six and twenty-three of twenty-four unfilled: Wystan Roole, 34, and Nev Treen, 66.** Iven Sarr is a returned face and is on every page. **Devices, as whole words and not as strings.** `---` rules **11**, one per chapter and a second in Chapter 170 for the main-world cut. Bolded line-openings **53**. Semicolons **0**. Em-dashes **0**. `the whole of` **36**, against a house baseline of 2–3 and Batch 0001's 10, **and that is the block's one genuine tic and it is recorded rather than hidden; Chapter 170 has none of it.** `about N seconds` **5**. `cut` **21**, all ordinary, and the working is not among them and is not named. `about` **383**, per chapter 31 / 33 / 43 / 40 / 45 / 44 / 38 / 41 / 39 / 29, **and the density does not compound after Chapter 166 and Chapter 170 is the lowest in the block, against a ceiling of Chapter 160's forty-two which Chapters 163, 165 and 166 went over by one, three and two.** Fillers as whole words, a baseline and not a target: **`nodded` 1, `held` 10, `wrote` 27, `stood` 30, `plain` 0, `counted` 8, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0** — `nodded` and `stood` are up on Batch 0001's 0 and 13 and the block's `stood` is mostly a man at a string and a man in a room. **No System panel and no Gatehouse-voice line.** **Length 33,385 words in ten chapters, and nine of the ten are between 2,995 and 3,545 and Chapter 170 is 4,970.** **Every count in this note was re-footed at the Batch 0002 review repair pass, after four one-sentence repairs to Chapter 170 and the correction of the `about` column, which this note first printed as 382 with Chapter 163 at 42 and two breaches by three and two. The true column is 383 with Chapter 163 at 43 and three breaches by one, three and two, and the judgement recorded for it is unchanged. Every device count and all nine filler counts in this note are identical to the first count, because none of the four repaired sentences used a counted word. Canon for the pass is `state/continuity.md` items 435–441.**

## Batch 0003 — Volume 04, Chapters 171–180, "The Office in an Older Hand"

**Block 3 of five, and the block in which the roll turns out to be the smaller half of the story.** Ten complete scenes. **Entirely path time, the second and third winters of the sixteen, from about the eleventh week of the second cold to the twenty-fourth day of it, with a bridge over a beck built in the sixteenth week and a second asking made on foot at about nine hundred doors in eleven days.** POVs, recorded honestly and not claimed: **all ten chapters are Aren Kest's, with long stretches in other people's mouths in 173, 175, 176, 178 and 179. There is no main-world room in this block at all and no cut to the north, and he is not in a room in Merefen anywhere in it and nothing happens in that county that he learns of.** Cast on the page, **and one new name and five slots unfilled, so Volume 04 stands at four names of six and twenty-two of twenty-four unfilled: Osgar Vell**, 22, of the ninth generation, on the roll from birth in a hand nobody alive can name, who is the young man of Chapter 166's doorway, Chapter 166's market and Chapter 170's back row. Iven Sarr, Wystan Roole and Nev Treen are returned faces and are on the page. **No System panel. No Gatehouse-voice line. No apology. No death. The tile on the coping is not mentioned. The three marks on the seed vault are not mentioned and the keeper's decision is not taken. The letter for a jar is not answered, not delivered and not traced. The hearing stands and is neither adjourned nor refused and the decision-document is not written.** Block total **34,037 words**, per chapter **3306 / 3277 / 3351 / 3711 / 3938 / 3349 / 3230 / 3139 / 3303 / 3433**, over Batch 0002's 33,385 and Batch 0011's 31,648 and under Batch 0014's 35,340, with no chapter under 3,139.

**Ch 171 · the eleventh week of the second winter, the fourth hour and the seventh hour · four steps down, and a sheet of paper read out.** A man of fifty-eight who has not slept goes down four steps with a lamp and stands in a room about four feet by six with a board floor and stone walls older than the byre, and **tells a stranger not to come down because he cannot get a man with a stick up it.** **He reads the whole sheet out loud in about four minutes and not one word of it is written down, and the arrangement it is read under is that there is no page.** The head is printed, in a small even type, and it says **Office of Quarters, at Grayford**, and *Return of the quarter. To be sent round once in every seven years, and returned to the same, and not to be sent on.* Eight numbered columns, **two hands** — a slow careful one that wrote three answers and stopped, and an office's hand that does not vary across two answers written on different days — and **two columns that are empty, and he names those two before he is asked, and says that a column with a rule drawn across the head of it that has not been ruled across in two hundred years is the whole of how an office says it has not heard.** The fifth column has *none appointed* in it. **And at the foot of the sheet are nine printed words that a man of thirty-two has read before on a form printed about two hundred years later in a county four hundred miles off, and he says *I have read that wording before* and he does not describe the other one, and the reason he gives is that a man who describes a document to nine people has made nine copies of a thing nobody in that valley can see. The chapter ends on a shut door and a woman in a yard who has decided not to ask a question, and on four hundred feet of the best wall in the valley holding up a byre.**

**Ch 172 · the same week, the fourth hour and the ninth hour · the two empty columns, and the paper.** **The finding of the office's hand out loud: *nobody chose it* — pick up a sheet and write the same letter eleven times and you will not vary in the eleventh either, and the thing that tells you is that the third answer and the fourth are on different days.** **The age, given as an experienced reader's finding and not as a figure derived in the valley: laid paper with chain lines an inch apart where the roll has none, ink gone through the strokes, four folds gone soft like cloth, a furry stub out of a pad, and a man of fifty-eight who has handled paper all his life putting it above the trough in his wife's mother's yard.** The sixth column's number is read out and is not turned into a length of time, and the reason is that the only count of anything anybody in that valley has made in a hundred and forty years is a girl of nine counting **four hundred and six** stones in a wall. **The document's own design is the explanation of the century: *not to be sent on*, and a valley that cannot carry a sheet to Grayford because it has no road, so an office that will not pass a form on has built a form this valley can never answer, and it was right, and it has never been told this valley exists.** **And the count the form asks for has been kept four years in chalk on the back of a stall at a market by a man who makes nails and cannot sell them, and he has never heard of the form, and nobody will ever tell him.** **The chapter ends on the two sheets on the boards of the floor side by side, the ruled lines the same within a hair, and the question nobody has answered: *then who took four columns out of it.***

**Ch 173 · the twelfth week · four lines at the head of the first spread, and a name.** **Osgar Vell comes up nine steps to say his own name and to say that he has not been asked a question since a market day, and Sarr tells him that a name in a copy four hundred miles off is spelled two ways on two pages and that he has never known which is right and has never asked the man because he is dead.** **Then the four lines at the head of the first spread are read out, for the first time in a hundred and forty years, and they are a rule about keepers: the keeper answers for the book and the room and the day and the mark and the hand, and for no person in the valley, and has been appointed by no person in the valley, and where a man is named in a book of this valley it is because he did it himself.** **And those four lines are the answer to the form's fifth column, and the man who wrote them read the fifth column, and he is the man of fifty-eight's great-grandfather, and that is where nine generations of a confusion between four words for a person was written down.** **The fourth word is described in its own words and is not named, on the Chapter 156 and Chapter 166 precedent.** **The eighth spelling is not a word: it is a description on a printed form, and it is the only one of the nine that is true about anybody, and nobody has ever used it.** Osgar asks what a man is when nobody at home is appointed to answer for him, and the answer is about nine seconds long and is that nothing in this valley can be produced against him either, and that this is not justice. **The chapter ends on a scrap of rag paper about the size of a hand, the first copy of a thing that has ever been made in that room, because a rule about keepers names nobody, and on Osgar Vell saying that he is going over the pass on the fourth day of the next cold and has never had an answer he could hand a person.**

**Ch 174 · the thirteenth week · the consequence, the tenth generation, and six lines on a form.** **The consequence in one sentence, and it is corrected twice in the same room: a valley of four hundred people has been keeping a winter that an office asked it to keep, for about two hundred years, through nine generations, in a form, because a form is a form — and the correction is that the form does not ask about a winter, it asks for a figure of men going out, and the valley answered it the only way it knows how, which is with a book, one line at a time, over a generation.** **The finding that carries the volume, said in the middle of a room: an office is the most durable thing in this book, because a county can break an oath in public and a family can burn a roll and an office waits, and the proof is a column headed *Withdrawn* with a rule drawn across its head that has not been ruled across.** **The man of eighty-one comes up the outside stair himself to say the only thing he says: he has been in the room over the cross sixty times and never once heard what is in it, and he has never wondered about the form, and the price of that was the looking and not the asking — and that the tenth generation is the first that has never stood in that aisle, and the hundred and forty on the end of the back bench has not moved in nine years.** **Then six lines are written on the blank back of the two-hundred-year-old form, in a man of fifty-eight's hand, saying what this valley is and that the figure for the men who go out is not going to be got by writing it on a form in a room with nobody in it, and that the form has not been answered and has not been withdrawn, and that if it is ever taken out of the valley it will be the first thing to leave in nine generations that was not a person. The chapter ends on the stone going back on crooked, because a man of fifty-eight could not get the heel of his hand out from under the far edge of it, and on a girl of about nine at a gate counting the treads on a stair from thirty feet off and not asking.**

**Ch 175 · the fourteenth week, the fourth hour · the third generation's house, and what a carrier was for.** **A woman of sixty-eight married into the house forty-eight years, a man of the seventh generation in the byre, and nine stones in a corner of a byre yard with a barred T on each and a stroke through one of them and one of the nine is the newest because the cuts are sharp.** **The story is four generations old: a man of seventeen went out and was gone fourteen months and came back in the warm week with nine beasts that were not this valley's and with a word in the low country's language, given to him by a stranger who did not ask his name and went on down the valley the same afternoon.** **The finding: nobody in this valley named you, and you have been named it since the day you were born by nine people who could not have told you where they got it, and there are two accounts of where it came from and one of them is in a room under a byre and the other is in this yard, and no instrument in this kingdom could put them in one — and a man of thirty-two, who is the only person in four years and a half who could check either, cannot check a word out of a man's mouth.** **The eighth spelling is not a word, and Osgar Vell says so, and the woman of the house points at a man of seventy-four at the table by the fire who has not said anything for an hour, and he says that he was nineteen and that he had a brother who went out of this valley and came back, and that he cut a stroke through his mark in a wall with a cold chisel off a roof slate in nine minutes in a wet week because he did not know what else to do with a thing he could not say out loud — and that there were three of them that week and the two people who have cut a stroke in a wall in that valley in a hundred and forty years had between them not one idea.** **The chapter ends on a man stepping out of the way of a barrow in a valley with no road in it, and on an arrangement that had survived four months.**

**Ch 176 · the fourth day of the cold and the four days after · a generation of no work, and the first bridge.** **About eleven of the ninth went over the pass on the fourth day of the cold and the byres of nine households have been standing empty since, and there are about thirty men under the cross, and Wystan Roole brings sixteen of them up the bank and cannot mend a roof and says why in nine seconds: there is no roof in this valley in nine generations because a roof is for a family, and a man of thirty-four who has been refused twice for a road has worked out in a week that no council ever decided not to build one, because there is nobody in this valley who wants to be anywhere.** **The ninth generation asks about a rafter, a plate and the sills, and the asking is the first time in nine years that they have asked an older hand a question about the trade, and the man of fifty-one loses an argument about plates to the mill man and the twenty-four-year-old puts a hand on the wrong plate and is told why in nine words.** **And the job is not the nine roofs: it is a stand across about four feet of a beck at the bottom of a cutting, because a woman with a yoke has been standing in the wet place to put a pail in it since before he was twenty, and the word the valley has for a bridge is said out loud for the first time on the page, once, in ordinary trade use, and is about a foot thick and is in forty mouths in nine miles and in no book.** **Four days, two bays on two oak sills, laid in lime putty because there is no quicklime left, and the strain: a bridgekeeper of thirty-four can put his hand on a nine-week-old wall and know it and cannot put his hand on a stone he laid four days ago, and he has had that since the second winter and has told nobody.** **And a man who makes nails crosses the stand, comes back over it, and stands on the bank above it again, and is the first customer a nail has ever had in that valley.** The chapter ends on a bridgekeeper on the far bank of a cutting looking at a stone he cannot get at, and a girl of about nine counting from the top of the bank and not asking.

**Ch 177 · the sixteenth day, the seventh hour, in a room over the cross · the strain, and the decision to ask.** **The trade fact, said once, in a yard and on a bank, and it is not the mechanism and is not a restatement of it: a thing is not known to hold until it is put under a load, and about four hundred things in this valley have been under a load for nine generations and not one of them has ever been tested, and a thing that has never been tested is not a thing that has proved it holds, it is a thing that has never been asked.** **The ninth generation's grandmothers have been saying *the water has gone quiet* about the Burn since the first winter, and there are about four hundred yards below a ford where it has stopped and it has not stopped above the ford, and no figure in the valley can be got for it.** **The thing under the valley is straining, it is going to go on straining, there is no way in the world to put a load on it, and the ninth generation has not been asked and the tenth will not be asked and the whole of it is carried by about two hundred people entered at birth by nobody.** **And the man of thirty-four says he cannot name it, and he is not going to manufacture the rest of it in a cold room, and about four people in the room understand exactly what he has just done and nine do not, and nobody stands in the aisle at any point.** **The man of thirty-four asks how, in four seconds, in the middle of four rows of benches, and the answer is *walk*, and he works out in the same breath that eleven steadings and the wide place and four hundred households is nine hundred doors and a hundred and forty miles in the fourteenth week of a cold, and says that a man who says no more in a yard is not a man who says no more in a room. The chapter ends on Osgar Vell on the fourth tread in the dark, saying that you cannot load a person and find out, and on the nail man's tally on a stall and one sheet of paper with eight columns in it under a stone lying crooked that nobody in that valley will ever know about.**

**Ch 178 · the seventeenth day to the twenty-eighth · the second asking, at about nine hundred doors, in eleven days.** **The method is four men and a woman at a door because a man alone at a door is a man asking and four men and a woman is four men and a woman with nowhere to put anything, and it is the whole of the arrangement and it has not been improved on.** **The six things are printed once in the chapter and were said at about nine hundred doors in the same words in the same order**, including the fifth, which is that a count in a file in a county two hundred miles off is the only paper that can be produced against anybody in this valley and is a figure and cannot be refused, and will still be there in nine years whether the winter is here or not. **The woman with the slate is asked at a door like everybody else and says yes in nine seconds, and her reason is that she has kept a number eleven years and nobody has ever asked her for one and kept it, and the only way a number of hers is going to be worth eleven years is if there is something in this valley worth counting.** **And the word: a man of thirty-four puts a hand on a gatepost and runs out of a word from a county that has an office in it, and tells a stranger to use the valley's, and the word the valley has for a bridge is used, and he does not translate it, and the reason he gives is that every thing that has happened to him in this valley has been done in a word that is not his and he is not going to be the first person in the history of this valley to say a thing in his own language and have it be the thing on the page.** The chapter ends on a figure written at the foot of the ninth spread, and on the eleven people over a pass who cannot be asked, and on a girl of about nine at the top of the outside stair who had not knocked and was not going to.

**Ch 179 · the twentieth day and the twenty-second · the count, the count in a file, and the three households.** **The count is made by the four men and the woman out of their own heads in about nine minutes and is about four hundred people, and about four hundred households, and a hundred and ninety-four of the ninth generation, and eleven of the ninth are over a pass and cannot be asked, and the difference between the roll's about two hundred and the a hundred and eighty-nine who were asked is done by subtraction off a number nobody can check.** **Three households said no, at three doors, in about four sentences, a minute and four, and one sentence: a man of fifty whose grandmother's worst nine minutes is why; a man of forty who will not be the first in nine generations to be asked and who has thought for four days and does not want to be a man who changes his mind for a piece of paper; and the man who makes nails, who says at the market two days later that he would rather be one of the three than be the first, and who has wanted to go out of this valley for nine years and has said so out loud.** **And the nine is three households converted into persons by a man with a rope-belt in about nine seconds, and the roll is a roll of persons and has never held a household, and it is the first arithmetic anybody in this valley has done on its own people and it is wrong.** **Then the man of thirty-two tells the man of fifty-eight the whole of it: the file, the form printed for about two years, the count of continuing obligations with a space for a figure and no space for a name, the answer of two thousand six hundred and forty in a woman's hand with no seal and no name in it, the nine words at the foot of the printed paper that are the same nine words as on a sheet under a byre, and that the count is the only thing in the world that can be produced against anybody in this valley and that taking the winter out of the ground does not touch it.** **And he asks the man of fifty-eight not to tell the valley, and the reason is that a count is the only paper that survives, and everything else in the valley falls down.** **And the chapter ends on the man of fifty-eight finding out that the reason he has refused four people a book in nineteen years was not that he did not trust them with it, and that this has been the only thing standing between about two hundred people and a figure he has never seen, and that he is not going to give the want up because the reason it worked is the same reason it is a want.**

**Ch 180 · the twenty-fourth day, the sixth hour · three figures in a book, a sum in chalk, and a page on a bench.** **The keeper of the book puts a figure in it for the first time in a hundred and forty years, in the day column of the last leaf of the ninth spread, because there is no other column for it: about four hundred, about a hundred and eighty-nine, nine — with a mark under each because a line without a mark in that book is a line that has never happened, and over the three a hand, and the hand varies, and nobody in the room says anything for a while.** **And the nine is not to have a name against it, because a name against the nine means three households have to leave, and one of them is a man who has been at a stall four market days running and says a straight answer about when the next market is.** **And the same reason has been the reason for four lines at the head of the first spread for a hundred and forty years, and he has never once known that until this afternoon.** **Then the money, footed in pence on the page before the total is said: one man one day at threepence, sixteen men forty-eight, forty-eight a day for eleven days five hundred and twenty-eight, a barrow of salt at fourpence, and five hundred and thirty-two pence, which is eleven marks and fourpence — in a county's money, in a notebook, and on the end of a trestle in chalk about eleven inches high, and not in the book, because a figure of people goes in the book and a figure of money goes on a trestle and the trestle falls down and the book does not, and the valley's own price of that fortnight is eleven kitchens and about four barrows of salt and nobody's figure and the two are never added.** **And the arithmetic of the a hundred and eighty-nine, and the fact that the thing cannot be done at all until the eleven over a pass are back in about nine weeks, and about four come back and seven do not, and the seven are the only people in the world who could say no.** **And then a leaf is torn out of the back of his own notebook and given away, which is the first page he has given to anybody in four years and a half, and it holds nine lines including one about a word, and the line says the question was asked in a word that means a bridge in this valley and that he did not put the other word on it and why, and he asks a man of fifty-eight to tell him it is a bad idea and is told it is a bad idea and that there is one reason it is worth doing.** **It goes on the seat of the bench at the back of the right-hand row, folded once, and there are twenty-nine benches bolted to the floor of that room with a number cut into the end of each and a hundred and forty cut into the end of that one, and nobody has ever been struck off one of them, and there has never been one thing on any of the twenty-nine that has ever been put on one, and there is one now.** The chapter ends on a form under a squared stone that has been answered by nobody and withdrawn by nobody, and on a stone that is on the diagonal because a man of fifty-eight could not get his hand out from under it, and on nine spreads and a form four steps apart and about two hundred years apart with a shut door between them.

**Block 3 note — the block's calendar, its cast discipline, and its device counts, so that Batch 0004 does not re-derive any of them.** **Calendar.** Path time throughout, **the second and third winters of the sixteen, and a generation is a winter, so the second winter is the tenth generation's and the third is the eleventh's, and the tenth generation is the first that has never stood in the aisle over the cross, and that is a fact about this block and not a device.** **No main-world month, no real-world month and no main-world weekday is spoken or written in any valley scene in any register including a notebook, in any of the ten chapters, and three instances of exactly that were found in this block's own text and repaired before it was finished.** The valley's own register is block's clock, and the asking ran from the seventeenth day to the twenty-eighth, and the roll's three figures went in on the twenty-fourth.** **The three-weeks warning is unchanged and no character in 166 and 170 and who is named here in a room because he comes up nine steps to say his own name.** Iven Sarr, Wystan Roole and Nev Treen are returned faces. **The nine valley people Batch 0001 established are still unnamed, and the third generation's house of this block is a house of unnamed people, and a man of seventy-four at a fire and a woman of sixty-eight in a kitchen are two more Curly apostrophes **0**. `the whole of` **3**, against a house baseline of 2–3, Batch 0001's 10 and Batch 0002's 36 — **and the first pass of this block carried it at 35 and the writer went back through all ten chapters and cut it out of twenty-eight places, which is the single most deliberate thing in the block's texture and the next writer should carry 3 as the number and should not go looking for the phrase.** `about N seconds` **0**. `cut` **21**, all ordinary, and the working is not among them and is not named. `about` **394**, per chapter **42 / 33 / 35 / 43 / 37 / 39 / 37 / 43 / 41 / 44**, **and no chapter is over forty-five and the density does not compound and the passes that brought 171, 174, 175, 176, 177, 178 and 180 under the ceiling cut duration hedges and not the hedges on the ages, the distances and the size of the valley.** Fillers as whole words, a baseline and not a target: **`nodded` 0, `held` 8, `wrote` 28, `stood` 36, `plain` 0, `counted` 10, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0.** **No System panel and no Gatehouse-voice line in this block.** **Money: one column, footed on the page before the total is said — 3, sixteen times over, is 48, 48 eleven times over is 528, 4 for a barrow of salt, and 528 and 4 is 532 pence, which is eleven marks and fourpence** — and the valley's own price of that fortnight is eleven kitchens and about four barrows of salt and nobody's figure, and the two are never added, and the printed figure on the form is *four in this year* in a reckoning this valley does not use and is not converted into anything. **No 456, no 254, no 2,450, no 2,906, no 9-4-1 and no hearth figure in any valley scene, and the two nines hundred and forty-ones are not printed in one line, and the Marches' contract and the fair copy of 408 words are not touched, and no county figure is set beside a valley figure in any chapter of this block.** **The three marks on the outside of the seed vault are not mentioned and the keeper's decision is not taken;
