## Batch 0002 — Volume 05, Chapters 211–220, "The City Under the Light"

**Ch 211 · the first day, the second hour, the eastern road and a paved lane · the frame, in a barrow-man's mouth, and a lamp.** Sixteen weeks in a valley that keeps no months and no hours, and a man whose hand was trained there walks into a place that keeps a standing hour and gets the hour wrong twice before anybody tells him anything, **once because he had a long shadow and it was the second hour, and once because a man going to the fourth hour is a man being told things and it was the third.** A man of about thirty with a barrow and a mule says the whole of the city's time-keeping in nine words and in the tone of a man saying a price — **we do not keep hours here, we keep days, from the last renewal, and if you want a number go and ask somebody and do not ask me** — and then says the rest of the frame in the same breath: **there is a book in this city with a figure of months written in it and it is not ours and whoever wrote it had months where he came from and it is the only page in four hundred years with the word on it and we do not use it and we do not argue about it.** The light does not turn and a woman of about fifty at a doorway says the word for it in a lane before anybody has said anything else to him: **that is the lamp, it comes up in the east and it stands, and do not stand in that lane looking at it, you are holding up a barrow.** And nobody improved on it and two people on a working lane had not looked up at all. The lane is paved and there is no gravel in it and a man of about forty at a cart reads the stick in about a minute and a half and says it out loud to the next man and the next man does not improve on it: **a man off a road carries a stick like that because a stick is for four hundred yards of gravel and there is not one yard of gravel in this city, and it is a description, and you can tell where he is from with that thing hanging off him and I have never in my life wanted to know less about anybody than I want to know about that stick.** He cannot put it down, because he cannot lean on it. The wharf is not a view and is doing four jobs, a lighter comes up under the quay twice in an hour and a half and is faster the second time, a boy of eleven takes his hands off a loaded crane for a second and a half nine times a day, and a man of fifty with a bad shoulder tells a stranger to stand where the rope is not. The bread oven is hot at the second hour and at the ninth and the same people are on it both times. **The money, footed on the page: a room three pence, a loaf a penny, a second loaf a penny. Three and one is four, four and one is five pence**, weighed on a small stone balance by a woman who says she would have taken his foreign coin in three counties and there is nobody in this one who would. And nine hours with the light not moving, and forty counted in the dark by a man who has not counted anything out loud in a valley in five months, and nobody in the city asked him one question and about four people wanted to.

**Ch 212 · the second day, the market at the third hour · recognition as the trade, and a description in four parts.** About four hundred people in a street of two hundred yards with glass on one side and reed and salt fish on the other, open on every day, because **a city that keeps a count of days keeps a market that opens when it likes.** A woman of about thirty at a reed stall says in eleven words what the street is for and then, in a second sentence, why, and does not say either again: **a name in this city is a person somebody can be shown, a name in a book is a person somebody can be shown, a name in about four hundred heads is not, because four hundred heads are in this city and will be in it next year, and I have said it to two men in four hundred years and one of them was you.** He is described four times in an hour and three of the four are right and the fourth is wrong about the future and he does not correct it. A woman of about fifty says to a woman of about thirty that there is a man on the glass side with a stick and that he is off a road, and the second woman says *how do you know that.* A boy of about fourteen works out from watching him walk forty yards that his feet go down before his body does, and a few people say that the truth was not the interesting part. **And there is a man of about thirty at a corner of that street with nothing in front of him who is the trade, and his price is a penny a name, and he has never been asked for one by anybody who is not standing in that street on a working day, and a man of thirty-two with a limp did not buy one, and that was the first thing a stranger had ever refused in that market.** Then the man of fifty with a waggon comes through and is described in four seconds and says his name twice, and both men stood in the same street within a quarter of an hour of each other and one of them is not a thing anybody can carry out of here. **The money, footed on the page: a pound of bread a penny, four feet of glass rod twopence, a cup and a piece of salt fish a penny. One and two is three and three and one is four pence**, and the glass rod is for no purpose at all and a man of forty at the stall says that not knowing what it is for was the best answer he had had in four years. **And the Stage 3 tax arrives as an ordinary working day and nobody notices it: he is given a cup at the fourth hour and holds it eleven minutes without drinking from it and loses the thread of a conversation two thirds of the way through and finishes it by asking a question he had prepared the day before, and about four people in that street watch it happen and say nothing, and in a city where recognition is the trade this is a way of being unable to be given a cup.** And then the man of fifty with the waggon tries him for an afternoon's carrying and pays him in bread and tells him why in about eleven words, and the twenty-six-year-old with lime on his hands tells him not to stand in the way of the second hod, and a man of thirty-two starts a count of days in a notebook he has not written in for four years.

**Ch 213 · the fourth day, second hour to ninth · a wharf, a furnace, a ladder, and an hour kept by other people.** Nine hundred feet of quay, a crane on a leg every ninety feet, a lighter worked from the side in the standing water, a rope walk, and a hull two thirds done for eleven days because the man who owns it is sixty and there is nobody behind him. **A man of thirty-two with a limp does not stop watching a crane, and the whole of the trade is the second and a half in which the man at the wheel takes his hands off a loaded leg, and the man has been doing it since he was eleven and says his name is not anything and that nobody has asked him for it in nine years and that a man who did not ask was easy to have on a quay.** The glass works: batching, not blowing, four men giving four right answers in nine seconds each and a man of thirty-four saying that a man with a stick has not once said one of them was wrong. **The tax again, as a yard: two hundred and forty feet of stone with nowhere to sit and nothing to lean on, a leg that is the same leg and is slower and is slower at the end of a run than at the start of it, and a man of thirty-four who solves it by putting his own hod down six feet short at the end of every run and picking it up again, eleven times in an afternoon, without once saying why or looking at him.** **And the lamp: a man of about forty puts his trowel down to refuse a stranger the reason and not the word, and says that anybody in that yard will say the word including a butcher, and that he does not know the reason and neither does the man on the ladder and the man on the ladder has not been asked either.** The ladder goes up past the parapet and stops, twice a day, and the shifts are on a piece of paper nobody has asked to see, and a man of thirty-two stands at the bottom of it and says nothing to either man, and a man of forty comes down and looks at him for four seconds and says nothing. And the hour: a furnace yard at nine men all stopping at once is quiet, and a man about thirty feet up says *ninth hour* without being asked. **And at the gate a man of fifty with a waggon says his name is not wanted and asks a stranger what he wants, and a man of thirty-two says work, and gets about eleven words back: a man I pay is a man I have had to write somewhere, and a man I write somewhere is a man this city has had to put in a place, and a place is a thing that can be asked about from four hundred miles off, and there are eleven people in this city who do it properly and one of them keeps the forms.**

**Ch 214 · the sixth day, the fourth hour, a lane that goes up and not down · the council of eleven, and eleven, said once.** A step with a hollow four inches across and two deep in it, worn by everybody, and a man of thirty-two who looks at the step instead of the door. **The door is the only door in this city that has never asked a man his name, and it does not do that out of manners, and the reason is that a door that asks is a door that remembers.** A woman of sixty finishes a sentence she started before he came in, and about four of the eleven say the two minutes were the correct two minutes and that a man who interrupts a woman of sixty in that room has been told more in two minutes than a man who waits gets in a fortnight. The clerk of forty's book holds what was asked and not what was said, and he does not read back, and a minute is a thing a body answers in and this book is not a minute. **The panel, at the door, in two lines: *Nothing here is owed to you and nothing here has refused you. You have not been told which of the two you are in.*** He does not write it down. Then a sentence about a count of refusals goes into the book on the woman's word and not the clerk's, and the clerk enters four things a year that are not about the business of the morning because she tells him to and nobody has ever asked her why. **And eleven: a man of thirty-two asks how many there are and then why eleven, and she puts her own pen down, and says, once, that nine is the number you use, where you are from, where anybody is from, that nine men and nine days and nine of something is a good number and is our number, that this city had nine for a hundred and forty years and every man who came up that lane wrote nine in a book when he got home, that after forty years there were nine men in four counties who had written the same number for the same reason and not one of them knew the number came from here, and that eleven is a number that means eleven. And she says she has said it once and is not going to say it again.** They do not refuse him. They never refuse anybody in that room. **What comes out of that room is a form, and the form is correct, and it is made by a man called Crane who is not one of the eleven and does not sit at that table and cannot be asked anything by anybody in it, and who has wanted to be asked to explain his forms about four hundred times in nineteen years.** And the two wrong questions any stranger asks, and the correct nine-word answer to each: what is it for, and a thing which is not for anything is kept going by the people doing it and not by the reason for it, and if the people go the reason is worth nothing, and in nineteen years she has never found out which happens first; and if you do not work, then you will be fed by a woman with a loaf and that is not an insult and it is a worse arrangement for you and a better one for us. And the day, put in as a count and not a date, and the ink pot shut at the point where a question costs more than it is worth. And the page of foolscap in the coat at a bend in the lane with a date on it he does not look at and one word under it, and four questions that went down the lane unasked. And a boy of fourteen on the step who gives a stranger the address of the man who keeps the forms and will not shake his hand.

**Ch 215 · the sixth day, the fifth hour, a bindle yard · Dermit Crane, the book, the form, and eleven words.** A yard with a roof on two sides and no roof on the other two and two hundred bundles of cord on racks, and a man of sixty-six at a bench with a nine-inch rule and a strip of whalebone about two hundred years old and the thinnest glue in the city, and he does not stop cutting for a stranger and has decided he will answer him later. **His name is Dermit Crane and the Dermit is his mother's family and is in nobody's mouth and nobody in four hundred people has ever asked him about it.** A man of thirty-two is told the whole of the arrangement in one breath by eleven people and is told that it took them eleven to do what Crane does in one. **And the book: every refusal this city has given for twenty years, on a bench under a roof, with a board over it, and the board is not off, and it cannot be shown to anybody because a book that leaves that yard is a book that has been seen and a book that has been seen is a reason somebody has for asking a second question, and there is nobody on earth who has ever asked a second question and then gone away. And that is the correct reason, and it took four hundred years to work out here and twenty years to work out in that yard.** **And the finding, about thirty-one words, said once, to a stranger, at the fifth hour, and he is not complaining: nobody outside this place has ever been told why we say no to anything, ever; nobody in here has noticed that either; I have got nobody to tell; and the bench is right.** Then the form: four minutes, a foot of the thinnest paper, five ruled lines and the fifth empty when it is finished, a pen cut down and not a quill, an ink pot that has never once been shut in twenty years, and eleven words — **we do not give work to a person we cannot name** — turned round and shown without being asked, which four people in that yard have said is the one thing in twenty years every visitor has said was the worst of him. **And the number is not in it, because a figure of persons is the only kind of paper that cannot be refused and this one has to be refusable or it is a lie with a stamp on it. And the name is not in it either, because he has not been given one and would not have been put on the paper, and because a piece of paper with a name on it is a piece of paper that can be asked about and a piece of paper with no name on it is a piece of paper that can be asked about just the same and takes longer.** And the two questions underneath both of them are the same question, and a man of thirty-two works that out in about four seconds. **And the price: nothing. A refusal is not a price and a man who offers for that paper would have to take it and then it would not be a refusal, it would be a sale, and this city does not sell anything to anybody and has never needed a rule about it.** And a man of fifty who went up a pass nine days and came back four and was told to take a jar away and came back twice would have been given a form and would have taken it away and come back twice and been right to, and has never been in that yard. And eleven words and about four hundred of them, all eleven, none twelve, and nobody in the city could check it and about four people have asked. And a man of thirty-two folds a refusal into four and puts it in a coat that already has a page in it, and has shown it to nobody in nine days and taken it out twice.

**Ch 216 · the ninth day, the fourth hour, the same lane · the same woman, the second form, and the finding that a form cannot hear.** He goes up the lane with two questions and asks one, and the woman of sixty does not look up, and refuses him in about four seconds, and the sentence is **I said that once, I said it once to a stranger in four hundred years and you are the stranger and you have had it, and I am not going to say it twice to a man who has come up a lane to make me say it twice, and that is what twice is for**, and about four of the eleven have said since that those four seconds were the shortest silence anybody coming up that lane has ever been answered with, and nobody argued with it. **And the question he came for: he has been refused, by the man who makes the forms, and he would like to ask it again. And she puts her hand flat on the table for half a second, and says: not because I will not hear it, because there is nothing here that can hear it, and if you ask me again I will send him a form, and he will make you a form, and it will be the same form, because it is eleven words and there is one way of saying it, and you will be holding two of them in nine days and they will be worth exactly the same and neither of them will be worth anything.** And she tells him, in advance, in a room with eleven people in it, that in about four years he will want to show it to somebody and will not be able to, and that the gap between the two is the whole of what this place is, and that it is not a secret and not a policy. At the fifth hour, down four hundred yards, the yard door is open, **and for the first time in about nine years a man of sixty-six says his name to a man he has already refused.** The second asking is made on purpose, and a man of sixty-six looks at a man of thirty-two for about four seconds and the whole of them went on whether to charge for the second one, and he does not charge, and four people in that city have said that this is the only time anybody in it has refused to be paid for a refusal, and that a man who has been refused once and comes back is a person, and that the city does not have a form for that. **The same eleven words, the same order, the same paper, the same hand, and the only difference is a fold four inches from the bottom, and the second thing he has said out loud in twenty years that was not about paper: a refusal made twice is worth the same as a refusal made once and it is not less, and there are about four hundred men in four counties in your country who have been told the same thing twice and went away and said the place would not be told, and you are the first one in years who has come back and asked for the second one on purpose.** And the whalebone, which a man of thirty-two asks to try, and is refused, and the reason is not that he would do it badly: **if you learn that, then in about four years there is a man in a county four hundred miles off who can rule a form in this city, and a form is the only thing this place makes, and the only thing this place makes is the only thing it has ever given anybody.** And two identical refusals carried flat up a lane in a coat, beside a page with a date and one word under it, **not joined, and he does not join them, and about four people in that city have said that the man with the stick has never once said the name of anywhere out loud and that this is the single most correct thing anybody in this city has done in nine days and it is also the reason nobody here is going to know anything about him before he goes.** And the nine days: about forty hods for a loaf, a market at the third, a yard at the seventh, nine places and none of them, and a man who works out in half a minute on the eighth day that he is the safest person in this city, and why, and does not say it out loud.

**Ch 217 · the twelfth day, the second hour, a bridge gate · Nesh Karrow, four years, three gates, and a thing she wants.** About four hundred people through a barrier of three bars in a day and nine of them turned back, and a man of fifty-five in a hut who has been in it nineteen years and has turned back about four hundred people and has not once had to raise his voice or been told by anybody above him what to do. **And the reason, given once, by a man of about forty at the winch at the far end of the bridge: you cannot ask a man at a gate where he has been, that is not a gate, that is a court, and a gate does not want a reason, and a man at a gate who wants to know where a man has been has stopped being a gate and started being a question, and a question at a bridge in this city is the one thing that has never been allowed to happen, and a gate is a machine for letting liars through, and it is one man and three bars, and it has been one man and three bars for four hundred years, and if the four hundredth man who ever came over that bridge said he was from a place with a name on it then this city has been in a book for four hundred years, and it has not been, and that is not because we are clever, that is because it costs nothing to let a liar through and everything to stop one.** **And a woman of twenty-eight called Nesh Karrow who has been carrying for four years, four days a week, is turned back and does not go: she turns round at about the fourth foot of the bridge and then stands there facing the water, and about nine people go past her.** She comes back up and tells a stranger she is the man carrying two of Dermit's and that she has counted him going past the gate eleven times because she counts, and that she does not have his name and is not going to ask for it, **because if she asked he would be right to say no and she would be a woman of twenty-eight who has just made a man of thirty-two careful, and she has been doing this four years and knows exactly how many people have made a man careful and it is not nine hundred.** **And the want, once, in one breath, in her own words: I want it to be a letter. A letter goes into a hand and the hand goes away and nobody has to be turned round at a gate for four years over it, and a letter is not a thing anybody can be shown, and this is not a letter, and I have known that for four years and I have never once been told what it is.** She will not say what she carries, and four people in that city have asked her and she has given four answers and four of them were right, and none of them has ever been asked it by somebody who could have done anything with the answer. Her arrangement in her own words: **nine of us, half of us women, none of us paid, because the only thing this city sends out is a thing that is carried, and a thing that is carried is not work, and a person who is not working is not a person anybody has to answer for** — and: **that is the arrangement and it has been the arrangement for four hundred years and I did not make it and I would like to go on carrying.** Nobody in the city says the carrying is the job and not the failing, and it is not said to her. **And a child of nine goes through the same gate in the same quarter of an hour with a bundle on one shoulder and the man in the hut does not stop it and does not look at it, and a woman of twenty-eight is turned back for the same reason, and nobody in the hut and nobody in the lane says a word about either of them, and a man of thirty-two with a limp does not ask the child anything and does not go up the far bank after it.** She is turned back at two more gates and he does not follow her to either. And the yard at the bottom of the lane is shut and empty four days early, and there is a board over a bench, and a man stands in it for about a quarter of an hour and does not go in, and the only thing in the world he wanted out of it was a man with a nine-inch rule.

**Ch 218 · the fifteenth day, the fourth hour, a yard past two gates · Osmund Cusk, a book about the outside, and a second column that is not turned round.** A yard that is not Crane's yard, and a book in two columns, the first a count of days from the last renewal and the second headed with one plain word meaning **carried**, which is not a trade and is not a job. **A man of thirty-two asks what the book is of and is told it is of the marks, and then asks what a mark is, and a man of sixty-one named Osmund Cusk does not look up and says no, and four people in that yard have said that this is the only answer anybody in that city has ever given to that question and that it has been given by four different men in four hundred years and that not one of the four has ever said anything else.** He has been at the bench nineteen years and the book was in the yard before him and nobody told him what it was for and he worked it out in a year and nobody has ever confirmed it, **and he has not asked what a mark is, and the reason is that a man who keeps a book for nineteen years and asks what is in it has admitted that he has not known what he was keeping, and then somebody gives him the answer, and then he has to decide whether to go on.** He knows what goes in it and does not know what it is. **Two men in this city keep a count of days and neither has ever been asked to stop, and each has known about the other for nine years because their books have a fold in them in the same place, and neither has ever said so.** The second column is refused in four words and not turned round, and a man of thirty-two understands inside the first second that he is not going to be shown it and is not going to ask. **And the child: a hand flat on a bench, a line and a bar and a figure, the book turned round about the width of a hand, one line written, the hand taken off the bench in the way a man takes a wet thing off a table, and a man of sixty-one who has watched about nine hundred children go up that lane in nineteen years and has not spoken to one of them and has kept the figure in his head and refused to enter it.** And the want, once, in about nine seconds, in a yard, in his own words, never said to anybody in nineteen years: **I have wanted for most of my working life for somebody to come and tell me to stop keeping this. Nobody has. It is not that nobody can. It is that there is no one in this city who can, and I have never once said that to anybody, and I have said it to you because you asked me what is in it and because you are a stranger and will be gone.** And his reason for the silence about the column, once, and it is nineteen words: **the word on the head of it is what we do to a thing and not what the thing is, and there is a scratch on the second leaf about the width of a thumbnail that I have looked at about nine hundred times and it is a thumb and it is not a mark.** **And a man of thirty-two puts his own left hand on that bench, palm up, and a man of sixty-one looks at it for a minute and a half, four times longer than he takes, and finds nothing, and says no, and then: it is not the same, there is no same, there is a book and there is a bench and there is a hand that comes down the lane about nine hundred times in a year, and you have a line in your palm and I have a book, and there is nothing in this city that joins those two, and if there were one of us would have found it, and I have been looking for nineteen years.** And the fifth question, the first in fourteen days that was not about a thing, and the answer: **it is one man, and the reason it is the same answer is that the answer has never been a decision. There is no decision in this yard. There is a bench and a book and a man, and a man does not decide. A man is here.** And a man of thirty-two walks out at the ninth hour knowing less about a mark than he knew at the fourth hour, carrying two refusals and a page and a line in his palm that is not one of theirs.

**Ch 219 · the nineteenth day, the third hour, a lane · the child, the mark, the reason the city does not name it, and four words that are not asked.** A man of thirty-two has been forty yards behind a child of nine since the second hour for seventeen days and has not closed the distance, and about four people on that lane have said that he is the only person anybody has been able to be near for nine days without asking a child a question. **The mark is a line and a bar and a figure and that is all it is and it has been all it is in four hundred years, and four men in that city have each refused him one thing and not another and none of the four was unkind and four of them improved on the answer the one before gave.** A woman of about thirty with a pail says the whole of the post in about nine words and then goes to work: **a name in a book in this city is a person somebody can be shown, there is exactly one person in this city who goes out of the gate, and if that person has a name then the name is a thing that can be carried out, and if it cannot be carried out then it cannot be a name, and the child is not a name, the child is a post.** She has told it four times in years and three of the four times were to men who came up a road with a stick. The child takes a hod eleven times in a yard and is not counted and is given a piece of bread off a sill and does not say thank you. **It is not pitied, and not because anybody decided not to pity it: pitying a thing requires knowing what the thing is for, and four hundred people in that city know what the child is for and nine hundred know what it carries, and not one of the two figures knows the other one.** And then the lane: the child stands and does not go and the man does not go, and **is that the far one** is asked a second time in a different country and answered in about three words without understanding, and then the child looks at his left hand for a while and he does not put it behind him and does not open it, **and the hand has a black line healed into the crease about a foot long that runs under the skin and does not stop at the edge of it, and the child's hand has a line and a bar and a figure on it, and neither of them says anything, and nobody in that city has ever worked out what was in the look.** **And the reason he does not ask, which is not a rule and is not a decision: he has had four words ready since the sixth day and a page of foolscap in a coat whose seventh line says a person and was looked at twice and is not finished, and he does not ask because the seventh line says a person and not a name, and a name in a book in that city is a person somebody can be shown, and a person who is asked what a mark is by a stranger in a lane is a person who has been asked, and four people in that city have said since that this is the whole of why and that the man did not work it out and did it anyway, and that this is the difference between a man who obeys a rule and a man who cannot be got to see one.** He writes in his notebook for the first time in about eleven weeks, a count of days and a line about a hand, **and does not write the seventh line, and does not go and get the page, and does not look at it, and about four people in that city have said that this is the only thing anybody in it has ever seen a man be frightened of.** And the child goes four hundred yards to a yard with a roof on two sides, and a man of sixty-six looks up, which is the fourth time in twenty years he has looked up at a child, and a man of thirty-two stands at the mouth of the yard and does not come in.

**Ch 220 · the nineteenth day, the fourth hour and a half, the same yard · the ninth asking, the ninth refusal, a pen that does not write, and ninety words.** A man of sixty-six checks a date in his own head and goes on, as he went on the first time, and then says **I want you to take one out to the west gate this afternoon**, and does not dress it and does not put it in a room. **And then, in advance and in his own words: I am not going to tell you what it is and I am not going to tell you where it goes and you are not going to ask me, and I would like that entered, and I would like the two of them entered together, and there is nobody in this city I can enter them with.** And **No**, said the child, in the time it takes to draw a breath, and about four people in that yard have said that a man of sixty-six has entered about four hundred refusals in twenty years and that the shortest of the four hundred was nine seconds and that the shortest of anything ever said in that yard was said by a child of nine to a man of sixty-six, and that four hundred years of a city making careful, correct, eleventh-word decisions came to that. And a man of thirty-two at the mouth of the lane did not move and did not call out, and the not saying was four seconds long.** And he works one thing out in nine seconds at the mouth of the yard, and it is this, and he has not written it down: **the man had said *a man of twenty-eight* and not a name, and the only person of twenty-eight in that city who is turned back at a gate four days a week is a woman who has been carrying for four years, and a man of sixty-six had known that, and had not sent her, and had sent the child instead, and had not said why, and had said in advance that he was not going to say why.** And then the book: the board off it, a page, a ruled space the right size and the wrong shape, **and nobody in that yard has worked out what shape a space for a person is, and there is not a column for it anywhere in the world this city has ever made or answered, and a form in a town two hundred miles off with a space for a figure of persons and nowhere at all for the name of a person has exactly the same trouble, and neither of those two things is in the same book and nobody has joined them and nobody is going to.** And a man of sixty-six keeps a pen in his hand and does not write, and has never once in twenty years not written. And then he says the thing, once, in trade terms, in about ninety words, and it is not improved on: **A man can be asked twice and can be asked it a different way the second time. A column cannot be asked anything at all. That is nine refusals in four generations and eight of the nine were given by eleven people in a room, and a room is a column. The ninth was given by a person. It is the only one of the nine I have never been able to put on a page, and I am not going to find a way to put it on a page, and that is not a complaint, it is a fact about a book.** About four people in that city heard it and none of them can say a word about it and have had nineteen days and have not got it, and about four of the eleven in the room at the top of the lane have never heard it and will not. **And a man of thirty-two stood at the mouth of that yard with four words ready that he had had ready for thirteen days and did not say them, and the count in a book on a bench was the same count it had been on the eighteenth day, and nobody looked, and about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand did not know any of it and will not.** And the child stays in the yard for about three hours and neither of them says a word for about nine hundred seconds, and a woman of thirty with a pail counts three hours of a man standing in a lane and does not ask, and he does not go in, and the child does not go out through a gate. And one man four hundred miles off is going to be told a number in nine weeks or so and the number will be right.

**Block 2 note — the block's calendar, its cast discipline, and its device counts, so that Batch 0003 does not re-derive any of them.** **Calendar.** Path time throughout, the first day of a count of days from the last renewal to the nineteenth, and the block's remaining days to the thirtieth of ninety are Batch 0003's. **Every day in the block is the city's own count: the first, the second, the fourth, the sixth, the ninth, the twelfth, the fifteenth, the nineteenth, and the hours, and the ninth hour and the fourth hour are the hours the city's work is done by.** **No main-world month, no real-world month and no main-world weekday is spoken or written in any of the ten chapters in any register including a notebook, and a sweep for the eleven month names, the twelve real-world month names and the seven weekday names returns zero.** The main world is not in this block except as a distance in four references that carry no date: a county four hundred miles off, a town two hundred miles off, a form in a bag, and a page with a word on it four hundred miles from here. The printed three-weeks warning is unchanged and no character in this block uses the word *failed* about a road, and **the block printed no drift figure and the ledger's conversion of ninety days into three months is referenced once, in a man's mouth, and is not performed on the page.** **Cast.** **One new name of six and five slots unfilled, so Volume 05 stands at four names of six and twenty-six of thirty slots unfilled, against the volume's planned five and twenty-four: Dermit Crane, 66.** Osmund Cusk, 61, in Chapter 218, and Nesh Karrow, 28, in Chapter 217, are spent Batch 0001 names and both now have pages and neither is re-described. The woman of sixty on the council, the clerk of forty, the man of fifty with a waggon, the man of forty at the wharf and the man of forty at the winch, the man of thirty-four with lime, the man of thirty who sells names, the man of fifty-five in the hut, the woman of thirty with a pail, the man of about fifty at the crane wheel, the man of about sixty with a boat, the man of about twenty-six, the man of about thirty with a barrow, the boy of ten and the boy of fourteen, are addressed by trade or by age. **The seventh child of the volume is a child, is unnamed, is not named in any of the ten chapters, and does not count, and is the same child as Chapter 210 and is the living anchor Block 0004's return is made through.** **Devices, as whole words and not as strings.** `nine` **189**, per chapter 10 / 4 / 19 / 17 / 15 / 16 / 28 / 15 / 34 / 31, **5.92 per 1,000, against the volume's six-block ladder of 2.87 / 4.58 / 7.31 / 5.73 / 7.26 / 4.17 — the second-highest in the volume, and the rise is the city's count of days, the ninth refusal, and a notebook.** `about` **360**, per chapter 43 / 41 / 37 / 34 / 29 / 31 / 33 / 36 / 39 / 37, **and no chapter is over forty-five.** `the whole of` **15**, against a house baseline of two or three a chapter. `about N seconds` **2**, one in Chapter 218 and one in Chapter 219, **and both are the two figures the block required, and the figure was forty on the first full pass and every other instance was replaced with a different true fact.** `about nine + noun` **1**. `in nine years` **0**. `cut` **3**, a ferrier's stick cut out of a fence rail, a man cutting a piece of glass rod at a stall, and a pen cut down and not a quill, all three read and all three ordinary, **and the working is not among them and is not named anywhere in the block.** `---` rules **51**. Bolded line-openings **130**. **Semicolons 0, em-dashes 0, straight double quotes 0, curly apostrophes 0, curly opening single quotes 0.** **One System panel in the block, in Chapter 214, two plain lines, no number, naming neither the city nor the lamp.** No occurrence of the word *Gatehouse*. Filler as whole words, a baseline and not a target, **with the basis named in both columns: `nodded` 0, `held` 3, `wrote` 14, `stood` 33, `plain` 2, `counted` 9, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0**, against Volume 05 Batch 0001 at 0 / 1 / 35 / 24 / 0 / 5 / 0 / 0 and Volume 04 Batch 0005 at 0 / 7 / 25 / 42 / 0 / 16 / 0 / 0. **A per-line bold parity check across every line of all two hundred and twenty chapter files returns zero, a duplicate-paragraph sweep across the ten new chapters returns clean, and both were run here and both are recorded as having been run.** Length **31,938 words in ten chapters** and no chapter is under 2,931.

**The ten endings, because the Volume 04 close's item 1 asks for the list and Batch 0003 should not re-derive it.** **211** on a lamp standing where it was standing and a woman who did not ask him anything. **212** on a waggon and a stick and a cup that was not his. **213** on a man coming through a gate with his name not wanted and asking a stranger what he wanted. **214** on a boy of fourteen on a worn step and a door that has never once asked him for anything back. **215** on a man of sixty-six who says goodnight to nine people in a yard and has never once said it to a man who is leaving. **216** on three pieces of paper in a coat and two of them that say no. **217** on an empty yard and a stranger four days early for a man with a nine-inch rule. **218** on a man walking out at the ninth hour knowing less about a mark than he knew at the fourth. **219** on a page of foolscap on a hook four feet away with an unfinished seventh line. **220** on a ledger turned round with the spine toward a man of sixty-six and a child of nine that did not go out. **Nine of the ten are not a refusal; the one that is, 220, is a no given by a person of nine years old in a yard, and that is the volume's whole engine.**

## Batch 0003 — Volume 05, Chapters 221–230, "The Count"

**Ch 221 · the twentieth day, the second hour and after, the eastern road and the paved lane · a man of forty-six, a satchel, and what a printed thing is for.** A man of about forty-six with a satchel and a stick and a list comes down the road for about an hour, **and he does not get the hour wrong, which is the first thing about him and is the only sentence in the chapter about him that is not a trade fact.** He is not a trader and not a man with a message and not anybody anybody has sent. **He leaves forms at doors: *I leave them. Four hundred doors and I leave one at each and I go on to the next. I have never once been asked to fill one in and I have never once filled one in, and I have been doing it eight years and I have left about three thousand and I could not tell you what is on the top of one of them.*** And the second sentence of it, which is the trade fact the whole block is made of: **a form is a thing a door can throw away, that is why it is printed and not written, a thing you write you keep.** The paper is printed and not ruled, about the size of a broadside with a little less paper than a broadside, and it is **ruled in six columns and four of the six are ruled for a figure and a man of thirty-two with a limp works that out in about half a minute in a lane and does not write it down.** The money, footed on a sill in a room the size of a cart: **the room two pence, bread a penny, a second loaf a penny, two and one is three and three and one is four pence**, and the woman who owns the room says *there are about nine thousand people in this city and there is not one of them who has ever asked me what the weight was in the column for*, which is the same sentence she says to a man with a stick on the first day of Batch 0002 without knowing she is saying it twice. **Recognition held without a beat dropped for it: four descriptions in a market, the fourth of them given by a woman of about thirty with a pail who says nothing at all and is the only correct one.** He is fed and not paid and works four days. And at the top of the lane a boy of about fourteen on a worn step tells him where the man who makes the paper is and tells him not to thank him. End: about four hundred places on a list, three hundred and ninety-nine of them names of places, **and the four hundredth a word he has never heard in eight years with the district column filled in like all the others and the ink dry.**

**Ch 222 · the twenty-first and the twenty-second days, the fourth hour, a bindle yard and a printed sheet · six columns, four figures, and a question nobody has asked in six years.** A man of sixty-six does not stop cutting, and then **he puts the whalebone down before he has been asked twice, which is the only time in twenty years and which is the whole of the visit.** The man of forty-six says what he is, in a yard, in a city of about nine thousand people, and puts a printed sheet on the bench: **it is the same series, four presses in four towns, about four hundred doors, and he has never once been told what the series is for and has never once asked, and the reason is on the page in his own mouth, which is that it is not on the list and the list is what he is paid for.** The sheet is ruled in six columns, five with heads and the sixth with no head at all and the same width as the other five, and the man of sixty-six reads the five heads and then the sixth and then the five again. **He says three things about it, all three short: it has four places for a figure and not one for a name and he has not got a way of saying no to a piece of paper like that and it has not occurred to him in twenty years that he would be asked to; the other side of it is in a hand he does not know and he is not going to talk about what is written on the other side of a piece of paper that has come into his yard; and he has not known what the series is for for about two days, which is the longest anybody in this city has gone without knowing something, and he has not asked.** Nobody improves on any of the three and about four people in that yard have worked out that the middle one was the one about the paper and that the man with the satchel did not hear it at all. **And a man of forty-six asks the first question anybody has asked a man of sixty-six in about six years, and it is *has anybody ever come here*, and the answer is no, in eight years, not once, and the man of sixty-six goes on cutting for a minute and does not answer it, and the silence is a man finding out that there is a second thing about a piece of paper that is worse than the first.** A city of nine thousand people does the four things it does on every day of a count of days, and a man of thirty-two with a limp is two hundred yards up a lane and is not told any of it. End: the sheet nine inches from a board and a book, and a man of forty-six going up a hill who looked at the lamp once and did not ask what it was.

**Ch 223 · the twenty-third and the twenty-fourth days, the second hour and the fifth · eight in the book, nine in his head, and four of the same figure.** The sheet has been on the bench about a day and he has neither written on it nor thrown it out, **which is a third place, on the right hand side of his own working, and about four people know about it.** He reads the five heads again and takes the board off a book and puts the book down on the other side of the bench, and **a man of sixty-six counts out loud twice, in a yard, to nobody, and both times it is eight, and a man of sixty-six has not counted anything out loud in about a year.** Then he counts the other one, **which is nine, and which is not in the book, and the nine is a refusal given on the nineteenth day by a person of nine years old that took the time it takes to draw one breath and that has no column in that book and has never had one, and the difference between the two numbers is one and nobody in that yard has ever worked out that he was holding both at once.** He counts nine without moving his eyes, the way other men do a sum they have done every day of their working life, **and the ninth of the nine is in a coat two hundred yards up a lane and the other eight are in a room with a bench too short for him in it and he has shown his to nobody for four days.** Then he writes, in four places, in about a minute and a half, **one, and one, and one, and one, and that is four of the same figure and it is not a sum, and a man fills in the spaces because the spaces are there, and a man of sixty-six has not written a figure on anything in twenty years and has now written four of them.** **And nine is a count of things this city has said no to and it is not a count of people, said once, in about eleven words, to a yard and not to the sheet.** A man of about thirty with a barrow and a mule stops outside the yard because a man of thirty-two with a limp is standing at the mouth of it **with the page out of his coat for the first time since the ninth day of a count he does not have, looking at the seventh line, and puts it back**, and the barrow-man says the truest thing anybody in that city has said about a stranger: *he has been standing in a lane for two hours with a page in his hand and he has not looked at the first six lines, and I have been going up that hill for twenty-three days and I have never once seen anybody in this city look at the first six lines of anything.* The sixth column with no head on it, a man of forty-six who has asked about it twice in a tone of a man asking for a price, and a woman of about thirty with a pail who says nine words at the mouth of the yard and goes on. End: a man of forty-six writes it on the back of his own list and not on the sheet, **and the sentence is the only part of this anybody outside the city can act on and it is on the back of a list.**

**Ch 224 · the twenty-fourth day, the second hour and after, the road gate and the eastern rise · four words, a bale of cord, and a figure that leaves.** **A gate is a machine for letting liars through and it is one man and three bars and it has been for four hundred years, and a man of fifty-five in a hut has turned back about four hundred people in nineteen years and has never once had to raise his voice, and about four hundred people have been turned round at that gate in nineteen years and not one of them has ever been told what the four words are for.** A man of forty-six walks up to the barrier with a printed sheet in his hand and is told *then turn round*, and turns round, **and nobody in that hut has ever worked out why a man with a sheet of paper in his hand turned round at a gate in a city he had been in for four days, and nobody in that hut is going to ask him, because a gate does not ask.** He goes four hundred yards up the lane and puts the sheet flat inside a bale of cord and reed and cords it over with about four turns through the loops that are already in it for that, **and says one word while he does it, and the word is *cord*, and a man of sixty-six says it in the tone of a man saying a price and then goes back to a strip of paper.** A bale is about four feet long and there are about nine in a yard at any hour and they are not numbered and they are not weighed, and about four people in that yard have said since that a thing this city cannot name is a bundle. He goes back down the lane and out through the road gate with a barrow and a bale on it, **and the man of fifty-five says nothing, and a child of nine goes through the barrier about a minute later with a bundle on one shoulder and the man in the hut does not look at it.** The tax as a working yard: a man of thirty-two with a limp walks nine hundred feet of paving four times between the second hour and the fifth hour and turns round at the end of it, and in a glass yard watches a gather go from the colour it should be to the colour it should not be and does not move and does not speak, **and a man of about thirty-four with lime turns round and looks at him and then at the gather and then back at him and says nothing and puts the gather in the mould.** A man of fifty-two comes down a ladder at the fifth hour instead of the sixth and stands at the bottom of it for about two minutes, and nobody has asked him in nineteen years what the bucket is for. End: **a sheet of printed paper in a bundle of cord and reed on a barrow going up a rise out of this city with four figures on it that are all the same figure and the figure is nine, and a book under a board nine hundred yards off that says eight, and nobody has put the two numbers side by side.**

**Ch 225 · the twenty-fifth day, the fourth hour, a yard at the end of a lane past two gates and a slope · the ledger turned round, and the city's mandatory midpoint.** A man of sixty-one has been at that bench nineteen years and the book was in that yard before him, **and on the twenty-fifth day he is not waiting to be told anything, and the reason has been in the city for two days and has come to him the ordinary way, which is that a man of thirty with a barrow and a mule said one sentence at the top of a hill and a man of thirty-four with lime heard it from a man of about forty at a cart and a woman of about thirty with a pail carried it four hundred yards down a lane without knowing what she was carrying.** He puts the pen down and does not say anything for a minute and a half, **which is the longest a man of sixty-one has ever sat at that bench without doing anything and about nine hundred children have put a hand on that bench in nineteen years.** The man of thirty-two puts the figure where it belongs and says he is not going to ask him a question about it. **He turns the book round, and the second column comes up off the bench, and a man of sixty-one refused that column in four words on the fifteenth day and would not say why and turned it round on the twenty-fifth without being asked twice.** The reason is in a man's own words and it is a want and not a policy: **he is the only man in this city with a book about the outside, the outside now has a piece of paper about this city on it that is wrong by one, and he cannot correct it and nobody outside will ever hold his book.** **The second column is in two parts: the first is a hand, and there are eleven of them and they are the same size and the same shape and they are not the same thing; the second is a road, written the way a road is written, which is from here outward, and a man of thirty-two who has spent four years with a road on a river four hundred miles off reads eleven of them in about a minute and a half and the eleven of them are not the same eleven and every one of them goes out of this valley and down the eastern side of it and across about a day of country and into a place, and not one of the eleven names a place anybody in that city can see from where they are standing.** He does not know what the column is for, has not asked in nineteen years, and does not say the reason twice. **And what the man of thirty-two could not use, worked out at the bottom of the slope, is eleven roads in four hundred years, which is a little more than one every thirty years, and a city that had a road out of it every thirty years is not a city anybody could find, and eleven is not a number anybody in this city chose by accident and a woman of sixty told him why in a room on the sixth day and will not tell him again, and a man of sixty-one has now told a stranger the same thing in nineteen words about a book and does not know he has said it, and the two are in two yards nine hundred yards apart and nobody has joined them.** A child of nine puts its hand on the bench with the second column still open. End: a man of thirty-two standing at a bench with a line in his palm that a man of sixty-one looked at for a minute and a half ten days ago and said was not one of theirs, and eleven lines of a column he cannot stop looking at.

**Ch 226 · the twenty-sixth day, the second hour and the fourth hour, a market and a yard past two gates · the city knows, and there is no outcome column.** **The city knows. That is the first fact of the twenty-sixth day and it is not a secret and it is not a discovery, and about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand have been out of the gate and about nine hundred know the name of one of the eleven and neither of those two figures knows anything about the other one.** A man of fifty with a waggon has been to four of the eleven and has never in nineteen years put two of them together in one sentence. A woman of about thirty with a pail has been to two and has a sister at one and has said so twice to strangers and never to a man of this city. **A boy of fourteen on a step has been to none of them and has the names of all eleven and gets them from about nine people, and there is no book in this city with the names of the eleven in it except a book about two inches thick under a roof at the end of a lane past two gates.** A man of thirty-four with lime says one of the eleven in the plainest register there is, while working, without stopping, and nine sentences in twenty-five days and every one of them about work. **Nobody in this city has ever asked how a road out of it and back again is made, and the not asking is not a rule and there is nobody who could make one, and a man of fifty-two, a man of fifty and a woman of thirty between them know seven of the eleven and have never said the name of a place in front of each other.** Then Cusk reads the eleventh line: **two marks on one line and one on each of the other ten, and the first of the two is a woman's and the second is a boy's and the boy would have been about nine, and the second mark is the same shape as the mark a child of nine put on that bench on the nineteenth day, and the figure fourteen is said out loud in that yard for the first time in nineteen years in the tone of a man saying a price.** **And a man of sixty-one says the other thing before anybody asks him: there are eleven lines and a hand and a day and a road and there has never been anything else on any of them in four hundred years, and there is no column for what became of anybody and there is not going to be one and he could not fill one in.** Nobody asked him. **A man of thirty-two with a limp was nine feet off with his hands at his sides and did not ask him, and the not asking was four seconds long, and a page of foolscap in his coat has a seventh line that says a person and has not been finished since a lane four hundred miles off.** End: a boy of fourteen at the mouth of the yard saying the only true thing anybody in that city has said about a book in four hundred years, **that line is older than me, and you are talking about a thing that is the same age as me and you have been talking about it as though it were a thing from somewhere.**

**Ch 227 · the twenty-seventh day, the fourth hour and the ninth hour, a bindle yard and a lane · the refusal to be a document, and the one reading.** A second sheet of the same series comes back clipped to the first, and **the object column on the first has a place name in it and the object column on the second is empty, and that is the only difference between two sheets of the same series that anybody in that yard can see.** A man of forty-six says in about nine seconds what the second sheet wants, in the plainest register anybody in that city has for a piece of printed paper: **it is asking the district for a number of people in it who know about a thing, and the office has not written the thing down, and an office that will not name a thing is not hiding it, it is doing the same thing you are doing.** Nobody improves on it and both of the two men in the room have missed what has just been said. He asks for a form, for nothing, to carry back and say that this city has declined. **A man of sixty-six who has written about four hundred pieces of paper in twenty years and has never declined to make one declines, and he does not say the same eleven words, and he stands up to say the reason, which is twenty-two words: a form is a document, a document is a thing a court can do something with, and he is not going to put a second one about this city into the same room in the same book as the first one.** And then the cost, said by the man with the satchel, standing, in about nineteen words, **and it is the best evidence in the volume that a refusal can be true and still be useless: it is worth nothing, the first one is gone, it went out on the twenty-fourth in a bundle and is in a book, and not filling this one in does not take that one back, and the room will still have the other one, and I have never once known which of the two things in a satchel was the one that mattered until this week and it was the one that was filled in.** A child of nine goes past the mouth of the yard where a man is refusing to make a document and does not look in. Then the reading, at the ninth hour, in a lane, with a hand flat on a wall: **what comes back is a list, and it is eleven lines and there are no words in it, and under the list there is a column and in the column shifts and against one of the shifts a man, and the man is fifty-two and he is on the third shift and has been on it for nineteen years, and under the eleven lines there is a decision four hundred years old that eleven people made in a room once, and what they chose was to pay it every day instead of once, and they chose it because paying it once could have been refused and paying it every day cannot.** The panel at the threshold. And one fact about a woman and a boy: **a route is a thing four hundred people kept a column for, and there is no column in four hundred years of anybody's book for what became of either of them, and a man of sixty-one said so the day before before he was asked and he did not ask.** End: eleven lines in a notebook in the inside pocket of a coat, **and a city of about nine thousand people that has been keeping a lamp the way a bridgekeeper keeps a wall, which is by somebody turning up, and it has not been told and is not going to be.**

**Ch 228 · the twenty-eight day, the second hour, a glass works and an east wall · Ivo Marrow, 52, and the two things, and the duckboard.** **He was not doing anything for the first nine minutes and about four people in that yard have said since that a man who has run out of things that are wrong is the most dangerous man in a glass yard and is not going to explain that and nobody has asked him to.** A man of fifty-two on a ladder four times a day for nineteen years turns round, looks at a stick for about two seconds, and says he has wanted to know what a stick is for for about eleven years and has not asked, **and that there is nobody in this city he could ask and it is not because of the light, it is because of what a man would be supposed to be doing while he asked.** His name is Ivo Marrow. **The thing he is good at is the wall: the wall is four hundred years old and is not flat and is not straight, and there are about nine places on it where a ladder will go and about nine where it will not, and he knows the nine and knows which of the nine is the one for a man with a bucket in one hand, and a man of thirty-four with lime has watched him do it about two thousand times and said so once, to a stranger, and not to him.** The tax: a man of thirty-two with a limp watches a gather go from the colour it should be to the colour it should not be and does not move and does not speak, **and a man of thirty-four puts a duckboard down under his feet without a word and has been doing it for five days and nobody in that yard has ever seen him do it for anybody else.** The two things, said once each, in the same conversation, in his own words, in a working yard: **there is a piece of paper with my name on it and the name of the man that was on it before me and the name of the man that was on it before him, and it is a list of the third shift in a drawer in a room in this city, and about four hundred people in this city could be asked what the third shift is and not one of them would be able to tell you, and I am not asking you for anything, and I have not said it to anybody in this city in nineteen years. And I do not want to die on it. I am fifty-two. There is a brother of mine at the low end of the river who thinks I am on a roof, and if somebody knew what the shift was, and if I did not want to be on it, then I would be able to say that, and there is nobody in this city I could say it to, and that is the whole of why I have said the other thing.** Nobody improved on either and a man of thirty-four did not turn round. A drawer is the correct place and not a wall, because a wall is a thing people look at. **A man of thirty-two then tells a man of fifty-two that he has eleven lines in a notebook and that he cannot use them, and a man of fifty-two says it is the first useful thing anybody has said to him about a list in nineteen years, and neither of them asks what the list is.** End: a man of fifty-two going up a ladder for the fourth time with a bucket in one hand and not looking down at anybody, and a notebook with eleven lines in it that the man with the stick cannot stop seeing.

**Ch 229 · the twenty-ninth day, the second hour and the fifth hour, a gate, a room and a bindle yard · the same sheet, a person asked a second time, and eight and two is ten.** **The series goes round twice and the man of forty-six says so at the gate before he has got through it, and a man of fifty-five in a hut does not say the four words the second time, and the four words were in his mouth and did not come out, and this is the first time in nineteen years a man has gone through that gate carrying a bundle without them.** The money, footed on a sill: **the room two pence and it is the same room at the same price and it is not a second price and the two nights are not a column, bread a penny, a bundle of waxed thread twopence, two and one is three and three and two is five pence.** A man of thirty-two has slept in that room for twenty-nine nights and has not been charged for twenty-eight of them and nobody in this city has offered to charge him and a man of thirty who sells names for a penny has worked out the arrangement in about a second on the second day and has never said it out loud. Then a man of sixty-six puts the sheet on the bench before the man of forty-six is through the gate, **and a man of forty-six says that a sheet that came back on the twenty-seventh is going back again with something on it, and a man of sixty-six says that he is going to write a figure in the four spaces and that it is going to be the same figure in each.** Then he asks a child of nine years old **the same question he asked it on the nineteenth day, in the same yard, in the same words**, and says the reason out loud in about eleven words, **and the reason is that the figure he wrote on the twenty-third was one higher than the number in his book and there is one refusal in this city he has never been able to put on a page.** **No**, said the child. It took the time it takes to draw one breath. **And the arithmetic is done out loud in a yard before the figure is written: eight in the book, and the child twice, and eight and two is ten, and the two is a person of nine years old who has been asked twice, and the ten is not a count of people and it is not a count of rooms and it is not a count of doors and it is a count of times this city has said no, and it is the only time anybody in that yard has put a count and a person next to each other and nobody in that yard has worked out that it is a document.** One, and one, and one, and one. The man of forty-six is told the same eleven words a second time, writes the same sentence on the back of his list a second time, and says the thing that is all of the day: **a room with two returns from one district is not a room with a problem, it is a room with a pile, and nobody in a room adds two figures from one district together and nobody in a room asks why they are different, and I have never once known which of the two things in a satchel was the one that mattered until this week and it was the one that was filled in.** End: **a child of nine that took its bundle off its shoulder and put it on again and did not go out that afternoon, and a man of thirty-two with a limp at the mouth of that yard who did not come in and did not call out and did not ask the child a second question himself.**

**Ch 230 · the thirtieth day, the second hour, the fourth hour and the ninth hour, a road, a glass works and a ladder · the finding, and the mechanic, and a thing a man of thirty-two cannot use.** The man of fifty-five says nothing and the man of forty-six goes up the rise, **and the twenty-eighth and the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth were three ordinary days and the only thing that was different about any of the three is that a man of fifty-two said two things in a glass yard on the twenty-eighth.** Then, at the fourth hour, **a man of fifty-two comes down a ladder for the fourth time and says three things while he is working, and does not stop and does not look up, and none of the three is to the man of thirty-two with a limp, and about nine men in that yard hear all three and about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand hear none of them, and nobody in that yard improves on any of the three and about four of the nine have not stopped working, which is the correct way to receive it in a working yard.** The finding, in about nineteen words: **we have begun filing a person as a class, that is the first time in four hundred years this city has done that, and we did it in answer to a form, and we did it out of nothing, and nobody in this city decided to, and a man with a satchel asked a boy a question twice because a figure was wrong by one, and the boy said no twice, and a man of sixty-six wrote down a count of times and not a count of people.** The mechanic, once, in his own words, about a place to stand a man in: **a man can be stood in a place and a man can be asked, that is the whole of the difference and it is four hundred years old and I have watched both sides of it from the same ladder, and a column is a place to stand a man in, it does not ask him and it does not hear him and it is the same whatever he says, and I have been in one nineteen years and I would not know today if it had changed on me.** And the third, in about nine seconds, with one look up: **and you are the same as the paper, and you have not noticed, and you have been fed and not paid for thirty days and there is nothing to show anybody about you, and that has been the best thing that has happened to you in this city, and it is not kindness, it is a line in a form with your whole life on the wrong side of it, and the man who filled it in did it because a figure was wrong by one and not because of you, and a man of thirty-four in this yard has been putting a piece of wood under your feet for seven days and neither of us has ever once said why, and that is the same arrangement and it is a smaller one.** A man of thirty-four turned a mould and said nothing. **A man of thirty-two with a limp stood nine feet off and did not say a word for a minute and a half, and could not use it, and has not written it down; and then he asked his sixth question in a glass yard and it was *a child of nine*, and a man of fifty-two answered it in nine words: no, a man of sixty-six put that in a count and he asked it twice because a figure was wrong, and if you want to take it out of the count you will have to go nine hundred yards and take it out of it yourself and you will not be able to, and I have not said that to be unkind and I would have said it about any of the nine of us in this yard.** End: a child of nine goes out through a gate at the ninth hour and a man of thirty-two does not go with it and does not call out; the eleven lines out on a table and the eleventh of them a man of fifty-two on a shift nineteen years old; and the feet of a ladder against a four-hundred-year-old wall.

**Block 3 note — the block's calendar, its cast discipline, and its device counts, so that Batch 0004 does not re-derive any of them.** **Calendar.** Path time throughout, the twentieth day of a count of days from the last renewal to the thirtieth, and the block's remaining days, thirty-one to sixty of ninety, are Batch 0004's. **Every day in the block is the city's own count: the twentieth, the twenty-first, the twenty-second, the twenty-third, the twenty-fourth, the twenty-fifth, the twenty-sixth, the twenty-seventh, the twenty-eighth, the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth, and the hours, and the second hour and the ninth hour are the hours the city's work is done by.** The fifteenth, nineteenth and sixth days are back-references inside Batch 0002 and are not re-derived. **No main-world month, no real-world month and no main-world weekday is spoken or written in any of the ten chapters in any register including a notebook, and a sweep for the eleven month names, the twelve real-world month names and the seven weekday names returns zero, and seven instances of a main-world weekday that the first full draft carried were found by reading the file and are at item 599.** The main world is not in this block except as a distance in references that carry no date: a county four hundred miles off, a town two hundred miles off, a form in a satchel, a road, a rise. The printed three-weeks warning is unchanged, **this block printed no drift figure, and no character in it uses the word *failed* about a road, and the ledger's conversion of ninety days into three months is not performed on the page and is not quoted.** **Cast.** **One new name of six and four slots unfilled, so Volume 05 stands at five names of six and twenty-four of thirty slots unfilled across the five batches, against the volume's planned five and twenty-four: Ivo Marrow, 52, first named in prose in Chapter 228.** Osmund Cusk, 61, Dermit Crane, 66 and Nesh Karrow, 28 are spent names and all three have pages and none is re-described. **The man of forty-six with a satchel, the man of fifty with a waggon, the man of about thirty-four with lime, the woman of about thirty with a pail, the man of thirty who sells names for a penny, the man of fifty-five in the hut, the man of thirty with a barrow and a mule, the boy of fourteen, the woman of sixty, the clerk of forty and the man of thirty-two who sells nothing are addressed by trade or by age, and the boy of fourteen is a child and is not the child.** The child is a child, is unnamed, is not named in any of the ten chapters, and does not count. **Device counts, on the page, with the basis named.** **`nine` 196, 6.52 per 1,000, per chapter 12 / 10 / 19 / 14 / 24 / 21 / 17 / 25 / 14 / 40** · `about` 367, per chapter 37 / 36 / 41 / 31 / 43 / 38 / 42 / 33 / 35 / 31, no chapter over forty-five · `the whole of` 23 · `cut` 1 · `about nine` plus a noun 38, thirty-one of them canon figures · `in nine years` 0 · `about N seconds` 0 · `two` 329 · `---` rules 49 · bolded line-openings 112 · semicolons 0 · em-dashes 0 · en-dashes 0 · straight double quotes 0 · curly apostrophes 0 · curly opening single quotes 0 · **one System panel in the block, in Chapter 227, two plain lines, no number** · no occurrence of the word Gatehouse and none of custodian. Filler as whole words, basis named in both columns: `nodded` 0, `held` 3, `wrote` 19, `stood` 20, `plain` 0, `counted` 13, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0, **and the reporting clause *a few of the people in that yard have said since that* is 35 in 30,038 words, between two and five a chapter, after the review repair pass cut it from 158 in 32,103**.

**The Batch 0003 review repair pass, in this note and not over it.** Twelve findings, twelve fixes, and the block's twenty-five deviations, ten endings, one name, cast and plot are unchanged. **Eight
