**The ten endings, because the Volume 04 close's item 1 asks for the list and Batch 0004 should not re-derive it.** **221** on a list of about four hundred places and one name on it that a man has never heard in eight years, with the district column filled in like all the others. **222** on a question a man of sixty-six asked for the first time in six years and did not answer, and a printed sheet and a board nine inches apart on one bench. **223** on four of the same figure on a printed sheet and a book that says eight, in one man's two hands at the same time, uncomputed and uncompared. **224** on a bundle of cord and reed going up a rise out of the city with four figures on it and a gate-man who did not say the four words. **225** on eleven roads and a man of sixty-one who has not asked in nineteen years and did not repeat what he said on the fifteenth. **226** on a boy of fourteen and a line in a book that is the same age as he is, and a keeper who said there was no column for anybody before he was asked. **227** on a man of sixty-six who has made about four hundred pieces of paper in twenty years and has declined to make one, and nobody in nine thousand people has heard that. **228** on a man of fifty-two going up a ladder for the fourth time and a notebook with eleven lines in it that the man with the stick cannot stop seeing. **229** on a figure of ten on a printed sheet going down a road, and a child of nine that did not go out. **230** on the feet of a ladder against a four-hundred-year-old wall in nine places out of the nine that will take a ladder, and a bucket in a hand. **Nine of the ten are not a refusal; the one that is, 227, is a man declining to make a document, and the refusal in this block that is a person is in 229 and it is the second half of that chapter and the figure is on the sheet after it, and the second time a person was asked something in this block and said no it was said by a child of nine in a yard and the man of thirty-two with a limp, who has a question ready for twenty-four days, did not ask it.**

**Ch 231 · the thirty-first day, the second hour, the fourth hour, the seventh hour and the ninth hour, a room off a lane that goes down to the quay, a bindle yard and a slope · nine of us who carry, a strip with nothing on it, and a column refused in a doorway.** **The room is not a room anybody made for this. It was a room for cord, and the shelf is about five feet off the floor and eleven feet long and about nine bundles of cord and reed are on it, and a woman of about fifty keeps the room and has kept it nineteen years and is not in it today and asking her is the same as asking the gate.** Nine people carry, half of them are women, none of them is paid, and a man of thirty-two with a limp asked for the number out loud and was given it in four words. **They are folding: a strip of paper about a foot long with five lines ruled across it and nothing written on any of the five, folded once across the middle and once again with a thumbnail, and nine people for three hours will get through about a hundred and forty.** A woman of twenty-eight puts a bundle down on the bench and starts folding and tells him in advance that he is going to ask her what this is and that she does not know and that three of her four answers in four years were wrong. He folds about ninety and tears the corner of the ninth and she takes it and looks at the tear for about a second and a half and says nothing. **The money is footed on the sill of the bench by her and not by him: paper three pence the hundred, glue four pence the pot, cord twopence the ball, three and four is seven and seven and two is nine pence, and the reed is not in it and has never been in anything, and a price gets made out of two things that are not the same thing and then somebody files it, and the room is not in that either and the room is two pence a night and bread at the second hour is a penny and that is the woman of about fifty's column and the two nights are not a column.** **He is handed a strip at about the fifth hour and nine minutes later cannot remember whether it has four lines or five, and waits until the sixth hour to look, and does not write the number down, and a man of thirty-four with lime has said out loud once that a man who is losing the thread of a thing he is holding can be told from nine feet off.** A man of thirty-four with lime says in eleven words that the strips are for the shelf and the four days in seven have not changed, and then says, in nineteen, that they go to people who are not told anything and that a man who is asked what is in a bale is a man who has started asking. **A man of sixty-one comes up a slope for the first time in nineteen years, stands in the doorway two minutes, and says three words — they want a column — and then the reason, in nineteen: a book about the outside is what a message system turns into when somebody starts counting, and I have got one and I have not been able to put it down in nineteen years, and a figure in a book is a figure in a return, and a room will take a number off you and not a name and those are the same transaction.** Two men who buy their paper out of one building and have never spoken stand eleven feet apart in a doorway. End: nine bundles corded and shelved, nine hundred feet of paving walked and walked back, a ladder on a four-hundred-year-old wall, and a count in a book under a board that did not move.

**Ch 232 · the thirty-third day, the fourth hour, the fifth hour, the seventh hour and the ninth hour, the same room, a glass yard, a gate · a mark in a corner, and a child that did not go out for three days.** **The mark goes in the corner of a strip of paper about a foot long in about a second and a half, and it is a line and a bar and a figure, and it is not ink and it is not a scar, and a man of sixty-one has said out loud in nineteen years that the marks in his second column and the marks that go on strips are the same shape and the same size and are not the same thing.** Nobody in the room asked the child what it was doing, and that is not because anybody decided not to. A woman of about thirty with a pail says the whole of the post in one breath and goes to work: **nine of us who carry and one of us who is nine years old, and if that one has a name then the name is a thing that can be carried out.** The child's day is given in full and it is an ordinary day: eleven hods in a glass yard, a piece of bread off a sill at the third hour and no thank you, four hundred yards of lane twice, two hundred yards of market and nothing bought. **A man of thirty-two with a limp stands at the door for about an hour and a half and does not go in, and on the previous day he came in and sat down, and that is the difference between the two days.** **It did not go out on the thirty-first, the thirty-second or the thirty-third, and a city of about nine thousand people has a child who does not go out three days running about once in four years.** A woman of twenty-eight says the thing she has wanted to say for four years, in nineteen words, in the room: **nine of us go out and about four hundred of us have been out, and not one of the two numbers knows anything about the other one, and I have worked that out about four times in four years and I have said it once.** He asks her the only question left in it and she says the number that matters is nine and he has had it twice. **He is handed a strip at the fifth hour and eleven minutes later cannot remember what the paper is for.** A man of sixty-six stands in a doorway nine minutes and does not look at the child once and says that looking at one of them is a thing he does not do twice in a day, and then says the thing about people who are not told anything. End: a child of nine out through the road gate with nine bundles behind it and a hut that said nothing, and a man of thirty-two at the end of the lane who did not go with it and did not ask it anything, the seventh time in thirty-three days a person in this city has been in front of him and not been asked anything by anybody.

**Ch 233 · the thirty-fifth day, the fourth hour, the fifth hour, the sixth hour and the seventh hour, the same room, a glass yard and nine hundred feet of paving · something comes back, and the reason he may not help, in nineteen words.** **A strip of paper about a foot long comes back into a city of about nine thousand people inside a bale of cord and reed with the cord neither cut nor retied, and a man of about fifty-five in a hut let it through three bars without the four words, and the four words are for bundles and this was a bundle.** The mark in the corner is a line and a bar and a figure, and it is the same shape and the same size and nobody in that room put it there, **and four people looked at it for about four minutes and not one of them said anything and a woman of twenty-eight put her hand flat on the bench two inches from it and did not touch it.** Nobody in the room can say what it is, and that is not concealment: it is that all four have been asked and have no answer, and a man of sixty-one has been asked the same question four times in nineteen years and has said no four times. A woman with a pail says nine words and goes to work. The work goes on around it: a woman folds, a man of fifty with a waggon counts cord and stops counting twice, a boy of fourteen looks at four people over a piece of paper and does not ask. **The man with the waggon says the one thing anybody said in that room in four minutes: I have been to four of them in nineteen years and I have never been asked how and I am not going to say, and I have never put two of them together in one sentence and I am not going to now, and that is not modesty, that is the only way a man keeps a thing he has not been asked about.** The man of thirty-two asks to hold it and is told no in one word, waits a minute and a half with his hand out, asks what it is called, is told in nineteen words that the fifth answer will be wrong, and is answered by a man of thirty-four with lime from a door about the word for the light being a plain one. **A man of sixty-six comes down the lane unasked and says the finding in about nineteen words, to the room and not to the stranger: you are the only person in this city that is in a book somewhere else, build this with you in it and two places have got a join in them, and a join with a person in it is a column, and a column can be filled in without asking anybody.** A man of thirty-two does not answer it, because a man of fifty-two told him seven days ago that he is the same as a piece of paper, and says eleven words that were not a question: **I am not asking to build it, I am asking whether a strip can be a road, and I know the answer to that from a bench in a hall four hundred miles off, and I did not need this room to find it out.** A man of sixty-six says then you did not need to be in it. **Nobody touches the strip for an hour and a half and a man of fifty with a waggon has had two marks in the corner of strips in his own cart nine years apart and has never been told why and has never asked and would like it noticed that he has never asked, because a man who asks that in this city is a man who has started asking.** End: the strip on the shelf with the nine bundles and not counted, and a duckboard put down on stone for a stranger for the twelfth day without a word.

**Ch 234 · the thirty-seventh day, the second hour, the fourth hour, the fifth hour and the seventh hour, a bridge with three bars, a bindle yard, a room at the top of a lane · a second person with a satchel, and a word nobody in that city has.** **He is turned round in four words for carrying a sheet of paper in his hand and works out in about two minutes that the three bars are for bundles and not for men, and cords the sheet into a bale with about four turns and says one word, and the word is *cord*, and a man of sixty-six says it at the other end of the same lane in the tone of a man saying a price, and the two of them have never seen each other.** The walk up the rise is two hours and he takes the satchel off his shoulder a hundred yards from the top and puts it back on. **The object column has a place name in it that a man of sixty-six put there on the twenty-third day, and it has a word in front of the place name, and nobody in that yard asks what it means and about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand people have not asked either and the not asking is four hundred years old and is not a decision anybody took.** The word is *eastern*. **A man of thirty-two with a limp read it and did not say it out loud and did not say what it meant and did not say where he had read it before, which is in a sheet of good paper in a bag in the ordinary post in a county four hundred miles off and in a copy on a shelf in that county, and the word is now in four places and nobody in any of them has joined any two of them.** A man of about thirty-one says the first thing anybody in that yard has said in four hundred years about a word on a printed sheet, in nineteen words, and then the other half: **there are two of us now who have carried a sheet out of this city and only one of us has seen this word and neither of us is going to say what it is, and I do not know what is in the four places and I have carried about two thousand of them in six years and I have never once known and never once asked, and the list is what I am paid for.** A woman of twenty-eight stops at the mouth of the yard, looks at the sheet, does not go in, and goes on to the gate: **a piece of printed paper in a yard is a question, and she had been asked one already that morning at a gate.** A man of thirty-four with lime walks past the sheet without looking twice. A boy of fourteen, in nine words: **it wants people and it will not say people.** A woman with a pail, in nine words: **somebody has filled that in and it is not the one who printed it.** End: the sheet taken away blank, a woman of sixty reading the word in a long room and not asking what it meant and a clerk of forty entering two lines on the strength of it, and a man of thirty-two walking nine hundred feet of paving.

**Ch 235 · the thirty-eighth day, the second hour, the fourth hour, the fifth hour and the sixth hour, a room at the top of a lane, a shut yard, a glass yard and a yard past two gates · a figure of persons, a drawer, and a second answer nobody said out loud.** A man of about thirty-one puts the sheet on the long table and the door does not ask his name. **A woman of sixty does not look up and a clerk of forty enters two lines and does not read them back, on the strength of an omission, for the fifth time in nineteen years, and she says one sentence of about eleven words: take it down the lane, it goes to the man who makes the paper, and that is the whole of what this room does and you have now been told it twice and you did not have to be told it once.** The yard is shut, and a man of sixty-six does not shut that yard, and nobody can say where he is on the day it is shut. The man of about thirty-one comes back and says what the four places want, in one breath, standing up: **a number of people, on every sheet of that series in four towns, and nowhere on any of them to write a man's name, and the both of the two instruments I have carried are the same instrument.** **A number of people is the one thing this city has never put on a piece of paper, and a man of sixty-six said on the sixth day of this count that a figure of persons is the only kind of paper that cannot be refused and that this one has to be refusable or it is a lie with a stamp on it.** Nobody in this city has been told what the object is, and the man of thirty-one says then it is a count of nobody, and that he has never carried a sentence in one of the four places, and that an office with a column for a sentence is a different kind of office. **The only figure of persons this city can put on paper is one already written down, and that is the list of the third shift in a drawer with a man of fifty-two's name on it, and nobody in that yard said it out loud and the man of thirty-two worked it out standing at a yard's mouth for eleven minutes and has not written it down.** **And there is a second answer and nobody said it out loud: to put a number of persons against that object somebody must put a name to the object, and one man in this city can do that with a hand, and he was standing at the mouth of a yard with a stick, and the second answer was in that room for about an hour and nobody in the room knew it was in the room.** He asks a man of sixty-one at a bench in about eleven words whether there is anything in this city that a number of people could be written against, and is told no after about four minutes, with the reason that he was not asked what for and was not asked, and that a man who is about to tell him is a man who has already decided. End: a man of thirty-one out through the road gate with a blank sheet, not turned round this time, and a man of fifty-five in a hut who has never written down which of the two was which.

**Ch 236 · the thirty-ninth day, the fourth hour, the sixth hour, the seventh hour and the ninth hour, a bindle yard · nine words where four hundred are eleven, and a ninth line under a board.** **He does it in four minutes and this is the first time in thirty-nine days a man in this city has done a thing in front of a stranger on purpose, and a man of thirty-four with lime has said out loud that a man doing a thing on purpose for a man with a stick is not showing off and is getting it right.** The paper is the thinnest in the city, about a foot long, ruled in five lines, the four not for a person and the fifth empty when it is finished, and the fourth of the five is the same width as the fourth of the five on the one he made for a man with a stick on the ninth day of this count, nine inches apart on two benches in two yards. He turns the paper round and puts it face down rather than holding it out, and has held one out exactly once in twenty years. **The refusal is nine words: we do not count what we will not name.** *That is nine words.* **And about four hundred of the eleven-word things are not eleven, and he said on the sixth day of this count that every one of them is eleven and not one of them is twelve, and he was wrong by a number and had been wrong by it for twenty years, and he found it out on the thirty-eighth day while he was not doing anything and is not going to lengthen a no to make it match a shelf.** **And then the second thing of the day, said while ruling the second form, in about eleven words, and it is the first of his that is about himself: I have been asked nine times in nineteen years and I have said no nine times in the same words, and I have wanted somebody to come back and ask me a different question for about eleven years and nobody ever has, and I am not complaining and I am not going to be.** The book is turned round, and the ruled space at the top of the page is the right size and the wrong shape, and **he does not write in it.** He turns a page and writes a line, **and it is the ninth line in a book that has had eight since before he came into it, and the count in it went up for the first time in a count of days anybody in this city is keeping.** *That is the ninth line in this book and it is not the ninth thing this city has said no to, and those are two figures and I am not going to put them in one sentence, and neither of them is how many of us there are.* And to the man of thirty-one: **no, the book says nine and my head says eleven and I have had both since the twenty-ninth day and I have not added them and I am not going to, and a refusal count is a count of things this city has refused and not a count of people.** **The four places on the sheet go out empty, and that is the first time a sheet of that series has gone back out of this city with nothing in the four places in a count of days any man here is keeping.** End: a child of nine out through the road gate, and a man of about thirty-one going up a rise carrying three figures and none of them.

**Ch 237 · the fortieth day, the second hour, the fifth hour, the sixth hour, the seventh hour and the ninth hour, a room at the top of a lane, a glass yard, a gate and nine hundred feet of paving · the power he already has, declined, and a road offered on terms with nothing in them.** **About two hundred and forty pieces of paper are on a long table, laid out in twelves, and they are the second half of the fourth sheet of a printed series cut along the fold in five cuts on the same whalebone, and a man of thirty-two with a limp counts them twice and gets two hundred and forty both times and does not say the number out loud and nobody asks him for it.** Nine hundred seconds is the longest silence in that room with a stranger in it and it is the same nine hundred seconds as the nineteenth day in a yard, and there are two of them and neither was about a person. **His left hand is warm at the fourth hour and he had been going to do a thing and did not do it, and it is the same thing he did on the twenty-seventh day with a hand on a wall, and it is the same hand and the same warmth, and nobody in the city saw him not do it.** A woman of sixty tells him the fifth time he comes up she will have said nothing at all, and then on the fifth time she says two things and a clerk of forty enters two lines and the ink pot is open for the fourth time in nineteen years, and the reason the pot was open is nine lines in a yard four hundred yards off and nobody in that room will ever be told. **A man of thirty-four with lime stands at the bottom of that lane for twenty minutes and does not go up it.** A man of sixty-six and a man of sixty-one stand in one room for the first time in nineteen years with both books, and both books have a fold in them in the same place four inches from the bottom and neither man has ever said so. **The man of sixty-six, in nineteen words: this city is going to have a mark in nine hands and a way of telling another place it is there, and there is exactly one person walking out of this valley who is in a book four hundred miles off, and we are not going to put him in the middle of it.** **And the man of sixty-one, in nineteen words and once: a road is a line and two hands and a day and a witness at each end who is not the man keeping it, and I have had four hundred years of a second column to look at and I have never once seen one of the eleven written in a hand, and I am not going to be the first and I am not going to let a man of thirty-two be one either.** **The offer, standing up, in nineteen words: a road, four days in seven, a bundle, no name, no figure, no hand, no wage, no clerk, and a witness at each end who is not you.** And the other half of it, and it is a document and not a speech: **it goes in a book under a board, it is not going anywhere, you are not going to take it, and there is no reason there should be a second kind.** A man of about thirty-one is turned round at the road gate on the last day of a round in about six years. A man of thirty-four with lime says a man who has been offered a thing by two people in a room is not in a position to write about it for about a day. The one System panel in the block. End: the four sheets in his coat, the ninth hour of the fortieth day as the last hour of a count of days this city keeps, and two books about four inches apart in two different books with a fold in each that have not been compared.

**Ch 238 · the fortieth day at the ninth hour in a city of about nine thousand people, and the eighth of Hearthmonth, YR 315, a Saturday, a market morning, at first light, in a town of about four thousand people · a hand flat on a kerb, a witness, and no line.** **It had not gone out on the thirty-first, the thirty-second or the thirty-third, and it had gone out on the thirty-fourth, the thirty-sixth and the thirty-eighth, and it came down the lane at the ninth hour of the fortieth and put its bundle on the kerb and looked at a man of thirty-two with a limp for about as long as it takes to count nine and then at his left hand, and he did not put it behind him and did not open it.** **And it put its own left hand flat on the kerb, at about the middle of it, on the cold stone, in the way anybody puts a hand flat on a thing to see whether it is warm, and the stone was cold on the other side of its hand too, and about a minute and a half later a man of thirty-two with a limp felt everything about a thing he has been building for four years stop being something he was holding.** **He was eleven feet off and did not move and did not put his hand anywhere and does not know what the eleven feet was for and neither does the child.** It did not say anything, nobody said anything to it, it did not go out through a gate, and it went down the lane. **A man of about forty at a winch stopped winding for the length of that minute and a half and did not look round and has not been asked and would not answer if he were.** The hour before that was an ordinary hour: eleven hods, a piece of bread, four hundred yards of lane twice, a market, a man of thirty at a corner of it, a ladder on a four-hundred-year-old wall, and a hut with three bars. **Four hundred miles off, at first light on a market morning, four people are standing at a crossing with no glass in its sill and they were not asked to be there and they are the four who would have gone out and not the four who would have been sent, and it is the second time in a year the same four have stood there.** **A man of thirty-two with a limp is at the low end of the sill and cannot get up the bank, and there is no line in the coping on either side of that sill and nothing on it and it was nothing before and it is nothing after, and a man of thirty-four with lime said so once about nine inches of lime in a stone course four hundred yards up the road and was not asked about it again.** The man of forty-seven says the four things and says them again, and then says the third thing he has said on a bridge in a year: **there was no line in this, I am the witness at this end and I have not been asked to be and I am not a road warden, and I am going to have the whole of that said in whatever anybody writes down, and there is going to be nothing in it.** He wants the hour said and says it twice and the second one louder, and there were two hours. A man of about nineteen holds a hod for an hour because a boy of fifteen told him to. A bench-board has a bill on it and the boy is not at it. End: **a man of thirty-two with a limp gets up the bank in about nine steps instead of one, and none of the four said a word about it, and one of the four is a man of forty-seven who is paid fourpence a week and has never once in about a year said a word to that man about how he gets up a bank, and he was asked about it once by a carter of thirty and he said the same four things.**

**Ch 239 · the eighth of Hearthmonth, YR 315, a market morning, and seven days in Weir Street, in a town of about four thousand people · the fever, and whose hands held the tools, and nobody asking about the morning.** **A carter of thirty gets him up the bank with a barrow and does not have to lift him, because he got on it himself and was not asked, and they do not say one word to each other on the way, and that is the only thing either of them has said about it.** The fever is a week and it is Stage 3's and it is earned by the stage. **A boy of fifteen held the tools for seven days, and the word tools was used once, by a man of forty-seven, in the tone of a man saying a price, and has not been used again in that county.** The ferrier's stick, ash, four feet nine, cut out of a fence rail in a county not on any map, for four hundred yards of road and nothing else, set in a corner where a man lying on his back could reach it, without a word, and not once put anywhere else. **A notebook with four pages filled in four years, one of them with no hour and no name in it, held for seven days and not opened, and given back flat and in the right order with the first leaf turned to the first page, and the right order is a thing a person can only get right by not having opened it.** Four sheets with four empty places and a place name and a word in the object column and no name on them, in a coat on a chair, and the coat put on the top shelf on the second day because there is a boy of fifteen in that house. **The tax: on the fourth day he is given a cup and asks a woman of about sixty what it is for, and about nine minutes later asks her again, and she answers both times in the same words and does not say the same words the second time and said it slower.** On the fifth day the stick is handed to him and taken back about a minute later because he could not hold it. The leg is the same leg and is not worse. **A man of forty-seven said the four things on the third day and did not ask what was in the four sheets, and a witness is not a man who asks, and he has been asked twice that week why he does not ask and says the same four things both times.** **Nobody asked him about the morning. A woman of about thirty with a pail walked two hundred yards to talk about a thing at a door and did not ask one question about the man in the next room. A man of fifty with a waggon came up Weir Street once with a barrow of salt and did not knock.** A boy of fifteen copied the four things onto the back of a bill he is not going to be given. End: **a market four hundred yards long and open, the salt coming over the first bay, the fourth bay being pointed, a bell with forty-one rivets rung by a boy and a carpenter, and a yard on Weir Street with about nine men in it and one of the nine who has not once said his brother's name and nobody on that yard has asked him why, and that is a cost and it is not a thing anybody in that yard has said out loud.**

**Ch 240 · the seventeenth day of Hearthmonth, YR 315, the sixth hour, a reach, Weir Street and a press · the reason written down and not the figure, and a strip still on a shelf.** **He got up on the ninth day, which is the seventeenth, and a woman of about sixty who has kept two rooms over a weigh-house for nineteen years has said that a house that works does not count its own days, and a carter of thirty did not ask her what she meant.** **The two unreconciled numbers are still on a page in the notebook and he has not written a figure on it, and he has got to them five times without writing a figure and has now been away long enough that getting to it a sixth time would be about a different thing.** The notebook comes out and there are eleven lines on the page above it with no words in them and the eleventh of them is a man of fifty-two on a shift nineteen years old, **and he could not stop seeing it in a city of about nine thousand people and he cannot stop seeing it in a town of about four thousand.** **He wrote one line, in about four minutes, in his own hand, the fourth page he has filled in in four years, and it is about a frame and not about a figure, and there is no figure on it and there is not going to be one: a city that keeps one hour standing has a frame that does not run away from this one, and that is a claim about the length of the interval and not about the length of the warning, and the length of the interval is a conversion somebody made and I cannot check it, and the claim is either the whole of what happened to me or it is nothing and there is no way at all to tell from here which.** **A warning in a file in a county two hundred miles off was printed in an office's hand two years ago and has said three weeks every week since and has not changed, and he has not got a copy of it and has never had one, and a man who has been away for a count of days he cannot name came home and wrote down why and not how much.** A man of forty-seven came to Weir Street and stood in a kitchen for half an hour and said the four things and did not ask one question, and a woman of about sixty has said that a man who does not ask is either the most careful man in a county or the only one in it who has nothing to ask. **The seventh line has said *a person* since a lane four hundred miles off and he took the page out on the eighteenth day and did not finish it, and that is the fourth time he has looked at that line and the fourth time he has not finished it.** The four words are still ready and have been ready for a count of days he could give in one number and could not. **The eleven lines are still eleven lines and there is no column in four hundred years of anybody's book for what became of a woman and a boy, and he did not ask, and the not asking took four seconds, and he has not asked anybody anything about it since.** A man of thirty-four with lime is not on the reach and has not been for a year. **The four sheets of paper went into a press on Weir Street on the nineteenth day and a boy of fifteen at the bench-board did not ask what was in them, and a man of forty-seven has never been in that room and has never been asked to be.** A bench of nine has not been asked anything since the crossing out and a clerk of about sixty entered nothing about a fever. End: **nine hundred feet of paving and a quay and about two hundred and forty strips of paper are four hundred miles off in a city of about nine thousand people, and one strip of the nine on a shelf in a room off a lane has a mark in the corner of it that nobody in that city put there and has not been looked at since the seventh hour of the thirty-fifth day, and a man of about thirty-one is about four days off a town two hundred miles off with a sheet that has four empty places in it and a word in the object column, and about four hundred doors on his list and about four hundred doors on another list in this county are the same four hundred doors and nobody has ever worked out how many, and a man of thirty-two with a limp put a notebook in a coat and did not look at the first six lines of the page, and nobody in that county has ever seen a mark in a child's hand, and one is about four hundred miles off on a shelf with nine bundles of cord and reed on it, and it is still there.**

**The ten endings, because the Volume 04 close's item 1 asks for the list and Batch 0005 should not re-derive it.** **231** on a man of sixty-one going back down a slope and nine bundles corded onto a shelf and a count in a book under a board that did not move. **232** on a child of nine out through the road gate with nine bundles behind it and a man of thirty-two at the end of the lane who did not go with it, and did not ask it anything, the seventh time in thirty-three days. **233** on a strip of paper on a shelf with nine bundles, not counted, and a duckboard put down on stone for a stranger for the twelfth day without a word. **234** on a printed sheet taken away blank up a rise, a woman of sixty who read a word off it and did not ask what it meant, and two lines in a book that nobody will ever say what they were for. **235** on a man of thirty-one out through the road gate with a blank sheet and not turned round this time, and a man of fifty-five in a hut who has never written down which of the two was which. **236** on a child of nine out through the road gate and a man of about thirty-one going up a rise carrying three figures and none of them. **237** on the fourth sheets in a coat, the ninth hour of the fortieth day as the last hour of a count of days this city keeps, and two books about four inches apart with a fold in each that have never been compared. **238** on nine steps instead of one up a bank, and four people who said nothing, and a man of forty-seven who said the same four things. **239** on a yard of nine men and one of them who has not once said his brother's name, and nobody on that yard has asked him why. **240** on a mark in a child's hand on a shelf in a room off a lane four hundred miles off that nobody in that county has ever seen, and a sheet going down a road with four empty places in it, and it is still there. **Nine of the ten are not a refusal; the one that is, 234, is a word on a printed sheet that nobody in the city asks about, and the refusal in this block that is a person is in 236 and it is a man of sixty-six refusing a form he made himself, and the power he declines is in 237 and it is a hand he does not put on a kerb, and the man of thirty-two with a limp, who has a question ready for more days than he has a count of, asked nothing on any of the ten days.**

**Ch 241 · the twenty-fourth day of Hearthmonth, YR 315, a Monday, the second, sixth and seventh hours, a room with a stove in it in a provincial town two hundred miles off · a tray that is not a file, a word the office printed itself, and four places with nothing in them.** **A tray is not a file and that is the reason four sheets of the office's own printed series have lain by that stove since the sixth of Embermonth in the year before: a man of about sixty has carried it out into a passage at the seventh hour of the evening and back at the first hour of the morning for twenty-two years and has never once looked at what is in it and has never been asked to.** The sheets are ruled in six columns, five with heads and a sixth with no head at all and the same width, and about four of the six are ruled for a figure, and nothing is filled in on any of the five that have heads. The heads are *Object*, *Date*, *Person having knowledge*, *Keeper*, and *How often*, the fifth has been the same head for two years, and about four people in that building have said a head cannot be changed without a decision and that no room in it has ever taken a decision in writing. **The sixth column has no head on it and is not a column and is not entered and is not kept, and a woman of about thirty-three who fills in that *Keeper* column about two hundred times a season said so out loud on the fourth of Embermonth in the year before, in a room, to a man who had brought a jar, and said it as a fact and not as a complaint.** A fifth thing comes in the ordinary post at the second hour: **the object column has a place name in it and there is a word in front of the place name, and the word is *eastern*, and the word is one the office printed, and the type for it has been in a drawer in that press room since the form was made two years ago and is set in the line with the heads of the five columns and is not used in any of them and nobody has ever struck it.** A woman of about twenty-nine, a clerk of the returns, read it twice and wrote two lines on a leaf of her own hand and did not read them back. A man of about fifty, a clerk of the press with about eleven thousand forms entered in thirty-one years, says three things and goes back to the press. **And it goes into the tray, because a return goes into the returns press, and a return is ruled for a figure, and a thing that is not a return is not a return.** End: **five things in a tray, four of them there five months, a man of sixty-one with a satchel and a small hammer he has never used who can find a thing in that building in about four minutes and who has not said one word about a tray in eighteen months and has not been asked.**

**Ch 242 · the twenty-sixth day of Hearthmonth, YR 315, a Wednesday, a month end, the second hour, the same room and a press room · the discovery, in a file, with nothing on the wrapper.** A month end is the only reason anything in that building ever gets read. **A man of about fifty had a tray out on the bench at the second hour with five things in it and did four of them in about nine minutes and read the four oldest, and he read the ones that had been in the tray longest, and a woman of about twenty-nine asked him why once in about nine years and he said that a thing that has been in a tray five months is a thing somebody has decided not to look at.** On the sixth line of each of the four, the line with no head on it, there is writing: **a county, a name that is not a market town, a number, and a line of words saying a body may be sued and may sue, and that it has a door, and that the door is on a lane, and four dates five months apart in one fair hand.** He does not enter it, because a line with no head is not a column and he has entered about eleven thousand of these forms in thirty-one years and has never entered one of those lines. **He put the four in a file. He wrote nothing on the wrapper.** Then a table out of a press, opened for the first time since the year it was made: **the name in the object column is not on it, and the county on the sixth line is on it, and a district is a set of market towns and a market town is a place where a thing is bought and sold.** He says it out loud twice and the second time to nobody. **And there were three sheets in that room from one place and two of them had a figure in them and one had nothing and the two with figures were in a pile together, and he looked at the two figures for about a minute and did not add them and did not ask why they were different, and he said it in nine words: two figures out of one place, I am not going to add them and I am not going to ask.** A woman of about twenty-nine says a return comes round twice and the newer of the two is the one that goes on and that a rule and not a judgement is the only kind of thing this office has ever had. **And nobody in that room multiplied the four either, and a figure repeated four times on a printed sheet is a figure entered four times because somebody was asked four times, and nobody in this kingdom has ever printed the total of them anything.** A man of about fifty says, in about nine words, the only sentence anybody in that building has said in about nine years about what a county is: **a county answers.** He stops in the middle of it and about two of them have worked out what the half after the stop is and neither has said so. End: **a tray going out into a passage with four things in it, and a fifth thing in a file on a shelf with the working papers, and nobody told what is in the file.**

**Ch 243 · the second day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Tuesday, the fourth, sixth and seventh hours, a lane off Weir Street, a room over a weigh-house, a door on that lane · a keeper of records, four questions that are not findings, a man at a door who does not knock, and a tenth letter that is not opened.** The copying season in that county is Hearthmonth and it is over by nine days and two women are still copying. **The office is fourpence a year, on a lease in a tradesman's hand, and the two rooms over the weigh-house are two shillings a month each and are the salt merchant's and not the office's, and those are two prices of two different things in two books in two different counties and nobody in this county has ever filed either.** The deed is thirteen words and says *for the keeping of what this county cannot be shown it has lost*, and a woman of twenty-nine has read it out loud to about four people in four years and a half and it has not improved in the telling. **A man of sixty-one comes down four hundred yards of lane and stands at her door for about forty minutes and does not knock, which is the fourth time in two years, and says nineteen words to the door and the door was shut the whole of the time: I have been in a building two hundred miles off eighteen months and I can find a thing in it in about four minutes, and there is a thing in it about a place that is yours, and it is in a file, and a file is a thing somebody has decided about, and I am not able to tell you what is in it and I am not going to try.** She saw him from the window and did not go down. **What he had come about, and did not say and could not have said if he had been asked, is four entries in a register that nobody can be served with, all four in her own hand, all four beginning with a district name, and all four entered as a question and none as a finding, and a keeper of records who enters a thing she means to do has made a plan and a keeper of records who enters a question has not.** She has not told the second copyist, who asked her once, about three months back, whether there was anything in the register she wanted, and was told no. **A fair copy and a working lie about four inches apart on a bench, and a body corporate can be sued and cannot be reached, and those are not the same and everybody who has worked in that room knows it.** A man of about nineteen comes down the lane to see what a man is doing at a door and does not ask, and he has an elder sister of twenty-two. **A letter has not been opened, and it is the tenth of a kind, and the day it is opened is the day this office is a body corporate that goes through a county's post, and the woman who said it has not said it twice.** End: **the reach open two hundred yards off with forty men on it and the salt over the first bay and a joint a foot and a half short that nobody measured, and a man of thirty-one two hundred miles away with about four hundred places on a list behind him, and about four hundred people in this town not knowing that a man of sixty-one had stood at a door for forty minutes and had said nineteen words to a shut door.**

**Ch 244 · the fourth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, the second, fourth and seventh hours, the same room · the figure, the district, and a woman who has been afraid of a column for eleven years.** **A return that is not one of the ordinary nine is a return that has been written on by a room and not by a press, and there are about eleven of those in about nine years and nobody has ever written a rule about them.** The object column has a name in it that this office made up about a hundred years ago and has never sent a form to, and a county beside it that is in a table in a press in the same building, and **the district is on the sheet because a sheet came in with it on.** **And in the second of the four places ruled for a figure there is a figure, and it is a figure of persons in respect of a district, and it is the figure this office has been keeping in a column with a head of its own since the year after the Sundering, and nobody in that room connected it to anything.** The number of persons the office would not print on an offer was asked for of a county in a return twice, about two years ago and again since, and it did not come, **and an office that will not print a number of persons cannot show that any person has not been instructed.** **A woman of thirty-three fills the second of four places in about a minute and a quarter, does not look up, and reads it back afterwards, and the reading is slower and not better.** She says one thing in nineteen words, and it is the only thing she has said in eleven years that was not about a column: **a figure of persons in a column is the only kind of paper in this kingdom that cannot be refused, and I have been afraid of this column since I was twenty-two, and I would like it noticed that I said it and that the figure went out anyway and that noticing it is what I have instead of stopping it.** And four or five words, which are the whole of what she wants: **nobody enters a family by a name nobody entered.** Nobody agrees with her and nobody refuses her, **and the not agreeing and the not refusing is the office entire and it has never once had to decide anything because a thing left the building anyway.** A man of about fifty says in nine words that there is no column in that form for a name and that changing the head is not hers to do. **Her note of nineteen words is face down in a book on the second shelf and has not been turned over in about five months, and a man who entered about eleven thousand forms in thirty-one years has walked past that shelf about four times a day for five months and has not once put his hand out to it.** **A hearing in that province for a day in Rainmonth for a delegation that cannot arrive, heard with nobody in it, still stands, is not adjourned and is not refused, and has now a file of one sheet opened beside it and not against it, and the district in that file is the district the return went out against.** End: **the bag goes out on the ordinary post, and this office is careful about what it prints and not careful about what it sends.**

**Ch 245 · the sixth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Saturday and a market day, the second to the seventh hours, the long room over the wharf · a special sitting, the bench's eighth thing, eleven words, and a reason entered twice.** A bench of nine sits on Saturdays, and a Saturday sitting begins about the seventh hour because the market is on from the second until about the sixth, and **a thing that is refused in a room is refused in a room and a thing that is refused on a market morning is refused in front of the people who live here, and this bench has never once been asked anything on a day that is not a market day and that is not procedure. And it sat on that Saturday as a special sitting, which is a thing it has done once in the nineteen years of that minute, and a special sitting is called by a person and the minute says which one and says what for: the reeve of this town called it at about the second hour on a sheet of a printed series addressed to a district of about nine market towns, and the line is at the top of the minute above the asking, and it names no person, and the clerk of about sixty read that line out first and read the asking second.** A reeve of this town carried a sheet of a printed series up two flights in nineteen words of her own and put it on the table, and the object column has a name in it that is not the name of this county and a district name and four empty places. **A market town is not a district and never has been**, in eleven words, and nobody argued with it for about nine seconds, and it is the third eleven-word thing that has decided anything in that hall. **The reason went in twice, and the reeve said the reason out loud first, and she asked for it twice because a bench that says no for money has refused a thing it could not afford and a bench that says no for anything else has refused a thing it does not want, and this county has never in the whole time of the bench got the first, and she is not going to let it put the second down in a book under a stair and have it read in a generation as the first.** And she asked for the count, and the count is on the page: **five askings for the crossing four hundred yards up this town's own road, a fifth of them brought up two flights and not put, a sixth in a Harvestmonth with a figure of forty marks on a page, a seventh on the thirtieth of Fallowmonth with the word consent in it four times, and now this. Five and one and one and one is eight things asked of this bench in nineteen years**, and in about forty years somebody is going to come up that stair wanting to know what this county thinks about roads and there is going to be one line in that book that answers it. **The clerk entered the reason twice and entered no names, and that is the first time in nineteen years a refusal in that minute has gone in with no name of any kind against it, and he did not enter that a man of forty-seven did not vote, which is the same thing a clerk does when he does not rule a line across an empty space.** A man of forty-seven says eleven words to the sheet and not to the room: **I have been the witness at two ends of two crossings in a year and I am not a road warden, and I have said that in this room before, and I am not going to be asked about a district either.** And the reeve, on the way out, in nineteen words: **I have said the wrong thing first for nine years and the wrong thing is the only thing that has ever got anybody to look at the right one, and if this county is on a sheet in a provincial town then this county is on it as a set of market towns, and a set of market towns is a thing you can count, and I am not going to sit here and be counted.** End: **a sheet with four empty places and a district on it going down to a press on a table in a room over a wharf, not answered, and the two marks in the chest under the window have not moved since the ninth of Fallowmonth in the year before last, and a bench of nine has been asked eight things and has said no to three of them for reasons and yes to four and has never once been asked to be a witness.**

**Ch 246 · the eighteenth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, the second, fourth and sixth hours, a room over a weigh-house with a door on a lane · the count refused, a money column footed in pence, and a fifth entry that is a question and not a finding.** The copying season ended eighteen days ago and two women are still copying, and a county that stops copying when the season ends is a county that thinks the work was the season. **The money is footed on the sill of the table before anybody says a total, and the addition is done by the woman who owns the room and not by him:** a sheet copied at a penny, a second sheet for the same person at a penny, a bundle of waxed thread at twopence. **One and one is two, and two and two is four pence, and nobody said four.** **And the two nights this office was open at the ninth hour in the season are not a column and are not added for anybody, and the reason given is that an office that works does not count its own hours.** **And the two prices of the same thing are never added: the office is fourpence a year and the two rooms are two shillings a month each and are the salt merchant's, both on a lease in the same hand on the same sheet, and she takes the addition as far as the two rooms at forty-eight pence and stops there and does not add the office's fourpence to it, and the reason is that one of the two is a price for the right to keep what a county cannot be shown it has lost and the other is a price for a floor that takes a tide up through it in a wet week. **The page as first written ran that paragraph to thirty pence and then said she did not add them, and the review repair pass made the line foot and made the not-adding true of the sentence that says it; see continuity item 641.**** A sheet of the office's series came into that room in the ordinary post in the spring with a word and a name and a district and four empty places in it, and a second sheet of the same series came to the same room on the sixth of that month and went up two flights to a bench of nine and was refused in eleven words and is in a press in a room over a wharf, and the two have been in a drawer together since the seventh and nobody has taken either out and looked at the other. **A reeve of this town comes up two flights for the sixth time in nineteen years with nothing in her hands and asks whether the county can give that office a number of its people, and is told no in about nineteen words: no, there is no column in this office for a number of people and there never has been.** And then the other half, longer, said once, including **a number of people in a column is the one kind of paper in this kingdom that cannot be refused, and I have a door on a lane and four years and a half of a body corporate that can be sued, and I have never once worked out what a county is supposed to do with a paper like that.** **The fifth entry goes into a register in her own hand at the sixth hour, under the rule, in about four minutes, and all five entries begin with a district name and all five are entered as a question and none as a finding, and a keeper of records who enters a thing she means to do has made a plan.** She wants somebody to write down the day the register becomes a roll and nobody writes it down because it is not the second copyist's column. **And he is given the register to look at and about nine minutes later cannot remember whether the fifth entry says question or finding, and the difference between the two is the whole of that room, and he does not ask her to read it again, and he puts the register down four inches from a sheet with four holes in it and neither of them has met the other one.** End: **a count refused, five questions in a book, nine not-askings and no tenth, and a county that is not a number.**

**Ch 247 · the twenty-second day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Monday and not a market day, the second to the fourth hours, the same room · nine sentences said once to somebody who had not asked, a refusal of them, and the reason.** A press with about four hundred documents in it and most of them gone out since Hearthmonth, a fair copy and a working about four inches apart on a bench, and **two presses within four hundred yards of each other, one of which can be produced on the order of a body corporate and one of which belongs to a yard and cannot be served with anything, and nobody in that room has ever put the two of them beside each other, and a second copyist has said out loud that they are the same press with two different heads on.** **He says nine sentences, once, to a woman who had not asked him for one of them, and does not improve on any of them and does not say a tenth.** The first is **I have been treating a refusal as a thing that had not happened yet.** The nine take in the book's nine and the man's eleven, the office's figure of persons on a Thursday, the bench's eleven words about a word, five questions and no number, a page with a seventh line that says a person looked at four times and finished not, and the eighth of the nine is that he did not know a no was a person until he was in a place that had nine of them and every one had been given by somebody who could not be asked a second time. A second copyist counted a silence of four seconds. **And she did not accept it, and the reason is longer than the nine sentences and is not an apology and is not a kindness: that is a finding, a finding has a day against it and a person against it, you have put a person in a column and given the column a head, and the head is a thing you decided about, and you decided it about yourself at a table in a room with a door on a lane without asking anybody whether the room was the right place to put it.** And: **I have five questions in that register and not one of them is a finding, and the reason is that a question can be asked a second time and a finding cannot, and you have handed me a finding about yourself and a date I have never had, and I cannot enter it, and if you had wanted it entered you were in the wrong room and I would have told you so if you had asked me to.** And the last of it: **I am not going to be kind about it, because a kind thing said at that table is the most expensive thing in this building and I have four years and a half of a body corporate that answers to nobody and I am not going to spend one sentence of it on a thing nobody asked me for.** The second copyist says the only other thing said in that room, which is that she has watched two people not say a thing to each other for four months and it is the longest sentence anybody has ever said in it, and that she is not going to be the one who breaks it, and that if either of them wants to break it they will have to do it in a room with no press in it. **Nobody asked him about the morning, he did not offer it, the not askings stand at nine, and the sentence she said in a gateway in another month is standing in the room and is not referred to.** **And then she asks him a question and tells him it is a question and not a finding before he answers it, and it is about about four hundred doors on two lists in two counties, and he has not seen the second list, and nobody added the two figures together.** End: **nine sentences on no page in that office, a notebook with nothing in it, and a man of forty-seven in a kitchen saying the four things for the fourth time in a year and asking nothing.**

**Ch 248 · the twenty-third day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Tuesday and not a market day, the fourth, sixth and seventh hours, a reach and a yard four hundred yards off · a quiet crossing season, a pointing carried into a second day, and eleven minutes at the mouth of a yard.** **It is a quiet season and the quietness is a figure nobody in this county has taken, and there is no column for it:** the reach had thirty men on it through the wet weeks and has forty on it now, the salt has been coming over the first bay since the spring, nine waggons have come up the channel road, the fourth bay is the last of four, and the frost is two months off. Three men stopped coming to work in that yard inside a year and none gave a reason, **and a man of thirty-four with lime has not been on that reach for a year, and four people in that yard have added the three of them up in their own heads and have not said the sum out loud, because a man who counts his yard and then counts it again in a week has made two figures where there was one.** **The joint on the parapet of the fourth bay is a foot and a half short because the man who began it went home at the fourth hour, and he has not come back, nobody has asked him, and nobody in that yard has ever measured it; and a line in the third course about nine inches long under about half an inch of lime has not moved, and nobody measured that either and nobody has said a word about it.** **And the pointing was begun at the sixth hour and was not finished on that day, which is the ordinary condition of a pointing course, and nine men in that yard have said so and not one of the nine has ever said why.** A waggon of stone comes up the channel road, is not for sale, stops at the wharf for an hour and a half and goes back, and **a carter of thirty says that a road open over a bridge brings people up a channel road who have not come up it before, and this county has never voted on it and would not know what to do with a vote, and a bench that votes on a waggon is a bench that has voted on a road.** **A woman of about thirty with a pail says one sentence at a door: a man with a satchel came through this market twice in Hearthmonth and went up the channel road both times, and nobody told her anything, and she is saying it because the asking after a man with a stick has stopped on the nineteenth of that month.** Then, at the sixth hour, he walks four hundred yards up the lane to the mouth of a yard on Weir Street and stands there for eleven minutes and does not go in. **One of the nine is holding a mason's line, and he is twenty-five and he owns the crews and the yard, and he is the one of the nine who has not once said his brother's name, and he says one working sentence to a man with a barrow and not to anybody else: that is a foot out and it will be a foot out on Thursday, and I have said it twice this week and I am not going to say it a third time, and I am not going over there to look at it.** Nobody asked him why. **And a man of thirty-two with a limp worked out in four seconds that he had been expecting not to be asked, noticed the working out nine minutes after he had done it, did not do anything about the nine minutes, did not take the notebook out, and did not write down what it cost.** End: **the fourth bay still a foot and a half short at the seventh hour, the salt on the first bay and the lane, the road open, and a man who has learned not to be asked not writing it down anywhere.**

**Ch 249 · the twenty-fourth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Wednesday and not a market day, the fourth hour and a half and the seventh hour, a crossing four hundred yards up the county's own road and a long room over a wharf · a bell rung by other hands, and a clerk who will not enter an absence.** The crossing is in municipal trust in abeyance since before the bench existed, the tolls are suspended by an instrument a court has found lawful and has said it has nothing further to say about at any time, **and so it has no owner and no money and no seat on that bench and no glass in the sill and no third seat**, and forty yards of tarred hemp went into the abutment on the fourth of Hearthmonth of the year before by four men and a boy and nobody in this county has ever dug for it. **The bell is nine stone of green-black bronze with a band of forty-one rivets and a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, and it is rung by a boy who has been the steward's apprentice for two years and three months and is still not good at it, and by a carpenter who is a hand and not a keeper, and neither of the two is paid by the guild and neither is a member of anything, and a bell rung by a person who is not paid for it and a person who is not a member of it is a bell nobody in this county can be asked about, and that is why it is rung.** **He stands nine feet off the abutment and does not go up and does not put his left hand on the dressed block or on the sill, and a sill with no glass in it is a sill anybody may put a hand on and nobody in this county has ever put a hand on that one.** **And the crossing carries nobody and has for four years, because the thing it is for is a thing that has to be agreed, and a crossing that carries nobody and a bridge four hundred yards the other way that carries everything are four hundred yards apart and a hundred yards from a market, and this county has one of each and has never put the two of them in the same book.** Two waggons of stone go up the channel road and do not stop, and the driver of the second looks at the crossing for about two minutes and says nothing, **and a crossing with no owner and no money has no way whatever of knowing how many went over it in a day, and a man with a satchel keeps a list of doors and not of waggons, and the two figures on the two lists are the same four hundred doors and nobody has worked out how many and nobody has added them.** **And the four times that crossing has been asked about are in a book on a shelf in a room over a wharf that is not a minute, with four names in it, and two of the four are the same man twice, and a clerk of about sixty says in nine words that a name in a subscription is an offer and an offer is not a minute and he has entered no minutes of offers in his life.** Then, at the seventh hour, he goes up two flights to the long room, where the bench is not sitting because a bench of nine sits on Saturdays, and asks in eleven words what the bench has decided about the Old Toll, and is told in about forty words: **nothing, that the four times are a toll and not a road, that the bench has never been asked about the road, and that a clerk who enters an absence is a clerk who has entered a decision, and nobody in that hall has ever taken a decision in writing.** End: **he did not speak, and the clerk entered nothing, and that is the first time in nineteen years a man has come into that room, asked a question about a thing in it, and gone out with nothing entered.**

**Ch 250 · the twenty-fifth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, the second hour, the fourth hour and a half and the seventh hour, a market and a reach, and the volume's last day · a word with no post behind it, a man of nineteen buying a piece of bread, four sheets in a press, a woman with a construction she has not used, and a strip of paper on a shelf.** **About four people in that market worked out, in the ordinary way, that a man of thirty-two with a limp has been in this county for five months and has been called something in four counties, and that the four are four different somethings, one with a carrier in it and one with a road in it, and that he has never once asked what any of the four means; and there is no post of that name in this county and no post of any of the other three where they were used, and a word with no post behind it is a word that can be given to anybody and is a word nobody has to be sorry for afterwards.** A man of about nineteen comes down the lane with an empty hod, buys a piece of bread, and does not stop at anything else, and he has an elder sister of twenty-two in a house two streets off. **A magistrate of this county, the reeve's elder sister, nine years on that bench, who has beaten two counts of persons with a form's own construction and has said nothing about either of them in that room and sat silent on the sixth of that month while a sheet with four empty places in it lay on that table, comes down four hundred yards of lane at the seventh hour.** Then: **four sheets of printed paper in a press in a room on Weir Street with a bench-board in it, in the press since the nineteenth day of Hearthmonth, and a boy of fifteen at the bench-board who did not ask what was in them, and the third refusal in a document in three volumes and the second time the same route has been refused in writing, in the same register and in a different sentence, and the whole of the difference is that the first was asked of him on a sheet in good paper and this one was asked of him in a room by two people.** **It has not been sent to anybody, and a document in a press in a county of four thousand people is the safest kind of document there is, because a county of four thousand people cannot be served with anything and cannot be sued by anybody and has no writ and no seal and no office.** He stands in that room for about four minutes with his hand on the outside of the press and does not open it, and then goes down the lane to a house forty feet from a door on that lane, **and the door was shut and it had been shut all day and he did not knock on it and did not go up the lane.** Then the reach, the salt, the fourth bay, a joint a foot and a half short, a seam that has not moved, and the bell at the fourth hour and a half by a boy and a carpenter. **He stands at the bench-board from the fourth hour and a half to the fifth hour and looks at a bill with a number on it and a rule under the number and a space under the rule, and the space is the widest of the four and the boy of fifteen has copied it, and he does not put a figure in the space and does not write anything at all, and the seventh line on a separate leaf says a person and this is the fifth time he has looked at it and the fifth time he has not finished it, and the four words he has had ready are still ready and he does not say them.** And the last scene: **a magistrate stands four feet off the bench-board for about a minute and says nineteen words to a man with a stick and not to a bench: I have had a construction ready since the second hour. I have had it since I read four empty places in a printed sheet in a room over a wharf on Saturday and I have not used it, and I would like somebody to write down that I did not use it, and there is nobody in this county I can ask.** Nobody asked her, and the construction is still there, and each of the two women who has an instrument of her own has not used it. **And the last image, and it is a thing in a place and not a sentence about a man and not a sentence about a city:** on a shelf eleven feet long in a room off a lane that goes down to a quay, about four hundred miles off, there is a strip of paper about a foot long lying with eight others of its kind, and in the corner of that strip there is a mark that is a line and a bar and a figure, and nobody in that room put it there, and nobody in that room has looked at it since the seventh hour of a morning in the spring, and nobody in this county has ever seen it, and it is a foot long and it is on the shelf and it is there.

**Block 5 note — the block's calendar, its cast discipline, its device counts, and its ten endings, so that a Volume 06 phase does not re-derive any of them.** **Calendar.** Main world throughout, the twenty-fourth day of Hearthmonth, YR 315, a Monday, to the twenty-fifth day of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, which is the volume's last day. **Every weekday printed in the ten chapters was counted from the chain at `outline/volume-05.md` §17 and checked against the day it names, and all ten are correct: Monday, Wednesday, Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, Thursday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and the two markets among them are the fourth and the sixth of Goatmonth and the eighteenth and the twenty-fifth, and the two non-markets among the block's own days are the twenty-second, the twenty-third and the twenty-fourth of Goatmonth.** The city keeps a count of days and no months and no character in this block converts one and no month of that city is spoken or written. **Cast.** **No new names and six slots unfilled, so Volume 05 stands at five names of six and twenty-four of thirty unfilled across the five batches, against the volume's planned five and twenty-four.** The one person the block could have spent a slot on and did not is Sabin Dain, a returned face addressed by age. **Devices, as whole words, with the basis named, and every figure re-counted after the Batch 0005 review repair pass at continuity item 644.** `about` **574**, per chapter **59 / 89 / 94 / 83 / 56 / 42 / 45 / 30 / 41 / 35**, and the column splits into five document chapters at a mean of 76.2 and five scene chapters at a mean of 38.6, and the five scene chapters are every one at or under the Volume 04 whole-volume ceiling of forty-five · `nine` **177**, per chapter 18 / 22 / 13 / 16 / 24 / 22 / 16 / 26 / 11 / 9, 5.80 per 1,000, the lowest of the volume's five blocks, and the reason is on the page · `the whole of` **27** · `cut` **0** · `in nine years` **4**, all four the same fact about a bench and none of them a filler duration · **`about N seconds` 5, basis *about* + a number word + *seconds*, and `about N minutes` 22 on the same basis** · `about nine` plus a lower-case word **46** in the block and every one of them a canon figure · `two` **274** as a whole word · `---` rules **45** · bolded line-openings **107** · semicolons 0 · em-dashes 0 · en-dashes 0 · straight double quotes 0 · curly apostrophes 0 · curly opening single quotes 0 · **no System panel in the block, and the volume's one was spent in Chapter 237** · `Gatehouse` 0,
