Filler as whole words, basis named in both columns: **`nodded` 0, `held` 3, `wrote` 17, `stood` 28, `plain` 1, `counted` 10, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0.** The reporting clause *have said since that* is 63 in the block. **Length 30,312 words in ten chapters**, per chapter 3083 / 2976 / 3045 / 3077 / 3167 / 3414 / 2961 / 3002 / 2802 / 2785, and no chapter is under 2,785. **Every count in this note was footed on the page before it was printed here. The block's three repairs and the eleventh worked example of this project's own process defect are at continuity item 635, and the four sweeps and the weekday check are at item 636, and every one of them was run and no check is reported here that was not run.**

**The ten endings, because the Volume 04 close's item 1 asks for the list and a Volume 06 phase should not re-derive it.** **241** on a tray out into a passage with five things in it, four of them there five months, and a man of sixty-one with a satchel who has not said one word about a tray in eighteen months. **242** on a file on a shelf with the working papers, and a tray going out into a passage with four things in it, and nobody told what is in the file. **243** on a man of sixty-one still on a lane and then not, and nine hundred feet between two places nobody in either has been told about. **244** on a bag going out on the ordinary post, and this office careful about what it prints and not careful about what it sends, and a woman of thirty-three who said four or five words and then wrote a figure. **245** on a sheet with four empty places and a district on it going down to a press in a room over a wharf, not answered, and two marks in a chest that have not moved since the ninth of Fallowmonth in the year before last. **246** on a count refused, five questions in a book, nine not-askings and no tenth, and a county that is not a number. **247** on nine sentences on no page in that office, a notebook with nothing in it, and a man of forty-seven saying the four things for the fourth time in a year and asking nothing. **248** on a fourth bay still a foot and a half short at the seventh hour, the salt on the first bay, the road open, and a man who has learned not to be asked not writing it down anywhere. **249** on a clerk of about sixty who entered nothing, which is the first time in nineteen years a man asked that room a question about a thing in it and went out with nothing entered, and a bell rung by two people who are neither paid for it nor members of it. **250** on a strip of paper about a foot long on a shelf eleven feet long in a room off a lane four hundred miles off, with a mark in the corner of it, and nobody in this county has ever seen it, and it is there. **Three of the ten are refusals, 246, 247 and 249, and that breaks the one-in-ten rhythm of the four blocks behind this one, and the two that are a person refusing a person are 246 and 247, and the one that is a clerk refusing to make an entry out of an absence is 249, and the seven that are not a refusal are a tray, a file, a lane, a bag, a press, a yard's mouth and a shelf.**

**Volume 05 close note — the three Series resolutions, and where each of them is on the page.** **`outline/series.md`'s Volume 5 resolution row has three items and the check is a count and not an impression: three delivered, none of them a gift, a rescue, an improvement or a conversion.** One, **the city remains sovereign and unreachable by the Crown**: Chapters 241 to 244, in a tray, a file, a drawer with unused type in it, a return, a district and a figure, and nowhere else, and the strip on the shelf is the only thing that came back and nobody in that city knows it. Two, **Aren's understanding of consent changes, and the change is a habit and not a belief**: Chapter 247 in her words and Chapter 250 in his not-writing, and it did not make him easier to be around and nobody was improved. Three, **Mara challenges his habit of treating refusal as failure and does not accept his answer**: Chapter 247, in about a hundred and fifty words across three speeches, the last of which is a refusal of kindness. **And the volume's last line is not a sentence about a man and not a sentence about a city, and it is a thing in a place, still there, that nobody in the county has ever seen, and the model is `outline/volumes/volume-03-close.md` §10 item 3 and Volume 03's last line was a road four hundred yards long and it is there.**

## Volume 05 close — page findings, and the four chapters whose meaning the close changed

**The close did not rewrite a single one of the fifty entries above. It changed the meaning of five specific pages and it records them here so that a Volume 06 writer reading the entries for those chapters inherits the close's finding and not the first reading.** The full record is `outline/volumes/volume-05-close.md` §2 and continuity items 646 to 652, and none of the five is repaired, because this phase writes fiction-plan and manuscript-state files only.

1. **Chapter 214 — the entry for 214 describes a sixth day on which the city is asked the first question and does not record that its dateline says the city has been asked nine times in four hundred years when the page's own arithmetic says eight before the ninth on the nineteenth day.** The finding does not touch the scene, the room, the eleven chairs, the reason for eleven, the door that has never asked a man his name, or the two lines a clerk of forty entered and did not read back. **A Volume 06 writer must treat the count as eight on the sixth day and nine from the nineteenth, and must not build anything on the dateline.**
2. **Chapter 226 — the entry for 226 describes a man of sixty-one turning his book round and a fourteenth-year-old line with two marks on it, and does not record that the narration calls him a man of sixty-six eleven lines after setting him as sixty-one.** The finding does not touch the eleven roads, the second column in two parts, the two marks, the absence of a third column, or the absence of any name in four hundred years. **None of that is affected and all of it is the volume's reversal, and the reversal stands.**
3. **Chapters 210 and 214 — the entries for both record a page with a date on it and a word under the date and do not record that the page's age is called thirty-five days and that the carried thirty-day month makes it fifty-four.** The thirty-five is the path figure the man is about to spend inside the city, and Chapter 233 uses it four times for that. **A Volume 06 writer must not use the page's age as a date and must not have any character convert a main-world age into a path interval or the reverse.**
4. **Chapters 231, 232 and 233 — the entries record the message system, the mark, the strip that came back, and the seventy-odd small counts, and do not record that the narration gives his time inside the city as forty days at `231:35`, `231:39`, `232:69` and `233:19` and as thirty-five days four times in the same chapter of `233`.** The finding does not touch the room off the lane, the shelf of eleven feet, the nine carriers, the nine pence, the nineteen words and sixty words in the doorway, the four minutes of looking and the hour and a half of not touching, or the finding about a join with a person in it. **A Volume 06 writer must not use either figure, and the city's count of days from the last renewal is a count and not a figure of weeks and not a figure of months.**
5. **Chapter 204 — the entry records a money column added in pence and footed at forty-two and a not-asking left out, and does not record that the same page carries a real-world month name in a main-world sentence.** The finding is a one-line repair and is the only calendar token of the five. **A Volume 06 writer may not carry the token forward and may not use a real-world month anywhere in this manuscript.**

**And one finding that is about the volume's prose rather than about a chapter's date: the volume names the length of its own speeches with figures that are not the lengths of the speeches, seven times out of eleven, and four instances check out exactly.** The entries above describe the speeches; this is a rule about the numbers attached to them. **A speech-length figure in Volume 06 is either footed or inside a character's mouth as a claim about that character, and the two may not be confused**, and the one place the mismatch is earned is the eleven-word things that are not eleven, which is canon and which Chapter 236 corrects on the page.

**Volume 05 close review repair pass — a page note, and it adds no chapter and changes no entry above.** This is a note about the documents rather than about any of the two hundred and fifty chapters, and it is here because the next batch inherits two of those documents as binding. **Five findings were applied and one was ruled out; the ruling is the one to read.** The review held that `outline/volumes/volume-05-close.md` §2.8 miscounted the age of the page at `210:43` — the fourteenth of Harvestmonth to the eighth of Embermonth — and gave fifty-three days elapsed and fifty-four inclusive against the close's fifty-four and fifty-five. **The close is right.** On the carried thirty-day month and the month order in `bible/terminology.md`, that span is sixteen days to the end of Harvestmonth, one into Fallowmonth, thirty through Fallowmonth, one into Embermonth and seven more, and it is fifty-four elapsed and fifty-five counting both ends. **The thirty-five days the page is called on the page is a path figure and not an error, and the close says so, and that part of the finding was never contested** — the thirty-five is the same number as the thirty-five days he is about to spend in the city, which Chapter 233 uses four times. **The two page defects the close did find in that neighbourhood stand and were not touched:** `210:43` and `214:98` both carry the thirty-five, and they are recorded as the one figure in the volume a reader can check with a finger on a month list.

**The other four repairs touch the Volume 06 plan, not Volume 05's prose.** The year labels in `outline/volume-06.md` are now YR 316 for every date from the turn at day 156 onward, which includes **the hearing at the ninth of Rainmonth, day 284, which was YR 315 on the outline's face and is YR 316 now, and whose day, weekday and block are unchanged.** The hearing's own figure of one hundred and thirty-four days after Volume 05's last day is what forced it: a day 284 that close to day 150 cannot be in the year the volume ended in. Four of five block frames were off by one and are footed. Two of the phase's own files failed the bold-parity sweep and are clean. Mudmonth is thirty days, fixed by the outline's own table before the outline admitted it. And two attributions that would have let a batch name the wrong clerk are separated: Alish Renn's want from Sarn Oyelaran's unsigned warrant, and Perry Hask's Block 4 hand-over from the Block 1 accident that nobody made and nobody was handed. **No chapter of Volume 06 exists and none is described here.**

No chapter beyond 300 exists and none is described below.** The close wrote no chapter summaries, because a close is not a batch and this file is one entry per batch; **what the close established about the fifty chapters is at `state/continuity.md` items 782 to 806 and `state/open-threads.md`'s section *Threads the Volume 06 close carries into Volume 07*, and the fifteen findings it made on the printed page are §2 of the close, one of which — the four rooms and four people, or five — is ruled on there and not here.** **A review pass then re-counted the close's own figures on the page and nine did not reproduce, and it corrected them without touching a chapter; the repair is close §13 and continuity items 807 to 809, and the corrected figures are the *roof* at two, the speech-length sweep at 143 and 29, the uncheckable class at fifteen referents carrying seven distinct figures, the other full-line italics at nineteen, and the weekday token column on a whole-word basis at Saturday 129 to Wednesday 11. ## Batch 0001 — Chapters 251–260, "The Summons"

*Main world, day 150, the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, to day 190, the fifth of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Tuesday and not a market day. Forty days and forty-one inclusive, twelve market days, six Saturdays at 152, 159, 166, 173, 180 and 187, and no bench scene, because the bench sits on Saturdays and no card wanted one and the volume's sitting is the last Saturday of the volume. 25,713 words as first written, **25,990 after two review repair passes, and the figure that governs is the later one.***

**Names spent: two of six, four slots unfilled. Ansel Rudd, 44 and Hester Cray, 38. The marshal is a return and is not named anywhere in the block. No other person is first named in prose. Alish Renn, Sarn Oyelaran, Mara Vey, Aren Kest, Tovan Kest, Lysa Fenn, Bram Ottery, Iven Sarr and the woman of thirty-three at the register are all returns addressed by trade or by age in this block, which is the volume's method and its cost.**

**Ch 251 · the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday, a market day, the second hour and the fourth hour and a half and the sixth hour · Merefen.** The market is on and forty men are on the reach and the bell with forty-one rivets in it went at the fourth hour and a half by a boy and a carpenter. **A summons comes up the lane in the ordinary post and is put on a sill in a room over a weigh-house with a door on that lane, and a woman of twenty-nine reads it standing up.** The sheet is the office's own printed series, six columns, five heads, a sixth with no head, and **the five heads and the form of oath are printed on the back of it, so a person is sworn on the back of a return.** It names a body corporate with a door, a number, the capacity to sue and to be sued, made out of a deed of thirteen words with no officer in it, **and in four years and a half nobody has ever been served at that door because a county of about four thousand people cannot be served with anything and has no writ and no seal.** The sheet asks for the register, the day-book, and a person having knowledge on a day in Rainmonth. **There is a line for the person served and a line for the office and both are ruled for a figure and neither is ruled for a name.** She enters the day, the hour and the door, on the fair copy and not on the working, and **does not enter a name and does not write *no person* either.** Money: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a carrier's hand for four miles twopence, a waggon kept an hour fourpence, **footed to eight pence in front of the second copyist**, and the fourpence a year and the two shillings a month are named and refused in the same paragraph. The two presses four hundred yards apart are set beside each other for the only time in the block. **A second copyist of about thirty says the one thing she has said in six years about a post she does not want** — that the day she opens the eleventh is the day this office is a body corporate that goes through a county's post, and that there is a tenth one here and she has known that for about two years — **and she does not open the tenth one.** **Change:** a body corporate that answers to nobody is now a body corporate that can be served. **Ends:** the lane quiet at the seventh hour, the market gone in, the bell already rung, and a man of forty-seven who was not asked to carry anything saying it out loud in a kitchen once, the following day, and not twice.

**Ch 252 · the twenty-sixth of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Friday, not a market day · the provincial town, the room with a stove in it.** **A proceeding is entered on the day after the return went out, and a proceeding is a question that has been given a day.** A woman of about twenty-nine who is a clerk of the returns **writes it on the back of a form, because the back of a form is where the form of oath is printed, and nobody in the room says what is on the sheet she is writing on.** She has wanted six years to sign a return and there is no line on a return for a signature. She asks **"Can a thing be undecided"** of a man of about sixty with a tray who has carried that tray for twenty-two years and has never been asked it, and he says he has never been asked that either, **and she writes the date anyway.** She writes a number and not the four words of the body's name, and **a figure into the line for a person having knowledge, because a figure is the only thing that fits.** **Then a man of about sixty with a tray puts the new file into the pigeonhole that already holds the standing hearing's file of one sheet with a district on it, because the returns shelf is four inches deep and the second shelf is full and his hands were full — and that is the first time in about nine years that anything in that building has joined a thing to a thing by accident, and nobody made the join and nobody was told.** The district has about nine market towns in it and one of the nine is a market four hundred yards long in the county that has just been served. **A man of about fifty who has entered about eleven thousand forms in thirty-one years comes in, is not asked anything, looks at the pigeonhole and does not ask what is under the bottom file, and goes down two flights without stopping at a drawer that has a word in it.** **Ends:** a tray into a passage at the seventh hour and back at the first hour, and a woman of thirty-three who was not in that room at any hour of that day and whose name is not in the pigeonhole or the file or the proceeding and is not going to be in any of the three.

**Ch 253 · the twenty-seventh of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Saturday, a market day · Merefen, the Archive.** The last market of the year. **The tenth letter is opened at about the third hour, in about a second and a half to open and about four seconds to read, and it has no sender.** Ten letters in about two years; the nine before it opened inside a week; the tenth has been on the second shelf since a day nobody has written down. Inside: one question, nine lines, from a market town in the district. **Nine forms went out, one came back, and the eight that did not come back have no register and no column.** The second half is one sentence: *And if there is a place on the sheet for the name of a person, will you tell me whether I am to write my own in it, or leave it, because I have left it, and I have left it nine times.* **A keeper of twenty-nine reads it over a copyist's shoulder, reads that sentence twice, and says nothing in the nine minutes she has to.** **The copyist enters it**, under a head of her own making, *Received without a sender*, three words, in a fair hand a quarter of an inch smaller than the keeper's, with four items under it: the day, the hour, the town, and the absence. **A thing entered in a day-book has a day against it, and a letter from a stranger entered under a copyist's own head is a finding about a market town, and nobody in that room has ever entered a finding.** The copyist's second thing in six years, **eleven words**: *It was never going to be the eleventh that did it.* **The eleventh does not exist.** **Ends:** a question going out on the ordinary post in about three weeks because a question is a thing that goes out and a finding is a thing that is produced, and no column in that office for a person who would rather not have answered it.

**Ch 254 · the second of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Thursday, a market day · the provincial town, a chamber two floors up.** He came in on the second of Thawmonth after four days, three on a hired horse and the last in a cart, **and the year turned on the road between a posting house and a bridge and the man who turned it over was a carter with a load of lime and did not know he had done it.** **A chamber is a room with a table of three in it, two chairs, a clerk's stool, a witness list of eight ruled lines with four names against them and four lines empty, and a form of oath that is printed on the back of a return.** **Hester Cray, 38, of the Crown, convenes, puts her own name in the office line for the first time on that sheet, and says her want once, in nineteen sentences, footed at nineteen, and nobody in the room improves on it: that a thing heard has to be entered, and an entry with a day on it in a proceeding with a date against it is a finding, and a finding is the only kind of paper that can be produced in a court four hundred miles off, and a question cannot be produced, and she has been in nine of these in nine years and every one of the nine is a figure and not one of the nine is a room, and she has never been in a room that could do it, and she does not know whether it is possible.** She asks for the asking to be entered. The clerk enters it, reads it back **once and not twice**, and Cray says **"That is right"** and does not ask for it to be taken out. **Money: a sheet a penny, a sheet for the list a penny, a clerk's fee for entering a proceeding fourpence, a light kept burning for a day twopence, a carrier's hand for four miles twopence, footed to ten pence.** A clerk's hand was not a part of that room. **A man of thirty-two with a limp spent the day in a passage with his stick across his knees, was not sent for, put his hand flat on a stone wall for two seconds and nothing came back, did not open a door, and had a four-word question he did not ask.** **Ends:** eight lines, four with a person against them, one of the four empty a body corporate with a deed that names no officer, and the woman of thirty-eight looked at that line for about a second and a half and did not fill it in and did not write *no person* on it either, and four hundred yards away in the same building a woman of twenty-nine did the same thing to a different line on the twenty-fifth of a month, and neither has been told the other exists, and nothing has happened between them.

**Ch 255 · the eighth of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Wednesday, not a market day, the second hour · the chamber, the long table.** **Ansel Rudd, 44, a member of the Culling Order and a classifier, is early, which is the whole of the first thing anybody says about him.** The head of the record carries the office: *Read into the record, at the second hour, of the office of the Culling Order, of the classifications of the kingdom made under the standing instruction, to be complete before the first of Longlight.* **The phrase is in the building and not in a mouth as a threat.** He reads about two hundred lines aloud for two hours and ten minutes, the object column first, and about nine of the two hundred lines have a word in front of the place name. **He says three things and all three are about a column** — the first column is the only one a person can fill in alone and he is not going to write in it twice in a day; the fifth head has been the same head for two years and a man who changes a head in his own hand has made a decision and he has not made one; the sixth has no head and so is not a column and anything put in it is a thing the building decided not to keep. **Nobody argues with him and nobody agrees with him.** The room is a room with a man reading and a clerk copying and a Crown officer writing down the time, the place and the number of lines. **She asks him one question and it is not about the four places** — *Is a crossing a place or a thing* — **and he answers it in nine words** — *It is a thing. A place is what the thing is at* — **and she writes the nine words down and does not read them back.** His want, once, to a clerk with a tray, **thirty-four words, footed at thirty-four**: *A classification that is late is a classification that can be argued with, and I have argued with nine of them in a year and I would rather be late than argue with ten.* **Nobody asked him what is in the four places on the form and nobody noticed that nobody had.** **Ends:** the schedule in a record two hundred miles from a fen county, with the second bay of a bridge in the object column and a word in front of the place name, and nine hundred people in that building who do not know.

**Ch 256 · the ninth of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Thursday, a market day, the sixth hour · the press room.** The drawer is the fourth down in a case and it does not lock and nine people in that building have known for two years that the word in it is not to be used. **A woman of about twenty-nine wants a word before a place and not a rule for the sixth, in fourteen words, footed at fourteen, and a man of about fifty says *set it*, and a boy of nineteen sets it in about four minutes.** The boy's own want is the eleven weeks to serve before the next sitting, **fourteen words to a man in a doorway, footed at fourteen, and the man says nothing and goes down two flights.** *Is it a real word.* / *It is a word.* / *That is not the same as a word anybody uses.* / *No.* He pulls the sheet wet at the fourth corner, carries it up on a board, **and is not in the room when the room is told what it has done.** Four people, nine seconds, one of them says *It has the word on it.* **The word is *eastern* and it is not defined and it is not going to be.** **Ends:** eleven weeks to serve, a word he does not use, and no column in that office for the difference between a word that is used and a word that is set.

**Ch 257 · the tenth of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Friday, not a market day · four rooms in one building on one day.** **A woman of about thirty-three, an aid to the register, is four feet off with a sheet in her hand and hears a man of about fifty say to a man with a tray that a man can stand in a room for two hours and be asked nothing and go out having done the work and not know that he was never asked. She says nothing back, and she has not been asked anything since she was twenty-two.** Then the four notices, late and separately, about four hours apart, in four rooms, and nobody joins them: the man of about fifty, who does not say a name; **a boy of nineteen told it at second hand, who asks *Asked a question by who* and gets nothing;** a woman of about twenty-nine who wanted the sixth column ruled for six years and says ten words to a stove about having wanted a rule in it for six years and is not asked a second question; and a man of about sixty with a tray, **twelve words**: *Nobody ever asked whether I would rather it went at the sixth.* **And in the same building, at the sixth hour, the woman of thirty-three fills in the fourth column of a form, which is headed *Keeper*, in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and has filled it about two hundred times in a season for eleven years, and two hundred is a count of askings and is not a count of persons and is not a price and is added to nothing.** Her note of nineteen words is face down in a book on the second shelf and is not turned over. **Ends:** the tray out at the seventh hour with four things in it, and nine hundred people in that building who do not know that four people said something on that Friday and that the four somethings are one thing, and that nobody in that building has ever asked what is in the four places.

**Ch 258 · the eleventh of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Saturday, a market day, the third hour and the fourth hour · a room with a bench in it and no window.** A man of about forty puts a sheet on the bench. **The matter is entered in the provincial court out of a deed of affiliation and it names him and it has been standing for a year and a bit and it is about a body that answers to nobody and a road that four people say he made and forty people say he did not.** His one sentence about an offer, **twenty-four words, footed at twenty-four**: *A person who gives evidence in the proceeding is not sentenced for the matter the evidence is about. That is the whole of it.* **The sheet carries two prices of the same fine and nobody in that room added them and nobody asked why they differ, and those are two prices of one thing and there is no column in that building for two prices of one thing.** He says he will give evidence before he is asked. **That is not the offer. The offer is the reduction** (ten words). His second thing, **twenty-four words**: *If you do not take it the matter stands, and a matter that stands is a thing I carry, and I am carrying four.* What goes in the book is four lines and the fourth is not on any form in that office: *Witness attended. Offered reduction of sentence. Declined. Evidence offered before the asking.* **Money: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a clerk's fee fourpence, a witness's day eightpence, footed to fourteen pence, a shilling and twopence, and the two prices of the fine are not in it.** Nobody in the volume says the offer was correct procedure and it is. **Ends:** a passage with a stove at the end of it, a minute and a half of standing, four words ready and not said, and nobody in that province knowing he had them.

**Ch 259 · the fourteenth of Thawmonth, YR 316, a Tuesday, not a market day, the second hour · a room on the third floor with no window in it.** He was sent for by a sheet with his own name on it written before he was in the building. **The marshal does not stand up, which is the first thing anybody has ever said about him, and expecting is not surprise.** *You have a mother.* And then the reason, without surprise: a woman went out of a valley in the year the Sundering happened with a boy of about one-and-twenty, **and about a year between the going out and the coming back, and there is no name in it, and there is a mark, and there are two marks on the eleventh line and it is the only line with two on it, and a copy of the list has been in a drawer in that building for about nine years.** The list is about eleven lines, **ruled in two columns in two parts, a hand and a road, eleven of each, and no third column and no column for what became of anybody**, and it is the same length as eleven lines with no words in them in a notebook in a coat on a slope four hundred miles off, and neither page knows about the other one. He reads it in about a minute and a half, and reads it again. The rest is **eleven drawers in four buildings and about nine hundred sheets, of which eight hundred he has never read, and it is his on the terms**: evidence in a proceeding he does not sit in, before a person who does not want him there, on a day he has not been told. **He does not say yes and does not say no.** The block's one unattributed two-line statement, in italics, two lines, no number in either, and he does not write it down and he has had four of those in four years and has written one and that one has no hour against it and no name in it. His one thing about himself, **seventy words, footed at seventy**, and the marshal's one thing back, **ten words**: *That is the correct way to be in a room.* **Ends:** the room he wanted to be in is two floors down, he was not sent for, he is not on the list, he has not asked to be, and a keeper of records with five questions in a register and not one finding was not told and is not going to be.

**Ch 260 · the fifth of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Tuesday, not a market day, the fourth hour and the fourth hour and a half and the seventh hour · Merefen.** He came in on the twenty-ninth of Thawmonth after sixteen days, four of them in a cart. Forty men on the reach on the fifth, because it is Mudmonth, and the fourth bay is in its third week of pointing and the joint on its parapet is a foot and a half short because the man who began it went home at the fourth hour and has not come back. **The crossing four hundred yards up the lane carries nobody and has carried nobody for four years, and he did not go up to it, and about four people in that lane have said since that a crossing that carries nobody is a crossing that carries nobody and is not anything else.** He goes down the lane to the weigh-house instead, and the door on the lane is shut, and **in a wagon arch forty feet from it he stands for about a minute and a half and says nine words to nobody and gets no answer, and the volume does not say what the nine words were and about four people have worked out that he said something and about two have worked out that it was nine words.** A woman of about thirty with a pail knocks the same door later in the evening, and it is not shut, and she has not said so to anybody and is not going to. **The bell goes at the fourth hour and a half: nine stone of green-black bronze, a band of forty-one rivets, a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, a boy who has been the steward's apprentice for two years and three months and is not good at it, and a carpenter who is a hand and not a keeper, neither paid by the guild and neither a member of anything.** He asks four people who keeps it and gets four answers and none of them is an answer, and the man of forty-seven says the same four things he has said four times and none of the four is about the bell. **Nobody in that county can answer, and that is the finding and not a gap: a bell rung by two people who are neither paid for it nor members of it is a bell nobody in that county can be asked about, and that is why it is rung.** He looks at the seventh line in his coat for the sixth time and does not finish it and puts the leaf back flat with the first leaf turned to the first page. **Ends:** the salt over the first bay for the ninth week, the tide under the wharf, a bell that went on the Wednesday and goes on.

**The ten endings, listed.** **251** the lane quiet, the bell already rung, and a man of forty-seven saying it once in a kitchen and not twice. **252** a tray into a passage and a woman of thirty-three whose name is in none of the three papers and is not going to be in any of them. **253** a question going out on the ordinary post because a question goes out and a finding is produced. **254** a line with no name on it, filled by nobody, four hundred yards from another line with no name on it, filled by nobody. **255** a schedule in a record with a word in front of a place name and nine hundred people who do not know. **256** a boy of nineteen with eleven weeks to serve and a word he does not use and no column for the difference. **257** four people who noticed separately and a tray with four things in it. **258** a passage with a stove, four words ready, and nobody in that province knowing. **259** a room two floors down that he was not sent for, and a keeper who was not told. **260** a bell that went on the Wednesday and goes on.

---

## Volume 06 Batch 0001 — review repair pass, and the two page figures the pass found and did not repair

**The ten entries above describe Chapters 251 to 260 as they were first written. A review of the batch returned fifty-eight findings; forty-one were applied and seventeen were ruled, and the full record is the repair entry at the foot of `state/batch-summaries.md` and continuity items 685 to 687. **The plot, the ten days, the ten endings, the two names, the two offers, the two money figures that are not added, the unattributed two-line statement, the debt discharged and the finding about the bell are unchanged, and the block's figures stand as re-counted after a second review repair pass: **25,990 words**, and `about` at 514, `nine` at 145, `two` at 252, and the durable record of both reviews is `reviews/volume-06/batch-0001.md`.** Three repairs touch what the entries above say about a chapter and are the only ones a reader of those entries needs.

1. **Chapter 254 — the entries say he came in on the second of Thawmonth after four days, three on a hired horse and the last in a cart. He now comes into the building at about the sixth hour of the first of Thawmonth, and the year turns on the road on the first between a posting house and a bridge, and the dateline and the paragraph agree, and Chapter 258's *nine days* in that building foots against it.** The distance between the fen county and the provincial town is **two hundred miles** in this chapter, in Chapter 256 and in Chapter 258, and the two instances of four hundred miles that stand are Cray's *produced in a court four hundred miles off* and the man of thirty-four's glass yard, both of which are canon and neither of which is the fen county.
2. **Chapter 255 — the schedule is about two hundred and forty lines throughout, not about two hundred, and the boundary oath-stone renewal that this chapter says is written down in a field in about twelve weeks — eighty-three days from day 163, which is day 246, and the eleven weeks the first repair pass claimed is a week short — is `outline/volume-06.md` §17's day 246, and the cut that it stands under is day 253, and the order is not reversed.** Cray's exchange with Rudd is **twelve words and the chapter now says twelve twice**, and the volume's one block-spine speech is bolded in nine paragraphs and is still nineteen sentences.
3. **Chapter 260 — the entry says he asked four people who keeps the bell and got four answers. He now says three of the four out loud: the mason of fifty and a half, a man of about twenty-six setting a course, and a carter of thirty. The fourth is the man of forty-seven saying the same four things, and the chapter now says that he has said them five times in a year to a man with a stick, and to a yard wall and to a bench-board and to nobody besides, and that he has been asked about none of them.** The paragraph that stood at `260:62` was eighty-eight words of ninety identical to `250:35` and is rewritten in its own words, and the return journey is four days and not fourteen, three of them on a hired horse and the last in a hired cart, which is the same four days and the same reason Chapter 254 gives.** The nine words in the wagon arch are still not told to the reader, the door is still shut at the fourth hour and open at the seventh, and the bell still goes on the Wednesday and goes on.

**And two findings on pages in Volumes 01 to 05 that this batch did not repair and that are recorded here because the entries above inherit them: `244:67` calls a man of about fifty's sentence about a district *about eleven words* and the sentence is seventeen, and `242:57` calls a twenty-word sentence *about nine words* and its own paragraph at `242:61` goes on calling them the nine words. Chapter 252 records the first on the page and repeats neither figure. The second was reprinted at `258:35` in the first draft of this block; the page now carries no figure at all where it carried the wrong one, so the wrong figure stops travelling, and Chapter 242 stands as closed prose with its defect recorded at continuity item 687, exactly as Chapter 244's stands. No chapter in Volumes 01 to 05 was touched by either repair pass of this batch.**

## Volume 06 Batch 0002 — Chapters 261–270, "The Classification"

*Days 191 to 231, YR 316. Twenty-three thousand one hundred and eighty-four words on first writing and twenty-four thousand five hundred and ten after the review repair pass. Zero names spent of six; six unfilled. **The per-chapter summaries below describe the block as planned and as written and are unchanged by the repair, which moved no event; the repair pass is summarised in its own section at the foot of this file.** Per chapter, before and after: 261 2,537/2,630 · 262 2,445/2,286 · 263 2,373/2,300 · 264 2,199/2,502 · 265 2,193/2,572 · 266 2,652/2,645 · 267 2,232/2,493 · 268 2,119/2,586 · 269 2,109/2,191 · 270 2,325/2,305.*

**Ch 261 · the sixth of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Wednesday, not a market day, the second hour and the second hour and a half, the third hour, the fourth hour, the sixth hour, the seventh hour · a chamber two floors above a room with a stove in it, and the first floor, in a provincial town two hundred miles from a fen county.** A schedule of about two hundred and forty lines, a week late, with room at the bottom, and a line goes in at about the second hour with **a ford on a made road in the object column**, because the object column is the only one of the six that can be filled in without a person being in the room. The other four places against that line are blank, **about four of the six are ruled for a figure, and nowhere on the whole of the sheet is there a place for the name of a person.** The fourth column is headed *Keeper* and is the only head on the sheet that is a person. The clerk of the returns stops with the pen on the rule for about a minute and a half and says one thing to nobody: *A place is a thing a person can be at* (ten words, no figure attached). **A woman of about twenty-nine who has wanted the sixth column ruled for six years says fourteen words to a press and not to a person, and a boy of nineteen at the stone asks her five words, *Whose column would it be*, and she says nothing and the boy did not have it after he asked and was not going to.** The building is four floors and about forty people in it and seven presses, about four hundred forms a month go out of it, nine counties, four hundred and nine parish rolls, and the light at the fourth hour in that month is on the floor, so the four hundred are read at waist height, and not one of the about forty is asked what is in the four places. **And at about the first hour, a floor below and before any of it, the woman of thirty-three filled in two forms in about a minute and a quarter each without looking up, and her note of nineteen words is face down on the second shelf of a case behind her, and nobody has asked her to turn it over and she has said nothing this morning about the fourth column and is not going to.** A tray with four things in it goes out at the seventh hour and comes back at the first. **Ends:** a rule about a late schedule that can only be applied to a person, and is therefore a want, and an office that has had two of those for two years and has printed neither of them.

**Ch 262 · the ninth of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Saturday, a market day, the second hour to the sixth hour · the ground-floor press room.** A man of about fifty is told to bring up a witness record and that is the whole of what he is told. The stock is in a drawer under the stone, about nine hundred copies of the office's own printed series in about forty bundles, and a witness record is one sheet of that series with the second column short, and he takes the top sheet off the top bundle without counting. **Three real things went into the fourth column and all three of them were real, and that is the whole of how it was done**: a form of the office's own printed series, a hand — the loop at the top of the column leans the same way on every one of about four hundred forms a month for eleven years — and a date, taken off a tray of about eleven days in about nine years rather than copied from anything, and nobody in that building has ever asked which of the eleven a day belongs to. **He did it in about nine minutes in the ordinary way, and the ordinary way is the reason it happened, and about four people in that building have said since that the villainy of this is thirty-one years of pressing type and that no man in that room did anything that he had not done four hundred times before.** A boy of nineteen asks seven words, *Is that one of the real ones*, and the man answers in **eleven words, footed at eleven**: *A head on a column is what a court can use.* **The boy asked about reality and the man answered about use, and neither of them has ever said so to the other one, and nobody thanked the man for the true thing he said, and a true thing said to a boy of nineteen is not entered anywhere and is not going to be.** He came past the register at the fourth hour and the woman of thirty-three was at the bench and he went by at about four feet and said nothing, and neither of them has said one word to the other in eleven years. **Ends:** the top bundle back in the drawer where the top bundle is, and nine hundred copies in nine counties with a form in them that has a head on it and nobody who has been shown it.

**Ch 263 · the fourteenth day of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Thursday, a market day, the fourth hour to the seventh hour · a room with a stove in it on the first floor.** The clerk of the returns reads the sheet up before he enters it, which is a practice nobody has written down, in about a minute and a quarter, and then asks one question and **the question is about the fifth column and not the fourth**, and nobody in the room noticed which of the two it was about except about four people who noticed it on a stair about two days later. **He entered the place in the first column in about four seconds and the day in the fifth in about two, and he entered the fourth column from the sheet without reading it out**, and about four people in that building have said since that a man who reads a sheet up in a minute and a quarter and enters a name from it in about a second read the two columns he can check. A form with four places ruled for a figure and nowhere at all for the name of a person is a form nobody in that room was taught to distrust, and **the only part of the arrangement that is broken is the part nobody has ever been shown, and nobody has been shown it because there is nothing to show: a person was never asked to be on the paper.** The tray went out at the seventh hour and came back at the first. **A woman of about twenty-nine asks six words of the man of about fifty at about the sixth hour, *Did you write that name yourself*, and he says no, and it was a true thing, and the not hesitating is the frightening part.** The sheet goes into a file of about nine sheets with nothing on the wrapper. **Money: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a clerk's fee for entering one classification fourpence, the tray charged to nobody because the man who carries it is paid at the year and a year is not a column. A penny and a penny is twopence, and twopence and fourpence is sixpence. Total: six pence**, and the six pence is not a figure of persons and is added to nothing. **Ends:** a man who has just had a name put in a column in his own hand and has not been asked about it going downstairs to ask a clerk about a tray, and the two questions being the same question, and neither of the two men having worked out that they are the same question.

**Ch 264 · the sixteenth day of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Saturday, a market day, the fourth hour, the fifth hour, the fifth hour and a half, the sixth hour, the seventh hour · a lane four hundred yards from a market in Merefen.** He comes into the lane because the market has gone in and a man who has been in a county for six weeks does not go up a lane to look at a thing, he goes down one. The door on the lane is shut and he does not knock. There is no owner and no money and no glass in the sill and no third seat, and a dressed block in the abutment with about forty yards of tarred hemp in it, and a bell a hundred yards off, **nine stone of green-black bronze, a band of forty-one rivets, a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, rung at the fourth hour and a half by a boy and a carpenter, neither paid by the guild nor members of anything.** He stands at the near end of the crossing for about nine minutes and does not put a hand on anything. **A road is a line and two hands, a date, and a witness at each end who is not the person keeping it; he has the line, he has both hands, he has a date four days off, and there is nobody standing at either end who keeps anything.** The witnesses are the difficulty, **and the last time a man went up that road the far end was a child of nine with a barrow, and this time it is a man of fifty-eight who keeps a book, and a child of nine had not been asked to keep anything and a man of fifty-eight has.** The second bay is being pointed into a second month, the joint on the parapet is a foot and a half short because the man who began it went home at the fourth hour and has not come back, and a clerk of a bench of nine was asked about it once and said that a clerk cannot measure a thing. **A boy of fifteen at a bench-board copies the empty space under a number as well as the number and does not know that he is doing the only thing in that county that a form does.** The man of forty-seven is found on the deck of the first bay and is asked a question and not a thing with a person in it and says yes, and then says nine words, footed at nine: **Nobody has ever asked me to hold an end.** **That is the first time in a year he has been asked a question and answered it in words that are not the four things, and the count on the page under that stair stays at eight and the bench is not asked anything.** **Ends:** a man who takes a printed form out of a drawer in a county he is going to walk out of, and nine days from that lane, and nobody walking any part of that road with him.

**Ch 265 · the twenty-fifth day of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Monday, not a market day, and the nine days before it · a made road, alone.** A stick that is ash and four feet nine, cut out of a fence rail in a county that is not on any map, and that he cannot lean on because leaning on it puts the weight through the wrong hip. He left at about the sixth hour on the second of that month and got to the other end on the twenty-fifth. **The road is made and it is not a good road, and for about nine hours of it on a good day a man can see that it was made by people who were not going anywhere and did not know who was going to use it, and a road that has to turn turns badly.** He came to a place where the road goes under a bridge on the fourth day and stopped under it for about ten minutes, **and there are about nine such places on that road and every one of them is in a list in a building two hundred miles off, and a man who has walked nine hours under nine bridges has been under the whole of a list and has not seen one line of it.** On the fifth day he said two things out loud, in italics, two plain lines, no number in either, naming no path, the roadmark, the light or the mechanism, **and he did not write them down and about four people do not know he said them.** He came into the valley on the ninth day at about the seventh hour. **There is no market in it and no market day and no calendar on any wall of it and nobody who lives in it has ever needed one**, and that is not a figure of speech, because a man who has come nine days up a made road out of a county with a bench and a market knows what day it is. About four hundred people, eleven steadings, four hamlets, a stream four people call the Burn, a room over a cross, a bridge with about two hundred and forty feet of stone on it, a mill with a man in it who cannot leave his wheel, a road about four hundred yards long made by hand, **and a man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work who said in a yard in a winter in a year before last that a road is not a thing you are given and a road is a thing you dig, and nobody has ever counted the length of that sentence and nobody has ever asked him to.** **Ends:** a room with a fire in it that a man of about thirty-one offered without a condition, in a valley where that is a thing nobody has ever written down either.

**Ch 266 · the twenty-sixth day of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Tuesday, not a market day in a county with a market, the seventh hour to the eighth hour · a room over a cross, four hundred miles from any county that is on a map.** The benches are bolted to the floor in four rows, there are twenty-nine, a number is cut into the end of each, and **the bench at the back of the right-hand row has a hundred and forty cut into the end of it, and the hundred and forty is a count of the times anybody has ever stood in the aisle to be asked, and no name has ever been struck off one of those benches.** The aisle is four feet wide and has gone three generations without being used, and **about four people in that valley have said since that a hundred and forty and three generations are two figures about the same aisle and that nobody in that room has ever put them side by side and that the man of fifty-eight could do it in about a second and has not.** Nine on the benches, about thirty in the room, about two hundred of the ninth generation at the back and not one of them in a seat. The ninth spread is about two hundred lines in one run of a page with a day and a mark and a hand against each, and a day against a line of that kind is the day the person was born, and about two hundred of that generation have never gone anywhere and have never been asked to. **A second column about the width of two fingers in the man of fifty-eight's own ink has eight names in it that eight people wrote themselves, and the ninth line is empty and is not ruled across and is not going to be.** The man who keeps it asks, in front of about thirty people, for the reading he has wanted for six years, and a man of thirty-four seconded it and a man of fifty-five did not and a woman of sixty-six did not and a man of eighty-one said nothing at all, **and nobody counted the hands and there is no column in that room for a hand.** Then the four lines at the head of the first spread are read out in that room for the first time, word for word as they stand at the head of that spread, and **they are not re-derived in Blocks 3, 4 or 5.** A man of thirty-four says what he has about them in three parts and all three are about a column, and a man of thirty-two with a limp who has been in that room a quarter of an hour understands all three and is not going to say so and did not. **A woman of sixty-six says fourteen words, footed at fourteen: *I have had my turn at it and I would not have it back*, and nobody asks her a second question, and the man of thirty-four does not and the man with a stick does not.** He says the six years out loud for the first time and says nothing else about it. **Ends:** a form of that county's own form folded once in the inside pocket of a coat over a chair nine feet off him, ruled in seven, with a column for a witness at this end and a column for a witness at that end, and about four people in that valley who cannot see inside a coat.

**Ch 267 · the twenty-seventh day of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Wednesday, not a market day in a county with a market, the seventh hour to the ninth hour · the same room, the same aisle.** The question is put by the man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work and it took him about four minutes to get round to it: **Stand in the aisle. I am going to ask you what you swore and you are going to answer and I am not going to ask you anything else.** The man of fifty-eight goes and stands in the middle of four feet of floor and the first thing he does is turn round and look at the bench at the back of the right-hand row and then look at the number cut into the end of it, and the room waits while he does it. The two hundred at the back came nine feet further forward and about nine of them did not. He said it in about nine seconds. **It is in the first spread in his own hand, eighteen words, footed at eighteen: *I swear to keep the book, the room, the day, the mark and the hand, and nothing else.*** A woman of about thirty who has carried a slate for eleven years asks whether the last two words mean what she thinks they mean, and he says that they do, and that she is the first person in nineteen years to ask him anything about it, and that she is not going to get a second answer. **Then he entered it, in his own book, in his own hand, at the head of the first spread under the four lines, because the four lines are a rule about keepers and a fact about a keeper goes under the rule about keepers, and he ruled a line to do it, and it is the first line ruled across in that book in a hundred and forty years and the first finding in that book in a hundred and forty years.** He offered it about four minutes after he had been asked and **nobody had asked him to offer.** **Nobody in that room asked him whether he could stand it afterwards. There were about thirty people in it and two of them were strangers and one of the strangers had come nine days up a made road and could have asked and did not, and the not-asking is not a kindness and is not a rule, and a room hears a thing once and a person can be asked twice, and that room had just used up the once.** **Ends:** a valley of about four hundred people gone to bed on a night with a hundred and forty cut into the end of a bench and a number ruled across the first spread in a hundred and forty years, and not one of them knowing that anything has been entered anywhere at all.

**Ch 268 · the sixth day of Greenmonth, YR 316, a Friday, not a market day, and the nine days before it · a made road, alone, and a house on Weir Street.** The nine days back were the nine days out and they were not the same nine days. He slept the last night in a barn with about nine other men and one of them asked him whether he was going as far as the town. **The sheet was on the table where he leaves things, undated by any man, dated the second day of that month, which is the day he went out, and it had been on that table for four days.** It is a sheet of the marshal's own office's printed series, and there are four sheets of the same refusal in a press in a house forty feet down that lane that have not been sent for about two years, and this is a fifth sheet of the same kind, and **it is the fourth refusal in a document in four volumes, and the two of those figures are not the same figure and nobody in that county has ever added them and is not going to.** The terms are the same terms and there is nothing in them: **a condition is not a price, and the marshal's office has never put a price on a thing and has never once pretended to, and a man handed the same four sentences a fourth time in writing has been told the truth four times by a man who is never surprised.** The object column has a place in it, **the crossing four hundred yards up that county's own road**, written the way that office writes a place, which is the name of the nearest thing anybody in that office has heard of, and the nearest thing is a ford nine miles off with a different name on it, and **in front of the place name there is a word, in the same type as the heads of the five columns, struck once about six weeks ago by a boy of nineteen who does what he is told.** He read the sheet in about a minute and a half and put it down and did not answer it. **Ends:** three columns on three pieces of paper in two countries — the seventh line of a page of a book four hundred miles off, the county's own form in the same coat, and the fourth column of a sheet in a building two hundred miles off — and nobody in that county has ever seen any of the three and is not going to.

**Ch 269 · the thirteenth day of Greenmonth, YR 316, a Friday, not a market day, the second hour to the fourth hour · a yard on Weir Street, a wet morning.** The yard belongs to a man of twenty-five who owns the crews and is not in it that morning, and the yard's rule is that nothing that belongs to a man goes in that yard's book and only a thing set, and **nobody in that yard has said one word about a family in about a year.** About nine men, about four hundred yards of yard, ground of stone and chalk and about nine inches of it under water by the second hour, and a wet week is a week a yard thinks and a dry week is a week a yard sets. **The bench-board is four feet off the ground and is not a table, and the rule in that yard is that a thing is set on it and not at a table, because a table is a thing four people sit at and a bench-board is a thing two people stand at.** A man of about sixty packs lime at the end of the yard, **because wet lime is packed and dry lime is dusted**, and he has done it for about nine years and he is not on the yard's book, and **he comes in out of the weather and reads the sheet upside down from about nine feet without moving his head, and says nothing, and about nine men have watched him do it about nine hundred times.** He wrote it on the bench-board in about eleven minutes, and the first column is what is given and what is given is a road, and the second column says *to the persons who may require this office to produce the same, and to no other, and to no person, there being none*, **which a man wrote out of a press in a wet yard and did not sign and could not.** In front of the place name in the object column he wrote the word, **and he wrote it because it is the word that goes in that column on that series, and he did not know what it was, and there is no line on that sheet for a man to write down that he does not know what a column is for.** **He did not put a hand on anything. It is daylight, it is the second hour, about nine men are within thirty feet of him, his left hand is warm at about the fourth hour every day and has been since a lane in a county that is not on any map, and it was about the second hour and he did not put it on a sill, a gate, a bench-board, a stone, a wall, a door or a man.** A man of about twenty-six setting a course asks five words at a bench-board and not in a room and gets five back, **and a thing two people agree about in ten words is a decision, and a decision made in a yard in the wet on a Friday is a decision with no room in it anywhere, and there is no column in this county for a decision.** **Money: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a sheet into the ordinary post in a bag twopence, a clerk's fee for entering a refusal fourpence, the bench-board at no rate and never has been; a carrier's hand for two hundred miles is not in the column at all because no rate for it has ever been printed in this county. A penny and a penny is twopence, and twopence and twopence is fourpence, and fourpence and fourpence is eight pence. Total: eight pence.** **Ends:** about four hundred people in a town of about four thousand people who do not know that a bag is going out of it in the ordinary post with a word on the front of a place name nobody in that town has ever said out loud.

**Ch 270 · the sixteenth day of Greenmonth, YR 316, a Monday, not a market day, the fourth hour to the sixth hour · the room over a weigh-house with a door on a lane.** The bag went on the Friday and it cost eight pence, added and footed in that yard and not in this room, and **a bag in the ordinary post is the first thing that has ever left that yard in the ordinary way, and a yard which sends nothing can be ignored and a yard which sends something cannot.** There were two people in the room and there would have been three. The keeper of records is twenty-nine and has kept this office four years and a half out of a deed of thirteen words at fourpence a year, **and in which keeper is employment and is not jurisdiction**; the second copyist is about thirty and is on a warrant not in the press and has wanted a post with her name in the day-book since the summer before last. The county's form is ruled in seven: **what is given. To whom, in the county's words. By whose hand. The day. The hour. A witness at this end. A witness at that end.** The seventh is a ruled space about two inches deep with nothing in it, its rule no more faded than the rule at the bottom of the third, **and it has been in this office's use for four years and a half and it has been filled with nothing on nine occasions.** He filled the first column in about four minutes, the second in about two, the third in a second, and then he stopped with the pen on the rule, **and read the second column back before he did anything else, which he did not have to do.** The day went in, and then the hour, separately, with the rule between them, because there is a fair copy on that wall nineteen years old saying no combined figure is entered in this office, **and that fair copy has never once been read out loud in that room by anybody including the keeper of records.** A witness at this end is the man of forty-seven and that name went in in about four seconds. **And the seventh column got a name in it at about the fourth hour and a half, and it is the name of a man of fifty-eight four hundred miles off who keeps the only roll in a valley of about four hundred people, and he did not enter it, and the second copyist entered it in about nine seconds and did not look up and has not asked for it to be taken out and is not going to.** The keeper of records said one thing about it, **fourteen words, footed at fourteen: *A name in a column of this office is a claim about a person***, and it was not a refusal and it was not an objection and it was about the office and not about the man. The third column says by whose hand, **and the hand is a second copyist of about thirty who has wanted a line in a book with her name in it for two years and has put her own name in the third column of a finding and another person's name in the seventh.** He did not argue with the fourteen words and did not thank her for them. **The day-book is the only book in that office nobody can be served with and it has nine entries in it of a thing that was not asked, and there is not going to be a tenth, and nobody entered one on that Monday, and the two of them were in the same room at the same hour and neither asked the other anything and neither is going to.** The finding was read back once by the second copyist, who stopped twice, and nobody asked for a second reading in nine years. **Ends:** a name in a column of a form in a room over a weigh-house is a claim about a person, and a claim about a person is the only kind of paper in this kingdom that can be produced in a room a long way off, and there is no column in that office for what is done to a claim after it has been produced, and about four hundred people in a town of about four thousand people do not know any of it and are not going to be told.

**The ten endings, listed.** **261** a rule about a late schedule that can only be applied to a person, and an office that has printed neither of its two wants. **262** the top bundle back in the drawer, and nine hundred copies of a form nobody has been shown. **263** two questions that are the same question and neither man knows it. **264** a form out of a drawer in a county he is about to walk out of, and a wagon arch, and nine words said to nobody three weeks before. **265** a bed offered in a valley without a condition, in a place where that is not written down either. **266** four lines read out in the room they were written for, and a man saying the six years out loud for the first time. **267** four hundred people gone to bed and not one of them knowing anything has been entered anywhere. **268** three columns, three pieces of paper, two countries, and nobody in that county who has seen any of them. **269** eight pence footed in the wet, and a bag going out in the ordinary post with a word on it. **270** a claim about a person, and no column in that office for what is done to a claim after it has been produced.


## Volume 06 Batch 0002 — review repair pass, and the six things the pass found that the block's own audit had called clean

**One batch, reviewed once, repaired once. The pass wrote no chapter, added no event and changed no plan. It found six things, five of them in the prose and one in the state files, and the block's own audit had recorded the worst of them as *not a defect*.**

1. **The narrator formula had replaced the scenes.** *About four people in that building have said since that* stood at seventy-four in the block against seventy in the larger Batch 0001, and quoted dialogue had fallen to 170 words in ten chapters with Chapters 265 and 268 carrying none. **Now twenty-five and thirty-eight, with dialogue at 224 and no empty chapter.** The block grew 1,326 words and the growth is scene.
2. **Six empty sections.** A doubled `---` rule in Chapters 262, 263 twice, 265, 266 and 267.
3. **The bell's full specification was written out three times** in the block, twice inside Chapter 264 alone. **Once now, in Chapter 264, and referred to in Chapter 268.**
4. **A repeat the project's own sweeps were structurally unable to see**, because both the duplicate-paragraph sweep and the near-repeat sweep are paragraph-scoped and the defect was two sentences in one chapter. **A clause-level comparison of a named pair is the basis that finds it, and it is now in the Batch 0003 prompt.**
5. **An eight-word shingle against the prior two hundred and sixty chapters is too loose a basis for this house voice** and returns a hit on roughly a third of sentences, because the register is built from stock phrases that recur by design. A shingle of that length reporting near zero is not a clean sweep.
6. **`state/current.md` contradicted itself three times** and carried five superseded entries above the live state. **Rewritten as one live block.**

**What the pass did not do is at continuity item 709, and it is the part a later writer needs: no name, no tenth not-asking, no *brother*, no definition of *eastern*, no System panel, no new money, no reconciled refusal figures, no measurement of the seam, no second reading of the finding, no third printing of the four lines, no named child, no walk on a road, and no edit to `outline/volume-06.md`.** The two outline defects stand and are flagged for an outline repair pass before Block 4.

## Volume 06, Batch 0003, Chapters 271–280, "The Column With No Outcome" (Block 3, days 232 to 272, YR 316)

**271 — The twenty-fourth of Greenmonth, YR 316, day 239, a Tuesday, not a market day, a field at a parish boundary.** A boundary oath-stone comes out of the ground and goes back; the face of it is about nine inches square with four letters cut into it and a figure nineteen years old. A clerk of about sixty arrives with a book that is not the book he has kept for nineteen years, and a magistrate of thirty and a reeve and a mason of fifty and a half and a man with a barrow and two men from the reach. **About four people in that field work out in the ordinary way that a bench of nine has no standing at a parish boundary and has never claimed any, and not one of them says it to the others.** The reeve says the claim, in the ordinary way, and says the stone is the only thing in that field that can say no to a man, and a man is not obliged to accept it. The clerk will not say what kind of book it is in a field. **He reads the day off the inside cover of the book in about two seconds and says the twenty-fourth of Greenmonth, and names the first of Longlight as the Tuesday they are all coming back for, and he wants the hour in the book at the time and not afterwards; the first printing of that speech gave the day of the field as the first of Longlight, seven days forward, and the repair pass corrected it.** **End:** the day is fixed, the words are a copy of a copy of something this county has never had, and the sheet goes down to a market in a bag.

**272 — The twenty-eighth of Greenmonth, YR 316, day 243, a Saturday, a market day, the reach, the yard, the long room over the wharf.** The fourth bay is finished and pointed. A joint on a parapet is a foot and a half short and nobody measured it and a clerk of nine years' standing was asked about it once and said a clerk cannot measure a thing, and he was right. A boy of fifteen copies the empty space under a number as well as the number, and nothing goes in it, and that is what the space is for. The bell goes at the fourth hour and a half and nobody in this county can say who keeps it. A door on a lane forty feet from a wagon arch has been open since the spring and a man with a limp goes up the lane and does not go in. **A bench of nine sits at the seventh hour and is asked nothing, and the count on the page under that stair is eight before and eight after.** A man of forty-seven says nothing for two hours and nobody asks him anything for two hours. **A man of about nineteen with a hod he is not carrying anything in has an elder sister of twenty-two in a house two streets off, and a man of about sixty packing lime at the end of the yard is not on the yard's book, and about four men have worked out where his lime comes from and about four have not; both paragraphs were rewritten by the repair pass, which found them reproducing Chapter 269 over about fifty words.** The clerk of about sixty says the first of Longlight is Tuesday and that he is taking the other book, and that he is not asking anybody, and the man with the limp says he will be there, and the clerk writes nothing down about that.

**273 — The first of Longlight, YR 316, day 246, a Tuesday, the renewal, in the open.** The clerk asks who is going to say the words and the magistrate says she has never spoken at a parish boundary and is not going to pretend she knows what is said at one, and the reeve says one word, and the clerk will not keep a minute of a field with nine people in it. **The magistrate reads four lines, in about eleven seconds, from a copy of a copy of something this county has never had, and nobody reads it a second time, and that was arranged before anybody came up the hedge by the reeve and not by the clerk.** A boundary oath-stone is a promise and a promise that can only be kept by breaking something else is a claim and not a record. **The clerk of about sixty kept the second kind of minute he has kept in nineteen years, and said, in thirteen words, that a thing an office can enter is a thing an office can classify, and nobody improved on it, and the man with a limp heard all thirteen words and wrote none of them down.** The entry describes what is at that boundary and nothing else: a crossing with no owner and no money, a sill with nothing in it, a dressed block with nothing in the stone that anybody has read, a bell a hundred yards off. **The word in front of the place name is read out loud in a field and asked about once.** Money: a penny, a penny, fourpence, twopence, fourpence, twopence — footed to **fourteen pence, a shilling and twopence**.

**274 — The fifth of Longlight, YR 316, day 250, a Saturday, a market day, two rooms on one day.** **In a chamber two hundred miles off, at the second hour, a length of made road in a fen county goes into a record with a place in the object column, a word in front of the place name, four empty places, and a sixth column with no head on it.** A man of forty-four who is a member of the Culling Order reads it and says he is not going to write in the object column twice in a day and does not explain himself. **The witness produced for the place at the third hour is the forged *Keeper* entry, and the man of about fifty who made it says the fourth column is his own hand in the way a man says the time, and nobody in that chamber has ever asked him what is in the four places.** A name is read out. **Two floors below, at the first hour, a woman of thirty-three filled in two forms in about a minute and a quarter each without looking up, and her leaf on the second shelf is still face down, and nobody went up or went down, and she does not find out.** In the fen county a market is on and a man with a satchel says the true thing about the four places a third time to a woman buying salt, and a carrier of about fifty with a firm of two carries a bag up the road himself and puts a sheet of the office's own printed series in the sill of a crossing, weighted with a stone off the bank, and asks nobody. Money: a penny, a penny, fourpence — footed to **six pence**, with two items left out of the column because no rate for them is printed in this county. **The description of the six columns and the footing line were both rewritten by the repair pass, the first for repeating Chapter 261 and the second because it was still the same nine words as Chapter 263's footing with a comma for a full stop; the total is six pence either way and is still footed on the page.**

**275 — The seventh of Longlight, YR 316, day 252, a Monday, the day before.** **A man of thirty-two with a limp goes up his own road and reads out of a sill a sheet with a place in it, a word in front of the place name, four places ruled for a figure, a sixth column with no head, and a woman's name in the fourth column with the leg of it run by the weather.** He knows the hand and not the woman, and a hand is a year and a half of watching a loop and nine shapes and a stroke left short. **He is asked one question by a man of forty-seven and gets forty-six words that are not the four things, and the list stands at five occasions.** A man of fifty-five at a barrier of three bars says the same four words and cannot say where he got them and does not want to, and he has turned round about four hundred people and let about four thousand through in nineteen years, and the two figures are two populations and are not added to one another. **He cannot get up the four-foot bank, gets about two feet, and sits down on the dressed block without putting his hand on it.** He goes over the sheet again and it gives him four things: a line that is late can be argued with, nothing has been costed, a keeper named in a county she is not in cannot say no, and a sheet that has no place for a person who is not a keeper does not know he came to a sill. At about the ninth hour he says nine words to a room with nobody in it: *A line that is late can be argued with.*

**276 — The twelfth of Longlight, YR 316, day 257, a Saturday, a market day, the fourth day after.** **The moment is not written and nothing in the chapter stands in for it.** The weather takes the sheet out of the sill. **The sill has nothing in it and had nothing in it the day before and has nothing under it now, and forty yards of tarred hemp that went in four feet down are not in it and nobody has dug for them and nobody is going to.** The dressed block is in the abutment with a line about nine inches long in the stone and not across a joint, unmoved, unmeasured, unruled across, and nobody in that county has put a finger on it. **A line of that length in a dressed block is the same length as a line in a stone course in another structure in this county, and that is a fact about two pieces of work done by the same hands, and no person in this county knows of the other one, and the two have never been in one book: that sentence is the block's only printed reference to the first seam and the block's ledger twice said the block did not mention it, and the ledger was wrong and is corrected at item 733.** **He gets about two feet up the bank and sits on the stone for about nine minutes and does not put his hand on the block.** Nobody heard anything. A man of forty-seven is in the toll house for about eleven minutes and is asked nothing and says nothing. A woman of about thirty with a pail says the ninth of her sentences at a door this year. **The block's one unattributed two-line statement, said out loud on the bank to a county that heard nothing, in two lines with no number in either.** **The illness in the closing pages runs about nine days and is the second in about two months, and the repair pass fixed this chapter's count of days between the promise in the field and the thing done in the eighth of Longlight, which was eight and is seven.**
