**277 — The fourteenth of Longlight, YR 316, day 259, a Monday, the reversal.** **Three pieces of paper on a table in a room over a smithy: a wet sheet out of a sill, a blank form of the same series, and this county's own form ruled in seven with a name in the seventh column.** The second columns are the same width and the fifth columns are the same width and both sixth columns have no head. **The fourth thing is not on the table: the list of eleven lines in a drawer two hundred miles off, a hand and a road, eleven of each, the eleventh with a woman's mark and a boy's mark on it and about a year between the first going out and the eleventh coming back, and no third column.** The finding, in four steps: a hand is not a person, it is what a person is when a column has a head on it; a road in a column with a head on it is a place, and a place is not a journey; **a document with a keeper in it and no outcome in it is not a record of a journey but a record of custody, and a record of custody is a list of what is held and by whom**; and the eleventh has two marks because two people were with the eleventh thing, and a mark is not a name and nothing in this kingdom says what a mark is. **So the thing he has been reading as a record is a list of what was taken.** And a form with no column for what became of anybody is not a form somebody forgot. **His mother is on that line and it is the eleventh and it has been the eleventh for about four months and he is not saved and not lost because there is no column for it.** He puts his own page of eleven lines with no words in them next to a drawer in his head for the first time. In the yard on the morning after, at about the seventh hour, the owner is twenty-five and would rather not be told, and a man of about sixty packing lime is spoken to by none of the nine. **The chapter runs from the seventh hour on the fourteenth to the seventh hour of the morning after, and the yard scene sat after scenes a day later than it until the repair pass moved it, and the dateline now lists three hours instead of a range.**

**278 — The seventeenth of Longlight, YR 316, day 262, a Thursday, a market day, the complication.** **The sheet goes on the table in the room over a weigh-house with a door on a lane and a keeper of records of twenty-nine says no, and then says that it is their shape with a place in it and no figure, and that they have never entered one. Eighteen words, footed at eighteen, and nobody improved on them, and he did not thank her and she was not thanked and did not want to be.** The second copyist does not look up. **The register has five entries, all beginning with a district name, all entered as questions, none a finding, and the fifth dated.** A rule nineteen years old on a wall has never been read out loud in that room and he asks whether it exists and is told it does and is told that he did not ask what is in it and that was correct. A leaf in the press has been there about a year and a half and was not mentioned and was not asked about. **The sheet goes back inside the coat and it is the only copy anybody in this kingdom knows of.** A woman of about thirty with a pail says one thing at a door and moves on. **The fever is on its ninth day, it began on the ninth of Longlight and it was over on the seventeenth, and a man last seen at the bench-board on the fifteenth has not been there two days; the first printing put the fever on its sixth day and the absence at six days, and neither could be true at once with Chapter 279 and Chapter 280, and all three are corrected.**

**279 — The nineteenth of Longlight, YR 316, day 264, a Saturday, a market day, the eleventh day after, the long room over the wharf.** **Nine people in the room at the fourth hour and a tenth in it who is on no roll of anything and has never once spoken in that room, and an aisle four feet wide between the long table and the wall that nobody has ever asked the use of.** The bench has not sat and does not sit until the seventh hour on a Saturday and on nothing else in the week. **A woman of seventy-two who came in with nobody and sat at the end of the bench for the fire stands up in that aisle at about the fourth hour and says one sentence: *A hearing is a column with a roof on it, and the roof is the part that does the damage.* Twenty words, footed at twenty. Nobody improved on it, nobody asked her a second question, and a man of about thirty-one on the bench asked her whether she wanted the fire drawn nearer.** **She is a woman of seventy-two and not the woman of sixty-six in the valley four hundred miles off; the block first printed her at sixty-six, with the same bench and the same aisle, and the repair pass moved her. Her dateline also gave her a seat on the roll of the bench of nine, which the chapter itself denied eighteen lines later, and the dateline is what a reader holds while reading the rest, so the dateline was corrected and not the chapter.** The clerk enters it in the minute with no head over it and reads the minute back once and only once. **On the eleventh day after the eighth, in the same room, a version of the last eight months in which he does not do it reads to him as the reasonable one, and he can see the shape of it, and the shape is the shape of a thing that would have worked, and the part he cannot get past is that in that version his leg is only a thing about his leg. The version now lists the sealed list of eleven lines staying in a drawer with his mother on the eleventh of them where the first printing listed a valley woman and a question nobody asked her, which had already happened and so was not a difference between the two versions.** Nothing came. It is not a vision and it is not a voice and there is no panel. **He tells one person, the clerk of about sixty, in forty-four words, and the clerk does not write it down, and he has never once been asked by anybody why he does not write a thing down, and he has an answer ready, and nobody in this county has ever wanted it.**

**280 — The twenty-seventh of Longlight, YR 316, day 272, a Sunday, not a market day, the claim and the fee.** **The fever was over on the seventeenth and he had been up ten days by the twenty-seventh, and he had not gone up the bank since the seventh and has twenty days of thinking about it for nothing; both figures are the repair pass's and the first printing said the fever was over on the nineteenth with five days up, which is eight days of arithmetic against a day the block had already called the last day of it.** **A man of fifty-five at a barrier of three bars is given the same four words and adds nothing and is not asked for a fifth thing, and he has done the three bars up and down about four thousand times in nineteen years and has said the four words to about four hundred people, and the two figures are two populations.** Then the man with the stick says one more thing, twenty-seven words, to a man who is not going to repeat it: ***The road she crossed has a claim on its own history, and it is not a claim against her and it is not a claim for her.*** The man in the hut does not repeat it, and has never been asked where he gets the four words, and about four people in that lane have said since that a man who is not asked has a much better chance of keeping a thing than a man who is asked. **The claim is stated and the verdict is not, and nobody is going to state it and there is nowhere to state it.** **The observation that a book can have no column for what became of anybody was made to him before he was asked, by a man at a mill wheel who cannot leave it, and that man is not asked by anybody in this county and is not going to be, and he is not asked because there is no road that gets there and not because anybody in a fen county decided it, and only one of those two is a decision and it was not made here.** In the yard on Weir Street at about the fifth hour, out loud, to nine men who were not listening: **the price of the thing done on the eighth is another crossing and he is not going to make it.** The reason is a crossing is a claim, and a claimed road can be claimed again by somebody with a different column and a different hand, and the road had one claim on it and the owner was standing in the yard. The owner of the yard is twenty-five and says the bundle in the press is not his and is not on his book and is not going on his book. **Nobody walked any part of that Sunday with him, and a yard that has sent one thing cannot be ignored and this yard has sent one thing and nobody is going to be asked about it and nobody is going to be able to take it back.**


## Volume 06 Batch 0003 — review repair pass, and the four of these ten summaries that were wrong in a way a reader would have seen

**The summaries above are corrected in place. Nothing was removed and no chapter shape changed.** Nine of the ten chapters had at least one paragraph changed and Chapter 273 had none. **The changes a reader would have seen, in the order they were made:** the woman who spends the volume's one sentence is a woman of **seventy-two** and not a woman of sixty-six, because the woman of sixty-six in the valley has a bench and a fire and an aisle four feet wide and a want of her own; the dateline of Chapter 279 no longer gives the tenth person in that room a seat on the roll of the bench of nine, which the chapter denied eighteen lines later; the clerk in Chapter 271 reads the **twenty-fourth of Greenlight** off the inside cover of his book and names the first of Longlight as the day the field is coming back for, instead of reading the coming day as the day they were standing in; **the fever has one run on the page, beginning on the ninth of Longlight, day 255, and over on the seventeenth, day 262, and lasting about nine days**, and the three chapters that gave it three ends now agree; the yard in Chapter 277 is on the morning after and not on the Monday, and the chapter's dateline lists three hours; **the man of fifty-five's figures are two populations, about four hundred people spoken to and about four thousand let through, and the twelfth of Longlight is about nine people turned round**; the counterfactual in Chapter 279 is about a drawer and the eleventh line instead of a valley woman and a question nobody asked her; and the two money footings still foot and stop at fourteen pence and six pence in their own words.

**And the three repetitions the block's own sweeps had called clear**, all rewritten in place with every fact kept: Chapter 272 on the man of about nineteen and his elder sister, which repeated Chapter 269; Chapter 272 on the man of about sixty packing lime, which repeated Chapter 269 with four words changed; and Chapter 274 on the six columns and Chapter 274's money footing, which were Chapter 261's sentence and Chapter 263's nine words. **A sweep that reports a block clean is a statement about the instrument, not about the block, and this block reported one clean and had four.**

## Volume 06, Batch 0004, Chapters 281–290, "The Parliament of Oaths" (Block 4, days 273 to 313, YR 316)

**281 — The twenty-eighth of Longlight, YR 316, day 273, a Monday, not a market day, the toll house and a round.** A man of about thirty-one with a satchel does a round of nine drops in a fen county and a sheet of the office's own printed series ends up in the sill of a toll house with a man in it. **The sheet is not a summons and there is no person served on it; it has a place in the object column, a word in front of the place name, three empty columns and a date in the fifth, and the date is the ninth of a month, which is a Friday, which is not a market day, and it is eleven days off.** He reads it once from the bench and puts it back on the sill under the stone, because taking it off a sill would be a decision and he has not made one. A man at one of the nine doors says a true remark about the rain to nobody and shuts the door on a sheet he has not read. A man of fifty-five at a barrier of three bars says his four words and adds nothing. **At about the fifth hour the block's unattributed two-line statement is said out loud with the wind behind him and the door open at the low end, and is not written down.** Ends: nine sheets are on nine doors in that county and the ninth of the nine is in a sill with a date on it, and a county that keeps a register of claims and a day-book of things that were not asked has three kinds of paper in it and a date nobody asked for is not one of the three.

**282 — The third of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 278, a Saturday, a market day, the long room over the wharf.** **The one bench sitting in the block, and it is the ordinary seventh-hour Saturday sitting, and the bench of nine is asked nothing at all and the count on the page under that stair is eight before it and eight after it.** The salt takes eleven minutes and a hedge takes twenty and a gate is refused without a reason. The magistrate does not use the construction she has had ready for about a year and nobody in that room knew she had one. A clerk of about sixty enters that the bench had not voted and enters nothing about how many of the nine wanted it. **At about the sixth hour a man with a satchel collects a round, and at the ninth of the nine he takes a sheet out of that sill and puts it in the satchel and goes on down the lane without looking at it.** The sheet goes into a building two hundred miles off and is read that evening and nobody asks where it has been. The second copyist of about thirty goes to the provincial town on the Monday on a warrant to produce; the second keeper of twenty-six is not going and the third post in the day-book is not signed, and the two women have never spoken about either.

**283 — The eighth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 283, a Thursday, a market day, the provincial town.** **Perry Hask, 34, a second clerk of the returns, is first named here and is the block's only new name.** A tray goes into a passage and comes back. A file of one sheet with a district on it and no person on it is handed to him and it is not a return, and there is no line in that book for a sheet. He asks a man of about thirty who is a clerk of that room and is told *It is a sheet*. **He enters it as a sheet, on the line for the district, and the book will carry a line that is not a return for as long as the book is kept, and nobody in that room will ever look at it again and the line will be there.** He goes down to the press room and says his want in eleven words and is thanked for nothing and refused nothing; the man of about fifty contradicts himself at the stone, retracts it, is told *You did*, and goes down two flights. The booking board in the passage on the second floor carries four cards of the same colour and the same word for the ninth of a month in four consecutive years, and a fifth card of a different colour, and nobody in that building has asked the question in the other direction.

**284 — The ninth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 284, a Friday, not a market day, the chamber.** **Two things in one room on one day and nobody joins them in a sentence.** The Crown's proceeding sits at the second hour with a table of three, a witness list of eight names, a form of oath on the back of a return, and about six people in the room. **A delegation cannot arrive and is not sent for and is not in that chamber and has not been in that building on that date in four years; its matter is in a folder on a board at the end of the room with a card on it and the word on the card is *stood*.** A second folder a foot away carries a card and the word *sat*. **Alish Renn, thirty, a second copyist from a fen county, came two hundred miles on a warrant to produce and is in the room as a witness and not as a copyist, and asks whether there is a seat, and is told there is a chair for the person before it, a stool for the clerk and a bench along the wall because the room is that shape.** Two of the six in the room are there because they are clerks. A man of about thirty-two with a limp is in the room because his name is on the sixth line in a hand that is not his and is not the office's. **The money column foots on the page to eight pence.** Ends: the finding at the end of that proceeding is a figure, and nobody in that building has entered that what was asked in that chamber is not a column and that what will be found in it is.

**285 — The tenth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 285, a Saturday, a market day, the room with the stove in it.** **A copy comes down two flights on a tray and a woman of thirty-three, an aid to the register and a member of nothing, finds her own name in a column with a head on it that she has filled in about two hundred times a season for eleven years.** The copy was made on the ground floor the day before by putting a filled sheet face down on a clean one and ruling the six columns again over the top of it and going along the lines with the same hand, in about nine minutes. **The nine shapes are hers and a stroke is left short at the top the way she leaves it short, and the weight of it is wrong, and that is the whole of what she has in about two seconds.** She says her want, which is the same sentence and has not got one word more in it than it had in the month she was twenty-two. **She then asks a question, and it is the first question anybody in that building has asked about that column in eleven years, and nobody answers it**, and the clerk of the returns answers a different question and says that is not what she asked. The copy is squared with two fingers and put in a tray by a person who has not been asked to put it in a tray. Her note of nineteen words stays face down and is not turned over.

**286 — The eleventh of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 286, a Friday, not a market day, the room with the stove in it, the third speech.** **A man of about fifty comes up two flights and stands in that room for about four minutes and says nothing at all and does not come up again.** A clerk of the Crown stands in the passage outside and does not come in. **A woman of about twenty-nine says a kind thing in five words and stops in the middle of it, and a woman of thirty-three says the third thing, and it is printed word for word and is not improved on: *I have been afraid of that column since I was twenty-two and I filled it in this year in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and you have now put my name in it again, and both of those are the same hand, and neither of them is mine. Do not thank me. I would like somebody to write down that I did not stop it and there is nobody in this building I can ask.*** **Nobody thanked her, nobody told her she had been right, nobody said it was not her fault, and nobody in that building asked her anything.** A second clerk of the returns offers her a form and is refused, and says he had to ask, and is told he did not. Ends: a table in that room has had a kind thing offered at it once since a woman was twenty-two and has refused it, and does not get one offered at it again, and nobody in that building has worked out how to do that on purpose and nobody has had to.

**287 — The seventeenth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 292, a Saturday, a market day, the chamber with the long table and the press room.** **The head of the record still says a schedule is to be complete before the first of Longlight, and the first of Longlight was sixteen days before, and about four people in that building have worked that out and none of them has said so to anybody.** The man of forty-four reads about two hundred and thirty lines in about two hours and his want is not said again. A woman of thirty-eight reads the first column of the first line of that schedule over his shoulder, says one thing about a sheet and not about a person, and is not asked a question about it. **A woman of about thirty is eight days in that town on a warrant to produce, in a room at the end of a second-floor passage with a bed a clerk of the Crown had made, and no second sitting has been entered and nobody has said otherwise.** A printed list goes out to nine counties and in one of about nine object lines there is a word in front of a place name, and that is the sixth printing of that word in this volume and it is defined zero times. A boy of nineteen with eleven weeks to serve says he set it and did not know what it was, and is told he set it, and nobody in that room says the other half of it.

**288 — The twenty-fourth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 299, a Saturday, a market day, the second sitting.** **The room has no window and takes its light off a lamp on a bracket and has done for about nine years.** A man of thirty-two with a limp is sworn on the back of a return and nobody asks him anything for about a minute and a half, and then he says eleven sentences before anybody asks him for any part of it and before the order of the marshal's office is read: what he did, on the eighth of a month in Longlight, on the strength of a line somebody else wrote, with no keeper at his shoulder and no rope and no second person in the room, and what it took, and forty yards of hemp four feet down, and a bell a hundred yards off that went at the fourth hour and a half the same morning, and a man of fifty-eight four hundred miles off who is not coming back and is not going to be told why. **The eleventh sentence announces that he has one more and is not going to say it. A clerk of the Crown made a stroke in the margin against each of the eleven, and the space after the eleventh is ruled and empty, and there is no rule after a twelfth.** The four words he has had ready since a day he cannot count are not said. **Nobody asked him why he began the way he began, and nobody is going to, and there is no line in that proceeding for a reason a witness had before he stood up.** A woman of thirty-eight enters the room as a room in the minute in her own hand, and has just watched the best possible version of what she asked for in Thawmonth performed by a witness, and it did not work. **The order is read at about the fourth hour, and a man of about thirty-one with a satchel says in eleven words that he has never once known what was in the four places, and nobody asks him a question about it.**

**289 — The first of Harvestmonth, YR 316, day 306, a Saturday, a market day, the court and the long table.** **The court accepts a temporary injunction against forced culling at about the fourth hour and a clerk of the Crown reads the term out: it holds to a day and after that day it holds if a local council renews it in public.** A woman of thirty-eight asks whether anybody in that county can renew it and is told there is nobody in that county at all, and asks for that to be written down, and is told it is in the ninth line and she did not hear the ninth line. **Two floors up the second hour and the third hour come and go and nobody reads anything into the record, and a clerk with a bad wrist sharpens a pen twice, and the man of forty-four is not in that room and his stove is cold and nobody has asked him where he is.** The money column foots on the page to seven pence. A clerk of the Crown asks a woman of thirty-eight whether a certain column is a column and she says yes in one word. **A woman of about thirty goes down two flights and out of the front door with a bag of her own, and nobody in that building said that the reason she was able to go was that the thing that was being held was over.** Ends: about four hundred people in a county two hundred miles off do not know that a thing they were frightened of has stopped being written down, and an office that has gone out of the ordinary way has not been written to and does not know that it has.

**290 — The eighth of Harvestmonth, YR 316, day 313, a Saturday, a market day, the county.** **A courier comes up the county's own road at about the second hour with about four hundred people in the market and does not stop in the market.** A courier is not a carrier and the two of them have never met. The sheet is a copy of a minute of a court and it says four things, and the fourth is one line at the foot of a printed sheet with no name against it and no office to ask. **The county reads it in a room over a weigh-house and it does not name a bell and it does not name a crossing and it does not name that county at all.** A reeve comes up two flights and gets to a true thing by saying the wrong one first. The magistrate is not told and has a construction ready and did not use it on a courier. The day-book stands at nine entries of a thing nobody asked and there is no tenth coming. **The office pays fourpence a year and that is the whole of what it has ever cost that county to be a thing with a door and a number on it.** The second copyist puts the courier's sheet into the press that can be served with anything, and a man of thirty-two with a limp takes it out of that press, puts it in his coat, does not ask what he is going to do with it, and puts it into a press in a room in a yard that belongs to the yard and cannot be served with anything. Ends: a county of about four thousand people read a minute of a court on a market morning and does not know whether to be glad, and a sheet that says so is in a press that nobody can be served with, and about four hundred people in that town went home that day knowing none of it.

## Volume 06 Batch 0004 — the block's ten endings, as a list, and the two figures attached to something this block never prints

**The ten endings.** 1. Nine sheets are on nine doors in a county and a date nobody asked for is not one of its three kinds of paper. 2. A sheet goes back down a lane in a satchel and is read two hundred miles off and nobody asks where it has been. 3. A book in a provincial town carries a line that is not a return and nobody in that room will ever look at it again and the line will be there. 4. The finding at the end of that proceeding is a figure, and what was asked in that chamber is not a column. 5. She is going to fill that column in on Monday from a roll without looking up, and she is not going to stop. 6. A table where a kind thing has been refused once does not get one offered at it again. 7. A word is not printed on a list any more and is not struck in a case any more, and a boy of nineteen is standing at the top of a staircase. 8. The figure at the end of it is the ordinary work of an office that has been doing this nine times in nine years. 9. An office has gone out of the ordinary way and does not know that it has, and nobody in that chamber is going to tell it. 10. A county read a minute of a court and does not know whether to be glad, and the sheet that says so is in a press nobody can be served with.

**The two figures attached to something this block never prints, one per figure, as the phase instruction requires them to be recorded.** One, **the four words** a man of thirty-two with a limp has had ready since a day he cannot count, named in `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0288.md` and not printed there or anywhere in this volume. Two, **the nineteen words** on a face-down leaf in a book on a shelf in a case behind a woman of thirty-three, named in `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0285.md` and in `chapter-0286.md` and not printed in either. A third, **the same four words** a man of fifty-five gives at a barrier, is named three times in `chapter-0281.md` and is not printed, and it is a standing canon figure from Blocks 2 and 3 and not a new one. **No other speech-length figure in this block is attached to something the block does not print.** The four figures that are footed are Chapter 282's fifteen words, Chapter 283's eleven words, Chapter 288's eleven words twice over, and Chapter 287's thirty-four words, which is the man of forty-four's want as first printed in Chapter 255 and footed there. **Chapter 285's first speech has no length figure on the page at all**, because the outline calls that want four or five words and the sentence is nine, and the block prints neither figure and does not repair the outline.

## Volume 06 Batch 0004 — review repair pass, and the four of these ten summaries that a change of date or a change of count made wrong

**What this pass did to the summaries above.** No summary above was rewritten, for the reason the Batch 0001 entry gives and Batch 0003's pass repeated: a summary that was true when it was written is a fact about the book and rewriting it destroys the record of what the block believed. **Four of the ten had a figure in them that this pass changed on the page, and a fifth had a figure that was wrong when it was written, and all five are corrected here, and continuity item 757 carries the ledger and item 755 carries the dates.**

1. **Chapter 282 is no longer a chapter whose last paragraph is a Monday.** The chapter is the third of Rainmonth, day 278, a **Saturday**, and its closing paragraph was headed as a Monday and carried a bench of nine sitting *that morning*, and the bench sits on Saturdays and on nothing else. **It is now the Saturday, with the bench, the clerk of about sixty, the tide, the salt and the bell inside it, and the second copyist's departure on the Monday is stated as ahead of it.** The chapter also no longer uses the *Nobody walked any part of that* frame twice; it uses it once, on the last line, where it is the answer to Chapter 281's.
2. **Chapter 287's interval was thirty days out.** The summary said the first of Longlight was *sixteen days* before that Saturday and it is **forty-six**, and the *about a month* beside it is *about six weeks*. The chapter also no longer narrates its own device count: the sentence that said *eastern* was the sixth time it had been printed and had been defined none of the six times is gone from the prose and lives in item 757, and what the prose says now is that the word is in the same type as the heads of the five columns and a man of about fifty at the press has looked at it every day for about a year and has not been asked what it is for.
3. **Chapter 288's and Chapter 289's elapsed figures were wrong and are now exact.** The second copyist has been in that building **fifteen days** at day 299 and **twenty-two days** at day 306, and Chapter 289's *about four weeks* and *for four weeks* are both of them twenty-two days, and the head's date is **sixty days** old rather than *a month*, and the head has been read about nine times in two months rather than in one. **Chapter 290 is the third chapter with a changed figure: she has been back in that room for three days, having come down the made road on the fourth of Harvestmonth, which is day 306 plus the four days on the road Chapter 284's money column already gave for the outward journey, and the three weeks and a day the two women have not spoken about is now named exactly.**
4. **The market crowd is a different number in three chapters.** The valley's **hundred and forty** is a count of askings on the end of a bench and the block's own prompt protected it, and Chapters 285, 287 and 288 had used it for the crowd at a market in the provincial town. **The crowd is about three hundred people in all three, and the block's four surviving *hundred and forty* are all *two hundred and forty* and are all the schedule.**
5. **Chapter 284's witness list summary was correct and one of the two figures in the item above it was not.** The item above these summaries records the block's first printing of 1,098 words of dialogue across 89 speeches, and the page is 1,111 across 91, and 23,745 words for the block and 1,023,773 for the manuscript. **The two figures that were wrong when the block was written and are right now are the ones the four summaries above do not carry and item 757 does.**

**What did not change in any of the ten.** No summary's beat moved. **The two proceedings are still never joined in one sentence and the companion file is still not removed, corrected or asked after. The delegation still does not arrive. The witness list still has eight names and six people in the chamber and two of the six are there because they are clerks. The woman of thirty-three is still not thanked, is not converted, has still not had her note of nineteen words turned over, and her want has not changed and is still nine words against an outline that says four or five. The man of thirty-two with a limp still says eleven sentences and does not say a twelfth, the four words are still not said, and the reason he went first is still a sentence in another month that this volume does not print. The injunction is still temporary, the Culling Order has still gone underground, the man of forty-four is still not in his room with a cold stove, and the county is still the last page and still does not know whether to be glad. A bench of nine was still asked nothing and the count under that stair is still eight.**

## Volume 06, Batch 0005, Chapters 291 to 300, "The Compounding" (Block 5, days 314 to 390, YR 316)

**Ch 291 · the ninth day of Harvestmonth, day 314, a Sunday and not a market day · the room over a weigh-house, a lane, a reach.** The block opens on the only Sunday in the volume. **A body corporate that can be served with anything by anybody who walks up a lane cannot shut on a Sunday without deciding something, and the keeper of records, twenty-nine, four years and a half out of a deed of thirteen words at fourpence a year, opened the door at about the first hour because a woman with a pail knocked on it.** The woman had said one thing at each of nine doors that morning and had told nobody that there was a room, and she told the keeper of records that she had not told the room, and the keeper of records did not ask her why she says things at doors. **A second copyist of about thirty is in that room and goes on the Monday at the sixth hour in a cart and has wanted a line in the day-book with her own name on it since the summer before last and has not asked for it in a form, and the two women have not raised it and are not going to.** **The keeper of records took the courier's minute out of the press and put it on the shelf, and the press in that room can be served with anything and a press four hundred yards up Weir Street cannot, and that is the second time she has decided where a piece of paper goes and neither decision is entered anywhere.** The reeve said the wrong thing first and got to a true one in about ninety seconds, as she always does. A man of fifty and a half came down a ladder because a bay wants nothing, and a boy of fifteen copied the widest space on his board. **Change:** the county's first act of a new era is a Sunday on which nothing can be entered, and the office does not shut, and the reason it does not shut is that a man came up a lane on Saturday with a bag. **Ends:** on Thursday the round comes up that lane, and the stone that has been sitting on the ninth sill since the twenty-eighth of a month in Longlight with nothing on it is put back down on top of a new one.

**Ch 292 · the thirteenth day of Harvestmonth, day 318, a Thursday and a market day · the lane, nine sills, a toll house four hundred yards up the road, two rooms over a weigh-house.** **A carrier of about thirty-one with a satchel puts nine sheets of that office's own printed series on nine sills, does not knock at any of them, and leaves the stone that has been on the ninth sill since Longlight on top of the new sheet.** He has never once found out what is in the four places and has said so out loud three times in six years and about four hundred people in that town have heard none of the three, and a woman with a pail told him she tells nine doors and not the room. **A woman of about thirty with a pail carried one of those sheets down the lane on her arm and put it on a table in the room over the weigh-house and did not read it.** **The keeper of records worked out the term of the injunction on the back of the courier's minute in pencil, small, in a corner, in about four seconds: it holds to a day and after that day only if a local council renews it in public, and there is no council in this county, and a bench of nine is not a council and has never been asked anything, and a magistrate does not renew anything in public, and there is no line in that office for a date against a thing that does not exist in the county.** Nobody asked her anything and she did not go four hundred yards to tell anybody. A man of fifty-five was in a hut at a barrier three hundred yards down the road and turned it down about nine times. **Change:** a date is now in pencil on the back of a court's sheet in a county that cannot do anything about it and has not been asked to. **Ends:** the ninth sheet is under a stone on a sill four hundred yards up that road and will be there on Saturday.

**Ch 293 · the seventeenth day of Harvestmonth, day 322, a Monday and not a market day · a press room on the ground floor, a room with a stove one floor up, a building of four floors and seven presses.** **The contested record goes out as a sheet of that office's own printed series with a figure of persons in the second column, under a head that says *Date*, and with the first column's space in front of the name of the place left empty, because the sort for the word in it has been in a drawer for two years, was struck once on a list that went to nine counties in the second month, and is not going to be struck again.** A man of about fifty, thirty-one years at that press, about eleven thousand forms, said the true thing about that column, and it is twenty words and foots at twenty. **A woman of thirty-eight came down two flights and said thank you, and a clerk of the Crown wrote the thanks in a margin in about four seconds in a hand that is not the office's, and a true thing thanked by the office now has a day on it and a person against it and is a finding, and that is the worst thing that happened in that press room in about two years and it took two words.** **The printer's mate of nineteen, who has eleven weeks to serve before the next sitting and wants to be a journeyman, was not in that room when the room was told what the drawer held.** The man of about fifty put a sheet under the press and said nothing else about it and that is the last time anybody in that building will say anything to him about a column. A clerk of the returns asked whether the returns book had a line for nine copies and was offered a second way of doing the thing and took neither. A man with a satchel offered to take nine copies early in a passage and was told they were not done. **Change:** the Crown's acknowledgement of the contest has gone out in the same shape as the thing that contested it, with a figure of persons under a head that says *Date* and nowhere on the sheet a place for a name. **Ends:** a woman of thirty-three fills in the fourth column of two forms from a roll in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and nobody in that room is watching her and she does not check.

**Ch 294 · the twenty-second day of Harvestmonth, day 327, a Saturday and a market day · the room with the stove in it on the first floor.** **A quarter ends in a ruled book nine inches by six and a quarter begins in it, and a woman of about twenty-nine who is a clerk of the returns carried a district from one quarter to the next in about four seconds, and a line is a line and lines do not have quarters on them.** **The thing that has gone out of the ordinary way in that building is a schedule, and a schedule is a count of places, and a district is a place, and a place does not stop being counted because the counting of it has been given up by somebody two floors up, and there is no column in that book for which office's habit it is.** A man of about thirty asked whether the schedule is still going out and was told *I do not know* and then heard the only sentence that woman of twenty-nine has said in that room in about six years, which is that nobody has told this room and that this room will go on turning the page whatever happens in the room it happens in, and then that she will put it in the book and that the book has four places ruled for a figure and nowhere at all for a name. A man of about thirty-one with a satchel asked the first question anybody in that room has asked about what a line is for and got an answer from nobody. **On the line for that district there is one entry that is not a return, entered in the second month as a sheet because there was no line for anything else, and the pen went over it in about four seconds and did not stop and did not go round it.** A woman of thirty-three filled in the *Keeper* column three times and put her hand flat on a book on a second shelf and took it off without turning a leaf. **Change:** a district is now counted for a fourth time by a room that has not been told, and nobody has asked the man who entered the sheet that is not a return. **Ends:** the county is being counted for a fourth time and the counting is not the thing that stopped.

**Ch 295 · the twenty-ninth day of Harvestmonth, day 334, a Saturday and a market day · the chamber the Crown sits in on the third floor, a board at the end of it, a passage on the second floor.** A chamber with no window, two candles in tin holders, taken off candles for about nine years. **On a board at the end of it are two folders a foot apart, and the first is a hearing entered for a delegation that cannot arrive with a card that says *stood*, and the second is a file of one sheet with a district on it and a card that says *sat*, and nothing has ever been sat in it.** **The wrapper on that folder is this quarter's and the card on it was written this week and the sheet inside is the same sheet, and the card is the only new thing in the folder and the only thing in it anybody can produce.** A woman of thirty-eight read the card, read the date on it, and put her hand flat on the board for about four seconds, and said the three things she could have done to a file and did none of them, and nobody thanked her for that either. **A clerk of the Crown came in with the wrapper and she told him there was no line on that board for a reason, and he put the wrapper back and wrote nothing and took nothing off.** The booking board on the second floor has four cards gone and one left, and a second copyist went home in a cart on the sixteenth of that month and nobody in that building has mentioned her since. **Change:** a matter that was never sat now has a card on it that says it was, and it will stay that way, and doing nothing to a file is a thing a person decides. **Ends:** a cart left that building on that Saturday afternoon and will be two hundred miles nearer by the fourth hour of a Tuesday in a month that has only just begun. **The nine sheets went onto the nine sills on the *thirteenth* of Harvestmonth, in Chapter 292, and came off them on the twentieth, and this chapter's dateline and its last paragraph said the seventeenth and were corrected by the review repair pass; the seventeenth in this chapter's money frame is Chapter 293's own date and is correct.**

**Ch 296 · the fourth day of Fallowmonth, day 339, a Thursday and a market day · the room over the weigh-house, and a reach four hundred yards down a lane.** A cart brought a sheet up the lane on the Tuesday and a woman of twenty-nine had it on a table since. **She read it at about the third hour: six columns and five heads, a set of market towns in the first column, a figure of persons in the second column, and a head over the second column that says *Date*. The figure is about nine hundred more than the town would have said, and the reeve got to the true thing by saying the wrong one first, and the true thing is that there is nothing in a figure to be wrong.** A county of about four thousand people cannot refuse a figure and cannot check one and has no writ and no seal and no office and nothing to show a thing to, and there is no line on a form in that office that a county can send an answer in, and the thing that is contested is a figure and a claim in that office is a claim about a person, and nobody there can make one into the other. **The sheet gives a day by which cause may be shown to an office two hundred miles off, and it is *about ten weeks off*, and this was eleven weeks until the review repair pass, which made it the same figure as the valley's eleven weeks in Chapter 297. The three week-figures in the block are now distinct and none of them is anybody else's: about ten weeks is the office's day, nine weeks is how long before that day the county was entered in a schedule it did not know existed, and eleven weeks is said in the valley's own mouth.** **She said the answer out loud: nothing, and nothing is the whole of what that office has ever been able to do, and she has a day-book for it, and it is the only book there nobody can be served with, and it has nine entries in it of a thing that was not asked and is not going to get a tenth and a tenth would not be a gift if it came.** The sheet went on the shelf and not in the press, and the register came down and was put back without anything entered, and the day-book was not opened at all that day. **A man of thirty-two with a limp took a leaf out of a coat at about the sixth hour and half and looked at a seventh line that says *a person* for about a minute and a quarter and put it back, and that is the sixth time in six months and it is not finished and there is nobody in that county he could finish it with.** **Change:** a county of about four thousand people has read a figure it cannot check and has answered it with the only instrument it has, which is a book that cannot be served with, and the answering is not in any book. **Ends:** a county entered in a schedule it did not know existed was told about it nine weeks after it was entered.

**Ch 297 · the thirteenth day of Fallowmonth, day 348, a Saturday, and not a market day in a county with a market, nine days off · a room over a cross in a valley four hundred miles from any county on a map.** **A man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work said the figure out loud, once, in the ordinary way, and it is eleven weeks, and the man of fifty-eight said *It is*, and nobody in that valley converted it into anything and the narrator did not convert it, and no character converts a calendar into a valley count or the reverse.** The book is on a trestle with nine spreads in it, one to a generation, kept nineteen years and by the men before him. **There is one finding in it, at the head of the first spread under the four lines, in the keeper's own hand, on a line he ruled himself with a straight edge off the back of the trestle, the first line ruled across in that book in a hundred and forty years, and about nine people in that room have seen the ruled line and nobody has asked the man of fifty-eight about it and nobody is going to, and he was never asked whether he could stand it afterwards.** Nine people on benches, about thirty in the room, about two hundred of the ninth generation at the back. A man of fifty-five asked about the ninth line of the second column and the answer was that it is not going to be ruled, **and he asked it in twelve words, which is his two sentences, *The ninth line is not ruled across.* at seven and *Then nothing goes in it.* at five, and the block printed *about nine words* until the review repair pass corrected the figure and left both speeches alone.** **The man of thirty-four asked whether the man who came up a road nine days and read a book aloud was coming back, and the man of fifty-eight said that he had not asked him that and was not going to ask the other one either, and that if he is asked a second time in that room he will not answer it in that room.** A hundred and forty is cut into the end of the bench at the back of the right-hand row and is a count of the times anybody has ever stood in the aisle to be asked, and the aisle is four feet wide and has gone three generations without being used, and nobody has put the two figures side by side. **Ends:** at the door a woman of thirty-six said to the man of thirty-four and not to the room that she will go down the road in the morning, and nobody asked her why.

**Ch 298 · the eighteenth day of Fallowmonth, day 353, a Thursday, and not a market day in a county with a market · a made road about four hundred yards long, a yard with about two hundred feet of wall, a mill at the low end of the water.** **Bessa Quill, thirty-six, keeps a bridge over the river with about two hundred and forty feet of stone on it, and she got up before the mill and rode four hundred yards down a made road nobody has come down and stood at a standing finish on the end of it for about as long as it takes to look at nine feet of grass twice and came back up with nothing, and the reason nobody knows she went is that a valley of about four hundred people wakes at about the fifth hour and she was back before it.** **She said her want once, in a yard, to a boy of about nine with a barrow and not to the yard and not to a stranger, and it is the only time she has said it, and the boy carried on to the mill and nothing is asked of him and he is not named.** **Nobody thanked her, nobody told her it would be all right, nobody gave her a reason, and a reason was available in about four kitchens that afternoon and none of it was given to her, and she was not put in a record and the day-book forty feet from a wagon arch did not get a tenth entry.** The man of thirty-four said her whole name in the yard, which is the first time it has been said in that yard, and asked her one question and got one word, and the question was not the one anybody wanted to ask. **Seven words were said to him after that and the seven foot: *Nobody is to be told I went.*** And a promise and an entry are not the same thing, **and the promise is *I am not going to tell anybody*, which is seven words and was described in the next sentence as nine until the review repair pass corrected the figure and left the speech alone,** and a valley of about four hundred people has an instrument for the second and not for the first, and the instrument is a book nobody will show her. **Change:** the road was gone down and came back from, and nobody in that valley was told, and the volume does not say that this is the last time any of them looks for him. **Ends:** about four hundred people in that valley went to bed not knowing, and the road is still there and the standing finish is still on the end of it, and there is no column anywhere in that valley for a road that was gone down and came back from, and nobody in that valley is going to look for anybody on it again.

**Ch 299 · the eighteenth day of Embermonth, day 383, a Saturday and a market day · a reach four hundred yards down a lane, a toll house a hundred yards from the end of the market, a yard on Weir Street, a barrier three hundred yards down the road.** A quiet season. The salt over the first bay on the tide since the spring and it is the salt merchant's and it is not the guild's and the two have never been in one column in this county. **The fourth bay is finished and pointed and a man of fifty and a half has been putting a finish on a finish for a fortnight.** **In the third course of the fourth bay, under about half an inch of lime, there is a line about nine inches long, in the stone and not across a joint, which has not moved and which nobody has measured, ruled across, laid a rule on or put a finger on, and about forty men worked nine feet off it every working day for a fortnight and none of them has ever mentioned it to another of them.** **At the fourth hour and a half the bell goes, in the present tense and on the page: nine stone of green-black bronze, a band of forty-one rivets, a dull red seam in the metal split lip to shoulder, chest-high, rung by a boy who has been the steward's apprentice for two years and three months and is still not good at it and by a carpenter who is a hand and not a keeper, on a line pulled together on the count of four, neither of them paid by the guild and neither of them a member of anything, and nobody in that county can be asked who keeps it and the answer nobody can give is the finding.** Nine men in a yard and a bench-board four feet off the ground and a press in a room at the end of it that cannot be served with anything and a bundle in it with nothing on the wrapper; three ordinary sentences about a hod, a space and a heap of lime. A man of fifty-five in a hut at a barrier said the same four words about nine times and nobody has asked him where they come from. **A crossing a hundred yards from the end of that market carries nobody and carried nobody for four years before anything ever happened to it, and there is no owner and no money and no glass in the sill and no third seat, and forty yards of tarred hemp went into the abutment four feet down on the fourth of a month in the year before and nobody has dug for it and nobody is going to dig for it, and in the face of a dressed block in that abutment there is a line about nine inches long, in the stone and not across a joint and not in a joint, under no lime of its own, which has not moved and which nobody has measured.** A man of thirty-two with a limp was on the bench inside and said one thing to the door, that it is on the same count, and nobody asked him about it. **Change:** the bell was rung and the volume asked who keeps it and nobody answered, and the bell goes on. **Ends:** a man of forty-seven was not in that market and has not been in it this month.

**Ch 300 · the twenty-fifth day of Embermonth, day 390, a Saturday and a market day, and the last day of the year · a market, a bench-board in a yard, the long room over a wharf, a page under a stair.** The bell went at the fourth hour and a half and goes on. **A man of forty-seven was at the end of a bench-board in a yard four hundred yards up that road with a man with a stick about nine feet off him, a yard wall behind one of them and nobody else in the yard, and he said the four things for the fifth time in a year, and a man with a stick asked him the same thing he has asked four times and got them and asked nothing else.** He is on the roll of a bench of nine with a vote and not an office, is not on a trade, has not used his vote since the day he was elected and did not use it then, has been a witness at two ends of two crossings in a year, is paid fourpence a week out of a private box, and holds nothing. **At about the seventh hour a woman of thirty-eight came up the outside stair on her own and put the term of the injunction on the long table and asked the bench of nine to renew it in public, there and that morning, as a matter of the county's own record and not of a court two hundred miles off, and it is a thing and not a figure of persons and the county can refuse it, and the magistrate did not use the construction she has had ready for about a year and nobody wrote it down for her.** **She said the bench's no and it is eleven words and foots at eleven: *No, because we have never been asked for anything at all.*** Nobody improved on it. **The clerk of about sixty entered that the bench did not vote on the line for a thing that was not decided and entered the reason under it in his own hand, and that is the reason on the page twice, once in the mouth of a bench and once in the ink of a clerk, and he has no line in that minute for how many times a thing has happened in it and has not gone looking for one.** Nobody thanked her for asking and nobody said the county was right. **A clerk of the Crown said *you will want it minuted that it was refused* and she said *I will want it minuted that the bench refused it* and he said *that is a different line* and she said *it is the same line with a person at the front of it*, and went down the outside stair without staying to see it written.** **At about the eighth hour the clerk went down four steps and put a ninth mark under eight on a page about nine inches by six under that stair, and he did not enter the number nine anywhere else, and nobody in that hall has ever entered that count on a form, and the count is a count of askings and is not a price and is not a count of persons and is added to nothing.** The minute was read back once and only once. **The man of forty-seven was on that bench and was asked nothing.** **Change:** the count of askings on the page under that stair is nine, a bench of nine has said no in eleven words to the first thing it was asked by anybody who was not in this county, and nobody in that hall has ever entered that count on a form. **Ends, and the volume ends:** a county of four thousand people with two crossings in it, the county's own figure that the two of them are four hundred yards apart, a line about nine inches long in the third course of the fourth bay of the one that carries a road over a river and a line about nine inches long in the face of a dressed block in the abutment of the one a hundred yards from the end of that market, neither of them measured, nobody in the county knowing of the other one, about four hundred people going home from that market not knowing that there are two, and there has never been a book in this kingdom with the two of them in it and there is not going to be one.

### The ten endings, as a list

1. **291** — the stone that has been sitting on the ninth sill since Longlight is put back down on top of a new one.
2. **292** — the ninth sheet is under a stone on a sill four hundred yards up that road and will be there on Saturday.
3. **293** — a woman of thirty-three fills in the fourth column without looking up, and nobody is watching and she does not check.
4. **294** — the county is being counted for a fourth time and the counting is not the thing that stopped.
5. **295** — a cart left that building on that Saturday afternoon and will be two hundred miles nearer by the fourth hour of a Tuesday.
6. **296** — a county entered in a schedule it did not know existed was told about it nine weeks after it was entered.
7. **297** — a woman of thirty-six says at a door, to one man and not to a room, that she will go down the road in the morning.
8. **298** — there is no column anywhere in that valley for a road that was gone down and came back from, and nobody in that valley is going to look for anybody on it again.
9. **299** — a man of forty-seven was not in that market and has not been in it this month.
10. **300** — the two crossings, and there has never been a book in this kingdom with the two of them in it and there is not going to be one.

### The three cards, and every deviation from them, counted

1. **Ch 291–295, the aftermath and the four documents.** **No deviation in substance and one in arrangement.** The four documents are a contested record, an injunction with an expiry, a schedule gone underground with a district that has not, and a companion file of one sheet, each in its own room with one person in it; **the Crown's acknowledgement is the contested record and not a fifth document, because the outline's §15 item 20 makes the acknowledgement a fifth thing and the prompt's card makes the contested record one of the four, and the only way to hold both is to let the acknowledgement be the contested record, which is also the volume's argument in one object. Judged as improving the book.** A man of about fifty is thanked for a true thing about a column and the thanks is worse and he goes back to the press, in Chapter 293. The printer's mate of nineteen is not in the room when the room is told what the drawer held and the type is not struck again, in Chapter 293. **The keeper of records is not thanked in any of the four rooms and no fifth person notices anything, which is the block's shape.**
2. **Ch 296–298, a county that has been counted and a valley that has lost a man.** **Two deviations, both recorded.** The ninth ask is not in this card's range on the page: **it is in Chapter 300, on day 390, because the block is allowed one bench scene and the prompt says that one is the volume's last and is the one the ninth ask belongs to, and Chapter 300 is the volume's last day and its last bench sitting.** Judged as improving the book, because a ninth ask at day 348 would have left the volume with a bench scene that was not its last and would have cost the man of forty-seven his once-more. **The valley's eleven weeks is printed as a figure said in the valley and is not converted, because it cannot be true of any date in this block on the chain and no batch phase repairs a source document; the arithmetic is at continuity item 764. Judged as the only honest handling available.** Bessa Quill is the only new face and her want is said once, in a yard, to a boy with a barrow.
3. **Ch 299–300, the two crossings and the last page.** **Three deviations, all recorded.** The outline's card says *a boy of seventeen* and the prose of two volumes says *a boy* with no age, and the block followed the prose and printed no age, because an age is a numeral. The card says *that nobody has measured in five volumes* and that is a narrator's reference to this project's own artefact and was not printed; the page says nobody has measured it. **And the county's own figure that the two crossings are four hundred yards apart is attributed to the county rather than stated flat, because the reach is four hundred yards down a lane from the market and the toll house is four hundred yards up the county's own road and the volume's standing figure is the county's, not the narrator's arithmetic.** All three judged as improving the book.

### What the block did not do, one line each, including the things it noticed and did not do

- **It did not join the four documents, and it did not put two of them in one room, which is the whole of the block's argument and the whole of its discipline.**
- **It did not print the figure of persons against the district, did not define the district, did not repeat or repair the eleven-word or seventeen-word figures on the sentence about a district in Chapter 244, and did not put the number of persons the office would not print on an offer anywhere near anything.**
- **It did not reconcile the five refusal figures, add any two of them, or add any of them to a figure of persons.**
- **It did not add about four hundred doors to about four hundred doors, did not work out how many there are, and did not say which county the older list is in.** The carrier of about fifty with a firm of two does not appear in this block at all, so the two carriers did not meet, and the courier of Chapter 290 does not appear either and is not in a room with either of them.
- **It did not print the word in front of a place name for a seventh time and did not define it, and the type was not struck again.**
- **It did not print the tile on a coping, did not mention it, and did not schedule anything for it.**
- **It did not name either line in a stone, did not call either of them a seam, did not measure either, rule across either, lay a rule on either, point at either, or use either as a door, a key or a mark, and did not repeat or vary the sentence in Chapter 276 that first put the two in one narrator's sentence.**
- **It did not dig for the forty yards of tarred hemp, and nobody in that block asks whether it is there.**
- **It explained nothing: no System panel, no lineage reading, no account of what a cut does to an anchor, no roadmark, no origin or maker or deathbed for the bell, and the standing limit was not paid again.**
- **It did not use the word *failed* about a road, a cut, a contact or a person, and the crossing that carries nobody is a crossing that carries nobody.**
- **It did not enter a tenth not-asking, did not thank the woman of thirty-three, did not convert her, did not change her want, did not make her explain anything, and did not turn her leaf over.**
- **It did not put a man and a woman on a road together, and nobody in the block walks any part of any day with anybody.**
- **It did not refer to, quote, re-tell, shorten or improve on the sentence she said in a gateway in another month, and it did not put her on a road.**
- **It did not spend the magistrate's construction, did not have her use it, and did not have anybody write it down for her.**
- **It did not ask the man of forty-seven anything a sixth time, did not get him the four things a sixth time, did not add an occasion that is not on the list, and did not make his fifth occasion a different kind of occasion from the four before it.**
- **It did not add a new final enemy, did not name a new office, council, order or mechanism, did not write a court or an Order as a character, did not give either a want, and did not have any council renew the injunction or refuse to.**
- **And the thing it noticed and did not do, which is the part a later writer needs: it noticed that the county's copy of the contested record carries the same wrong head the press room found, and it left the county not noticing it, because a fifth noticing would have been a fifth person and the block is four. It noticed that the district on the returns book is being carried into a second quarter by a clerk who has worked out that her room's habit and another room's habit are two things, and it did not put those two rooms in a sentence, because nobody in the block is allowed to do that. And it noticed that a Crown officer of thirty-eight came two hundred miles to be refused in eleven words, and it did not have her say one word about a column, and it did not have her be thanked.**

### The Volume 06 Batch 0005 review repair pass, per chapter, and the figures it moved

**A review of the ten chapters, the five state files and the one prompt returned eleven findings requiring repair and two ledger figures that did not reproduce, and all are applied. Nine paragraphs changed across seven of the ten chapters. No dateline moved, no card broke, no money total moved, no name was spent, no ending changed, and no chapter in Volumes 01 to 05 was touched. The full record is `state/continuity.md` items 776 to 781; this is the per-chapter index and the four figures a later writer is most likely to copy.**

- **Ch 291 — nothing on the page changed.** Its forward-reference, *on Thursday of that week*, is the sentence that proved the delivery in Chapter 295 to be the thirteenth and not the seventeenth, and it was right and is untouched.
- **Ch 292 — the fever count, once.** The man of thirty-two with a limp is on day 318 and the sentence said the fever had been out of him **sixteen** days, against **eleven** on day 314 in Chapter 291. Four days elapsed and five were counted. It is now **fifteen**, and the two figures are eleven and fifteen and the interval is the four days the chain gives. **One doubled `---` rule collapsed, which was the first of seven.**
- **Ch 293 — the money frame, once.** The office's **fourpence a year** was inside the same sentence-chain as the footed column and narrated the non-addition, and requirement 6 says that figure prints standing alone with no second price anywhere near it. **The fourpence a year is not in this chapter now**, and the paragraph carries the non-addition on its own footing. **The column is untouched: penny, penny, penny, fourpence, twopence, and the addition and the total of nine pence are on the page exactly as they were**, and this chapter keeps the aphorism, which is one of the two that survive in the block. **One doubled `---` rule collapsed.** The fourpence a year is printed sixteen times across twelve chapters of the volume, at Chapters 251, 252, 254, 260, 270, 278, 284, 289, 290, 291, 292 and 296, and in four paragraphs the two shillings a month sit in the same paragraph with it, at Chapters 251, 254, 260 and 289, which is Blocks 1 and 4's frame and is closed prose. Item 770's claim that it is printed once in Chapter 291 was wrong on the count. In this block it stands in three chapters, 291, 292 and 296, and in each of the three there is no second price in the paragraph.
- **Ch 294 — nothing on the page changed.** One doubled `---` rule collapsed. **Its noticing, a clerk of six years working out that her room's habit and another room's habit are two things, is not about a document, and it is one of the five rooms in the question the close has to rule on.**
- **Ch 295 — four paragraphs, and the most-changed chapter in the block.** One, the **dateline and the last paragraph** put the delivery of the nine sheets on the seventeenth and now put it on the **thirteenth**; the twentieth and the seventeenth at the money frame are correct and stand. Two, the **delegation and companion-file paragraph** reproduced Chapter 284's paragraph over about thirty words with three substitutions and is re-voiced with every fact kept, and **this repair also removed the loose twelfth instance of *about four of the people*, which is why the exact phrase is 11 and not 12.** Three, the **money frame** shared seventeen eight-word shingles with Chapter 293's and is re-voiced in full, and the aphorism is gone from it, and **both columns still foot on the page and neither total moved.** Four, the clause that said a chamber **has held** one thing on one Friday and one other thing on a Saturday **has held two things** was the narrator counting his own structure, which Batch 0004 recorded as a standing fault, and the count is gone, **and the same clause said the fen county was four hundred miles from this chamber when it is two hundred, which is the class of error Batch 0004 found seven of, and it is two hundred now.** One doubled `---` rule collapsed.
- **Ch 296 — one figure.** The contested notice's day by which cause may be shown was **about eleven weeks off** and is now **about ten weeks off**, because Chapter 297 says *It is eleven weeks* in the valley and a protected figure may not carry a second meaning. **The valley's eleven weeks is a standing unrepaired source defect and is untouched.** The three week-figures in the block are now nine, ten and eleven and none of them is anybody else's. One doubled `---` rule collapsed.
- **Ch 297 — one figure and three rules.** The man of fifty-five asked about the ninth line **in about nine words**, and his two sentences are seven and five, so it is now **twelve**, and both speeches are unchanged. **Three doubled `---` rules collapsed, the only chapter in the block with more than one, and each of the three left an empty section.**
- **Ch 298 — one figure.** Bessa Quill got a man in a yard to promise her a thing **in nine words**, and the promise is *I am not going to tell anybody*, which is **seven**, and the speech is unchanged. Her own sentence in the same scene is already footed at seven and the two sevens are now the same figure.
- **Ch 299 — nothing on the page changed.** Its bell specification and its Saturday-in-a-market-month sentence are the volume's own machinery and were read against Chapters 209 and 276 and kept.
- **Ch 300 — one paragraph.** The aphorism stood twice in this chapter, eighteen lines apart, and is now once, at the close. **The line it was removed from keeps every fact about her: nine years in that building, a finding at the end of nine of them, a figure at the end of every one, and her knowing since the fourteenth of a month in Thawmonth what the ninth would be, and her coming up the stair anyway.** The eleven-word refusal, the clerk's entry, the count going to nine under the stair and the man of forty-seven asked nothing are all untouched.

**The four figures the block's own ledger got wrong, which are the four a later writer is most likely to copy.** Quoted dialogue is **1,591** words in **143** speeches, not 1,597, and no speech was altered by the pass, so the six words were never on the page. ***About four people* is 11 and not 12**, and the loose variant is now zero, and the basis is the exact phrase. ***About N* units are seconds 17, minutes 15, hours 3, years 20** on a basis of *about* plus one to three number words plus the unit, and the block's recorded 15 / 6 / 0 / 16 is not reproducible on any basis this project has written down and is superseded rather than corrected. **Saturday was recorded as 27 against a page that carried 28, and the repair removed one Saturday and one Friday from the clause in which the narrator was counting his own device, so the figure now matches for the first time and did not match when it was written.** And one description was wrong rather than one count: the unattributed two-line statement is four, at Chapters 259, 265, 276 and 281, and only Chapter 265's two lines begin *Somebody stood in that aisle once*; Chapter 259's begin *Nobody has said out loud what a list of what went out is for.*

## Volume 07 — Batch 0001 — Chapters 301–310, "The Room That Is Listed"

**The block.** Main world and path time, day 390, the twenty-fifth of Embermonth, YR 316, a Saturday and a market day and the volume's first day and Volume 06's last day, to day 430, the fifth of Frostmonth, YR 316, a Thursday and a market day. Forty days and forty-one inclusive. Five market mornings printed. **23,778 words in ten chapters.** The frame is counted from `outline/volume-07.md` §17 and not from the prompt, and all ten datelines are exact. **A path is on the page for the first time in two volumes, and it is the Ninefold Winter, and it is a valley four hundred miles off any county that is on a map, and it has about four hundred people in it and a woman with a slate and a keeper of a roll, and it is a different place from the city four hundred miles off behind the reader, and nothing in this block is sent to that city.**

### The ten chapters

**Ch 301 · day 390, the twenty-fifth of Embermonth, a Saturday and a market day, about the fifth hour · the fen county, and a path.** The bell goes at the fourth hour and a half and nobody in that market looks up, and a waggon of salt stands at the end of the channel road for an hour, and a reach four hundred yards down a lane has about forty men on it, and a yard four hundred yards up that county's own road has nine men and a bench-board and a press nothing can be served out of. **A man of thirty-two with a limp asks a man of about nineteen with an empty hod to stand at one end of a road for about four minutes, and tells him the whole of what he is witnessing, which is that a man said a date and an end, and the man of about nineteen asks no second question.** The road opens, and it is not made with a hand on anything and nothing was broken. **On the far side there is a valley, and the first person he meets is a woman of about thirty with a slate, and he answers her ordinary question with somebody else's grief in about a second and a half — a book read out in an aisle, a line ruled across it in a hundred and forty years, about two hundred people who have never left the valley, a leg he cannot get up a bank with, and a road with nobody at his shoulder — and he knows in about a second that it is not his.** He says, before anybody has asked him: *I am not right, and I would like somebody to tell me what I have taken.* **She says nobody is going to tell him that and that he will have to ask a man and then believe him.** **The man who keeps the roll is behind the door and he is about fifty and his name is Marek Ollen and he has kept it since he was thirty-one, and the roll is a long sheet folded in four with a day and a name and a mark, and there is no column for anything else and there never has been one. He is the witness at the far end and a witness at the end of a road is not the person who keeps it. He tells Aren that the answer to the seventh line is a trade and not a name, and that the line wants the other thing.** He puts his finger on nine ruled days with nothing in them. **Change:** a man has been entered in the only record a valley of four hundred people will ever be in, inside a week of arriving, in a roll with a column for a day and a name and a mark and no column for the day a person goes. **Ends:** *I do not know* — the first time anybody in that valley has been told in words that the nine days are not known, and it was told to a stranger on the day he came.

**Ch 302 · day 394, the twenty-ninth of Embermonth, a Wednesday, and not a market day in a county with a market · the room over a cross.** Nine people on twenty-nine benches bolted to the floor, about thirty in the room, about two hundred of a generation that has never once left the valley at the back, and an aisle four feet wide that has gone three generations without being used. A man of fifty-eight keeps a book of nine spreads under a trestle, and there is one finding in it in a hundred and forty years and it is not asked about. The business of the morning is forty feet of stone in a channel and it has been argued four times. **He is asked, in front of the room, to say what his end of it is like now, and he answers with a grief that is not his: sixteen men, four of them with nowhere to work, a road of four hundred yards with a standing finish and about nine feet of grass at the end of it, and a leg, and nobody at his shoulder.** About four of the thirty notice. He says the sentence again. **Two men hear it. The man of thirty-four corrects him — that is his, and it is said better than he says it, and the part of it that will have to be given to him by somebody else is that he does not know when he does it — and the man of about fifty refuses, in eleven words' worth of plainness, to say which of two accounts of a man are right, because about four hundred people on his sheet have never been asked him either.** **Change:** he is entered in the day column with a mark that is a gate, and there is nothing to enter about him under either of the other two columns and nobody invented anything. **Ends:** a roll that has a line for coming in and no line for going out is a roll a man can be in for as long as the man who keeps it leaves the line alone.

**Ch 303 · day 399, the fourth of Wolfmonth, a Monday, and not a market day in a county with a market · the same room over a cross, the seventh hour.** **The room wants a number and the only thing in four hundred miles that knows the answer is a roll, and a roll cannot be made to say its answer out loud in one line without a man deciding which of nine hundred lines is a person here now.** There is a second roll, and the second roll is a copy of the first, made by the keeper once a season for about nine years, and the two differ in nine places a season and the difference is nine ruled days. **His want is said once, to a man with a limp and not to the room, and it foots at twenty-four words: *I have written down everybody twice and once was enough and now I have to know which of the two I was right about.* Nine faces and no answer.** The woman with the slate says her want to the roll and not to a person, and no figure is printed on it. **And the third thing is the thing nobody puts on the table: the forgetting is not entered, and the reason is not a decision, and there is no column for it and there never has been, and a man of fifty-eight spoke to nine of about two hundred people of that generation in about eleven years and could not tell two of them who they were and wrote neither of them down.** **Change:** a keeper of a roll says the true thing about a third thing to a sheet of paper in front of nine people, and the true thing is that a person is on a sheet or a person is not on a sheet and there is no third thing. **Ends:** there is a roll of who is in a valley and there has never been a roll of who is known to whom, and nobody in that city can be told which of the two they would have to be asked for.
